Geoff Nixon is a writer on CBC's national digital desk in Toronto. He has covered a wealth of topics, from real estate to technology to world events.

articles.title: Northern Samar Prov’l Hospital limits referrals amid bed shortage
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY—The Northern Samar Provincial Hospital (NSPH) has exceeded its maximum bed capacity, prompting the provincial government-run facility to ask partner health facilities and the public to…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY—The Northern Samar Provincial Hospital (NSPH) has exceeded its maximum bed capacity, prompting the provincial government-run facility to ask partner health facilities and the public to limit referrals to patients needing specialized or higher-level medical care.
In a public advisory on Thursday, NSPH reported 372 total bed admissions, compared with its 302 implementing beds and the 150-bed capacity authorized by the Department of Health (DOH).
The hospital, which is based in Catarman, said it currently has no available beds for additional admissions as it continues to operate beyond its maximum capacity.
NSPH appealed to partner hospitals, health facilities, and the public to refer or bring to the provincial hospital only patients who need specialized or higher-level care services.

It also asked referring facilities to stabilize patients before dispatch to NSPH to help ensure patients arrive in a condition suitable for transport and that available resources can be prioritized for critical and emergency cases.
The hospital said the cooperation of referring facilities and the public is needed to ensure that patients with critical and emergency conditions receive immediate and appropriate medical attention.
The NSPH is Northern Samar’s main referral hospital, serving patients from various municipalities across the province.
The provincial government also operates eight district hospitals across Northern Samar, each with a capacity ranging from 50 to 100 beds.

Hospital bed capacity refers to the number of beds available for patient care. When admissions exceed a facility’s capacity, hospitals may not be able to take in new patients, particularly those requiring emergency or specialized services.

In such situations, referring hospitals are generally expected to provide initial assessment and stabilization, when medically appropriate, before transferring patients to a higher-level facility. This reduces risks during patients’ transport and allows the receiving hospital to prepare for those who require specialized care./coa

articles.title: Rainfall helps reduce air pollution from Indonesia wildfire – Pagasa
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Rainfall is a factor in lowering air pollution levels linked to the wildfire in Indonesia, according to a Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Rainfall is a factor in lowering air pollution levels linked to the wildfire in Indonesia, according to a Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) specialist.

In a phone interview with the Inquirer on Friday, Pagasa specialist John Manalo noted that the direction of the winds carrying the air pollutants was more leaning toward the Visayas and Mindanao as the southwest monsoon (habagat) continued to prevail over parts of Luzon.
“Yung mga pag-ulan na associated sa habagat ay nakakatulong para mas mabawasan yung concentration ng mga air pollutants. Mayroong pollutant deposition na nangyayari,” Manalo explained.
(Rains associated with the southwest monsoon will help in reducing the concentration of air pollutants. Pollutant deposition occurs.)
“Yung epekto nito sa respiratory system ng mga makakalangap ay bahagyang mababawasan yung air pollution na malalanghap nila dahil din sa mga pag-ulan na yun,” he added.
(The effect on the respiratory system of those who breathe in this air is slightly reduced because of those rains.)
The southwest monsoon was forecast to bring rains over the western section of Luzon on Friday, Manalo said, adding that the rains may decrease over the weekend.

Currently, air quality monitoring stations in all 16 cities and the lone municipality in the National Capital Region showed low PM2.5 air pollution levels between 20 and 41 as of 6 a.m. on Friday, according to data from the Environmental Management Bureau (EMB).
Further, air quality monitoring stations in Meycauayan, Bulacan; and Santa Cruz, Zambales showed low PM2.5 air pollution levels between 17 and 35 as of 9 a.m. on Friday.
PM2.5 refers to fine particulate matter measuring 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter.

“Mababa yung air pollutants dahil sa pag-ulan for a certain period of time. Kapag kasi naging dry ulit, magkakaroon ulit ng dispersion and then possibly na naman umabot ng Luzon [yung pollutants],” Manalo explained.
(Air pollutants are lowered due to the rains for a certain period of time. Once it’s dry again, there will be dispersion and the pollutants may possibly reach Luzon.)
Meanwhile, according to Manalo, only isolated or scattered rain showers were forecast for most of the Visayas and Mindanao on Friday.
“Pero, dahil localized lang, yung magiging epekto nung pagkababa ng air pollutants dahil sa pag-ulan ay limited lang din dun sa area mismo kung saan umulan,” he added.
(But, because it’s localized, the effect on the lowering of air pollutants due to the rain may also be limited in the area where the rain occurs.)
International media have reported that the fire in Indonesia has burned in recent weeks and may be exacerbated by a looming stronger El Niño. /jpv

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
The cast of Heated Rivalry is getting hotter by the week, with the Canadian-made hockey drama recruiting three more stars for its second season roster.
Due South star Paul Gross also joins smash hit hockey drama shooting in Greater Toronto, other areas

Heated Rivalry, a production of Bell Media's Crave streaming service, became a global phenomenon in its inaugural six-episode season, after being picked up by HBO in the U.S. and internationally, and catapulted the careers of its lead stars — B.C.-born Hudson Williams, U.S. actor Connor Storrie and Quebec's François Arnaud.
Rookie cast members announced Thursday include:

items: Ukrainian-American actress Milla Jovovich, star of the Resident Evil franchise and Luc Besson's sci-fi classic The Fifth Element.
Kevin Zegers, originally from Woodstock, Ont., who had a recurring role in the CW series Gossip Girl, Paramount+'s The Madison and films such as Transamerica.
And, Canadian film, television and theatre stalwart Paul Gross, known for the CTV-CBS series Due South and the films Men With Brooms and Passchendaele, both of which he also wrote and directed.

blocks.text: "I'm so glad I don't have to keep these three a secret any more," Nova Scotia author Rachel Reid, whose Game Changers books inspired the streaming series, commented on an Instagram post about the casting announcement.
Heated Rivalry author Rachel Reid just made a big donation to rural libraries. Here's why
The series follows the secret romance between two young rivals on the rink — Shane Hollander (Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Storrie) — as their careers are taking off.
Gross, who recently starred in the Stratford Festival production of Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot, is set to play hockey league commissioner Roger Crowell.
Zegers will play Coach Wiebe, head of the Ottawa Centaurs — the fictitious team Hollander plays for.
Jovovich will take on the role of Dr. Galina Molchalina, a Russian-speaking therapist who supports Rozanov.
"Let's bring up the heat baby," Jovovich said on her Instagram account.
New cast includes Schitt's Creek star
Bell Media previously announced that Season 1 actors Robbie G.K., Sophie Nélisse, Christina Chang and Dylan Walsh, among others, would return to their roles.
The production has also drafted an array of Canadian talent for the new season, including:

items: New Brunswick-born Charlie Gillespie will star as Ottawa Centaurs forward Troy Barrett, who falls for team social media manager Harris Drover, played by American actor Justice Smith.
Daniel Diemer, known for Percy Jackson and the Olympians, is cast as hockey player Ryan Price who falls for aspiring musician Fabian Salah, played by Welsh actor Shaheen Jafargholi.
Schitt's Creek star Emily Hampshire, who grew up in the Montreal area, joins as sex shop worker Vanessa, a confidante to Fabian.
Canada's Drag Race Season 1 winner Priyanka is in the role of Tarek, a friend of Vanessa and Fabian.
Heated Rivalry Season 2 cast announcement sparks criticism from some fans over body diversity

blocks.text: Hampshire, in an interview with CBC Montreal's Let's Go last week, said that series creator and director Jacob Tierney is one of her "oldest and bestest friends."

"I've been in every single one of his things, so it would be sad if I wasn't in this one," she told host Sabrina Marandola, noting that she actually made an uncredited voiceover appearance in the show's first season.

Hampshire said the phenomenon of Heated Rivalry is beyond anything she saw with Schitt's Creek, the CBC show that also garnered a huge international audience and went on to sweep every major comedy category at the 2020 Primetime Emmy awards in its final season.
LISTEN | Heated Rivalry's Emily Hampshire on going from one Canadian hit series to another:
Let's Go10:32In conversation with Schitt's Creek and Heated Rivalry star Emily Hampshire
Despite its popularity, Heated Rivalry is not eligible for this year's Primetime Emmys, but Storrie is up for his first-ever award for his hosting gig on Saturday Night Live in February.
Heated Rivalry did, however, dominate this year's Canadian Screen Awards, collecting 13 statuettes, including the prize for best drama and Williams's win for best lead performer.
Tierney confirmed on Aug. 17 that shooting of the second season had begun. It's set to premiere on Crave in Spring 2027.

articles.title: Pacific leaders issue joint rebuke over China missile test
articles.summary: KOROR, Palau – Pacific Island nations condemned a Chinese missile test into their midst in a joint statement agreed Thursday, despite pressure from Beijing on Palau, the host of a regional…

blocks.text: KOROR, Palau – Pacific Island nations condemned a Chinese missile test into their midst in a joint statement agreed Thursday, despite pressure from Beijing on Palau, the host of a regional leaders’ meeting.

The Pacific Islands Forum summit communique, read by Palau’s President Surangel Whipps to a late-night news conference, calls for at least 24 hours’ notice of any intercontinental ballistic missile testing.
The statement was agreed by 17 of 18 forum members, with Naoero, formerly known as Nauru, dissenting.

China gave only a handful of nations short notice before test-firing the intercontinental ballistic missile in July, flexing its military might in a region where it has long sought to expand its influence.

The missile landed in international waters near Taiwan ally Tuvalu and Naoero, sparking immediate outrage from Pacific countries who hold bitter memories of nuclear testing by the US, Britain and France decades earlier, and have declared their waters a nuclear free zone.
The summit’s communique says leaders “register concern on the recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test which overflew a number of members without adequate notice”.

It called on “all states undertaking ICBM testing to ensure transparency and reassurance including through the provision of advanced notification of a test, at least 24 hours, in accordance with international practice”.
Beijing said the test launch was “a routine arrangement of China’s annual military training”, and that “relevant countries were informed in advance”.
Naoero switched diplomatic ties from Taiwan to Beijing two years ago, and has been reluctant to criticise China, a significant infrastructure lender to the region.
On Thursday, the Chinese foreign ministry accused Palau of “hijacking” responses from other Pacific nations.

“Palau has repeatedly hyped the issue, maliciously hijacking the positions of other Pacific Islands Forum member countries. This scheme will not succeed,” ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a news conference in Beijing, before the Pacific statement.
“I think the message from the forum is clear, transparency needs to happen,” Whipps responded.

The United States conducts ballistic missile tests in the Pacific under a defence agreement with the Marshall Islands, which Palau and Australia’s leaders said Thursday was “very different” to China’s test because adequate notice is given.

Palau invited its diplomatic ally Taiwan to the forum as an aid partner, among a dozen non-Pacific countries including China and the United States that participate in sideline events in different capacities.
Beijing bristled at the presence of Taiwan Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung at the opening ceremony.
Beijing claims self-ruled Taiwan as part of its territory, and China’s Pacific envoy Qian Bo told reporters on Monday there would be “consequences”.
Taiwan hit back saying its role in the Pacific, where it has three diplomatic allies, stops China from “having full control”.
The friction at times overshadowed Pacific nations’ focus on the region’s most pressing issues, tackling climate change and transnational crime.

Australia, the largest forum member and the Pacific’s biggest aid donor, pledged AU$600 million ($432 million) to boost satellite and drone aerial surveillance to help track and intercept “narco subs” bringing increasing volumes of methamphetamine and cocaine through island waters.

Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape said he had raised concerns about new US visa bond charges for Pacific citizens travelling to the United States in a sideline meeting with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.
Landau pledged $60 million to improve fuel security in the Pacific, to alleviate soaring prices caused by the Middle East crisis.
At the forum’s closing ceremony, secretary-general Baron Waqa said the Pacific faced significant challenges and had shown it would act together.
“The bonds between us must remain stronger than the forces that seek to divide us,” he said./dp

articles.title: UN to vote on adopting new world map that shows Africa’s true scale
articles.summary:
Togo-sponsored resolution calls to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland

The UN general assembly will vote on Friday on a resolution for the world to…

blocks.text: The UN general assembly will vote on Friday on a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.

Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said the resolution was sponsored by Togo and backed by countries including the African Union’s 54 other member states. He did not specify the total number.

blocks.caption: The 1569 map by Gerardus Mercator (1512-1594) has remained the global standard. Photograph: Stock Montage/Getty Images

blocks.text: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality,” he said.

UN resolutions are non-enforceable but if the vote passes, it could lead to an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology, given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.
The layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later it remains the global standard.

Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.

“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.
Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.

Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This, they say, has reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.

One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.

blocks.caption: The 2018 Equal Earth Map. Photograph: equal-earth.com

blocks.text: Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign is promoting the use of the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.

Some analysts agree too. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.

He added: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”

blocks.caption: A map of Africa from Mercator's atlas dating between 1595-1602. Photograph: Royal Geographical Society/Getty Images

blocks.text: Togolese authorities hope the vote will go the same way as another African Union-backed decision at the UN this year. In March a Ghana-sponsored resolution to describe the slave trade as “gravest crime against humanity” passed, with 123 states voting in favour. Three states voted no and 52 abstained.

Ghana’s success has given supporters of the map cause to believe in a favourable outcome. Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.
Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say, why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”
He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

articles.title: Visayas, Mindanao grids placed under red alert on Sep. 4, 2026
articles.summary: The Visayas and Mindanao power grids were placed under red alert status on Friday, September 4, 2026, amid limited power supply, the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) said.

blocks.text: Published September 4, 2026 9:47am
The Visayas and Mindanao power grids were placed under red alert status on Friday, September 4, 2026, amid limited power supply, the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) said.
In an 8 a.m. advisory, the Visayas grid will be under red alert from 3 p.m. to 10 p.m., while a yellow alert will be in effect from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m. and from 10 p.m. to 11 p.m.
The Visayas grid had an available capacity of 2,233 megawatts (MW) against a peak demand of 2,504 MW.
NGCP said eight power plants were on forced outage in September, while more power plants had been unavailable since the past months and years.
Seventeen other plants were operating at derated capacities, resulting in a total of 815.8 MW unavailable to the grid.
The unavailability of the Visayas' large coal plants TVI 1 and PEDC 3, as well as limited or unavailable power imports from Mindanao, contributed to the alert declarations.
Meanwhile, the Mindanao grid will be under red alert from 1 p.m. to 9 p.m., while yellow alert will be in effect from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. and from 9 p.m. to 10 p.m.
Mindanao had an available capacity of 2,549 MW against a peak demand of 2,592 MW.
Eight power plants were on forced outage in September, while more had been unavailable since the months and years.
Six other plants were operating at derated capacities, leaving a total of 784.5 MW unavailable to the grid.
The unavailability of Mindanao's large coal plants GNPK 1 and 2 and TSI 2 contributed to the alert declarations, NGCP said.
“A red alert status is issued when power supply is insufficient to meet consumer demand and the transmission grid’s regulating requirement,” the NGCP said.
“A yellow alert is issued when the operating margin is insufficient to meet the transmission grid’s contingency requirement,” it added. — RSJ, GMA News

blocks.text: DINALUPIHAN, Bataan – Raging floodwaters swept away nine houses near Pita River in Barangay Pita in Dinalupihan town on Thursday.
It is still unclear whether there was anyone inside the houses during the incident.
Dinalupihan Mayor German Santos confirmed that hundreds of residents living near the river were asked to evacuate to shelters operated by the municipal disaster risk reduction and management office.
Dinalupihan, the only landlocked municipality in Bataan, is among the hardest hit by flooding spawned by Habagat.

articles.title: 46 containers fall overboard in waters off Batangas
articles.summary: LUCENA City— The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) has warned marine vessels to exercise extreme caution after 46 containers fell overboard from a cargo ship sailing in the waters off Calatagan, Batangas.…

blocks.text: LUCENA City— The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) has warned marine vessels to exercise extreme caution after 46 containers fell overboard from a cargo ship sailing in the waters off Calatagan, Batangas.

In a Thursday (Sept. 3) report, the PCG-Southern Tagalog District said M/V Span Asia 39 encountered rough sea conditions, with heavy and continuous rolling, at around 11 a.m. as it approached the waters off Calatagan.
The vessel was reportedly navigating near Hamilo Point, about 1.5 nautical miles from the nearest shoreline, when its container lashings were reportedly loosened.

As a result, 30 of its 20-foot containers, 11 of its 40-foot containers and five open-type containers toppled into the sea, the PCG said. No reports have been released at presstime which describes the shipments lost in the waters.

The PCG-Batangas station immediately issued a navigational warning to vessels operating in Batangas waters, urging them to maintain a safe distance from the floating containers and to take all necessary precautions to ensure safe navigation.
The PCG also deployed a drone to conduct aerial assessment, monitoring and verification of the reported locations of the containers.
At around 2 p.m., while M/V Span Asia 39 was maneuvering toward the Manila North Anchorage Area, another container fell overboard and subsequently sank, according to the report.
The PCG said BRP Malapascua, its 44-meter multi-role response vessel, would be deployed to accelerate search, drift-tracking and containment operations for the missing containers.

The Marine Environmental Protection Force-Southern Tagalog also identified key marine protected areas in the surrounding waters, including Taytayin Cove, Santelmo Cove, Pico de Loro (Cutad) Cove and Fuego Point Marine Sanctuary, for monitoring and mitigation of possible ecological and coastal impacts.

The PCG sub-station in Nasugbu was directed to establish on-scene command and control in the incident area and lead response operations, with assistance from the local government and the local bantay dagat (fish wardens).

According to the vessel’s master, M/V Span Asia 39 departed from the Davao International Container Terminal in Panabo, Davao del Norte, on Aug. 31, carrying 332 container units bound for Manila North Harbor./dp

articles.title: [In This Economy] Should Filipinos’ ‘consumption culture’ be blamed for the weak peso?
articles.summary: BSP Governor Eli Remolona did not say that consumption is the enemy. Instead, the underlying message is that our country as a whole needs to find better ways to finance our investments.

blocks.text: On September 2, the peso-dollar exchange rate closed at P62.50 per dollar, yet another all-time low. This time last year, we were still at around P57.3 per dollar, implying a 9% drop.

Policymakers are becoming increasingly alarmed by the peso’s steady depreciation. On August 27, at the Senate briefing of the Development Budget Coordination Committee (DBCC), the economic managers were asked if there’s any way we can rein in the exchange rate.
Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) Governor Eli Remolona Jr. explained why the central bank cannot simply force the peso back to P60 per dollar.

At best, he said, the BSP can slow down a sharp depreciation by selling part of the country’s dollar reserves. In doing so, the BSP can make the peso dearer vis-à-vis the dollar, and therefore strengthen the peso a bit.

But the BSP cannot afford to sell too much of our dollars. Macroeconomic prudence dictates that we should always set aside an ample supply of “international reserves.” Governor Remolona rightly warned,“Mauubusan tayo ng reserves. Mauubusan tayo ng dollars.” (We will run out of reserves and dollars.)

As of end-July, the country had $103.3 billion in gross international reserves, or foreign assets (mostly dollars) the BSP can readily deploy, enough for 6.7 months of imports and related payments. While substantial, that amount is not bottomless.

Therefore, the BSP can only do so much to arrest the continual slide of the peso. After all, their primary mandate is to ensure low and stable inflation, not to manage the exchange rate. We’ve experimented with the latter in the 20th century, but that proved to be disastrous—especially since we’re not nearly earning enough dollars.

That brings us to Remolona’s other remarks. He told senators that he wished our exports were stronger, so we can earn more dollars, possibly through the proposed Pax Silica or the Luzon Economic Corridor. The more dollars flow into the country, the stronger the peso will be against the dollar.

Remolona added that the country’s saving rate is rather low. Then came the sound bite that provoked outrage in some circles: “Medyo mahirap sabihin ’to… pero mayabang tayo eh. May consumption culture ang tawag.” (This is rather difficult to say, but we are boastful. It is called a consumption culture.)

Predictably, many people were triggered. Labor coalition Nagkaisa said workers should not be blamed for buying basic necessities. “Food, transportation, electricity and medicine are not a ‘consumption culture.’ That is survival,” they said. Gabriela Women’s Party Representative Sarah Elago echoed this and said people cannot save because wages are too low.

IBON Foundation, meanwhile, said that such a comment was “astoundingly entitled, and bordering on willful ignorance.” They added, “Would be nice if economic policy was in the hands of folks who have a more than rhetorical grasp of the daily distress faced by the majority of Filipinos.”

The issue blew up on social media, but here let’s try to make sense of all this. While the BSP governor could have chosen his words better, essentially he’s correct. On the other hand, while critics are right to raise concerns, they also inadvertently put words in Governor Remolona’s mouth.
To start with, if you don’t know yet, the Philippine economy is indeed consumption-driven. The data show it plainly.
Figure 1 below shows that in 2025 as much as 73% of total spending in the economy, as measured by GDP or gross domestic product, was accounted for by consumption spending by the private sector.

blocks.caption: Figure 1.

blocks.text: From a macroeconomic perspective, intense consumption means that our country can only save so much. In fact, the Philippines’ overall saving rate—national savings as a share of national income—was just 30.1% in 2025. That’s quite low compared to Singapore (40%), Vietnam (37% in 2024), and Indonesia (35%).
Lower savings also mean lower resources for investment. Not coincidentally, we also have one of the lowest investment rates in the region.

But even with meager savings, we can still pay for investments if we earn enough resources from abroad. This is why Governor Remolona referred to the concept called “current account.” Roughly, it’s the difference between dollar inflows and outflows.
The problem is that we’ve long had a current account deficit, meaning that more dollars are pouring out than coming in (see Figure 2 below).

blocks.caption: Figure 2.

blocks.text: Figure 3 below shows that while we have a large current account deficit, many neighboring ASEAN economies enjoy current account enjoy surpluses instead.

blocks.caption: Figure 3.

blocks.text: The reason for the Philippines’ current account deficit is that remittances from overseas Filipinos and earnings from the IT-BPM sector are not nearly enough to offset the outflow of dollars for, say, import and foreign debt payments.
Low private savings, coupled with a current account deficit, means that there’s really not enough resources to fund investments in the country.

I think this is what Governor Remolona was trying to say in the Senate. That’s why he put emphasis on the need to grow exports as a source of dollar earnings. This will be increasingly important since inflows of remittances are not as strong as in past decades, and the income of Filipinos in the IT–BPM sector face many threats like US protectionism (“onshoring”) and artificial intelligence (AI). Tourism, by the way, is another potential source of dollars for us.

To be sure, a current account deficit is not inherently bad. But if it’s too large, then it becomes a cause for concern. If we earn enough dollars from abroad, we can abate the current account deficit and pay for more investments here at home. At the same time, it can help reduce the pressure on the peso to further depreciate—the original concern raised by senators last week.

The problem is that many people focused too much on Governor Remolona’s remarks on consumption: “Medyo mahirap sabihin ’to… pero mayabang tayo eh. May consumption culture ang tawag.” Admittedly, Remolona could have chosen his words better, and deemphasized the saving rate angle (to some people, that sounded like the BSP was blaming ordinary citizens’ lack of saving).

But in fact, Remolona never said that Filipinos must further scrimp on money or tighten their belts amid these challenging times. Saving by individuals at the micro level is different from saving by countries at the macro level. Lack of savings at the national level can be augmented by exports, remittances, and income from abroad.

I would add that while we’re borrowing from abroad, it’s best to put that money in productive and worthwhile uses. This is why it’s infuriating to know that a large part of public investments has gone to corruptible flood control projects or farm-to-market roads or multipurpose buildings.

Remolona drew more criticism when Senator Risa Hontiveros asked why Philippine inflation exceeded that of several neighbors. He cited our lack of domestic oil and said economies with AI industries could partly compensate. He himself called the comparison “oversimplified.”

There is a grain of truth here. An economy with high-value technology exports can earn more dollars, attract investment, and raise productivity. The International Monetary Fund has noted that the global AI investment boom is already boosting demand for Asian technology exports.

But AI does not directly make imported oil cheaper. Data centers also consume tremendous amounts of electricity: the International Energy Agency estimates that global data-center electricity use surged by 17% in 2025, while AI-focused centers used 50% more.

blocks.caption: Why Energy Secretary Garin says Pax Silica is ‘too dangerous’ to plug into grid

blocks.text: A better formulation is that strong, export-oriented technology industries can help an economy absorb an oil shock. In fairness, Remolona did mention a couple of times in the Senate briefing the urgent need to boost exports. AI is one possible source of productive capacity and dollar earnings. But by no means is it a substitute for energy security or a magic cure for inflation.

In conclusion, I agree that BSP Governor Eli Remolona’s Senate statement needed more precision. He was hinting at an economic logic that makes a lot of sense, but also difficult to communicate—hence prone to misinterpretation.
Governor Eli Remolona did not tell workers to skip meals or medicine. That’s not what he said, and that would be both cruel and economically silly. Let’s avoid putting words into his mouth.

He also did not say that consumption is the enemy. Instead, the underlying message is that our country as a whole needs to find better ways to finance our investments—what private saving cannot rescue, maybe a boost in exports, remittances, or incomes from abroad can.

Ultimately, if we want higher national savings, we should ensure stable incomes and better-paying jobs for Filipinos, more efficient firms, sounder public finances, and financial institutions that channel savings into productive investment. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics (UPSE). His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler.com. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. articles.title: Inflation slightly cools to 6.1% in August 2026
articles.summary: Though inflation remains on a downward trend, price pressures persist as bad weather keeps the cost of some food items high and the Middle East conflict pushes up fuel prices

blocks.text: BASIC GOODS. People buy vegetables at the Paco Market in Manila on March 11, 2026.
Rappler
Though inflation remains on a downward trend, price pressures persist as bad weather keeps the cost of some food items high and the Middle East conflict pushes up fuel prices

MANILA, Philippines – Inflation in the Philippines further eased to 6.1% in August, marking the fourth straight month of decline from a three-year high of 7.2% in April, the Philippine Statistics Authority said on Friday, September 4.

The August rate was slower than the 6.2% recorded in July, as lower electricity and meat prices and a stronger peso helped offset higher food prices brought about by bad weather, as well as elevated fuel costs.
But average inflation from January to August stood at 5.2%, remaining well above the government’s target range of 2% to 4%.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) had projected August inflation to settle between 5.5% and 6.5%. It said higher prices of rice, vegetables, fruits, and fish, partly due to unfavorable weather conditions, as well as elevated domestic fuel costs, were among the factors pushing inflation up. These were expected to be partly offset by lower meat and electricity prices and the peso’s appreciation.

The BSP’s Monetary Board recently raised the benchmark interest rate by another 25 basis points to 5% on August 27, its third consecutive rate increase as the central bank sought to prevent elevated inflation from becoming more persistent.

At its August meeting, the BSP lowered its forecast for average 2026 inflation to 6.1% from 6.4%, although it substantially raised its 2027 forecast to 5.4% from 4.5%. The central bank expects inflation to return closer to its 3% target midpoint by 2028.

In that meeting, the BSP cited the need to take “preemptive monetary action” to confront the possible inflationary impact of severe El Niño conditions as well as potential wage hike adjustments, including the stalled “historic” Metro Manila wage hike. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Volkswagen board approves plan to cut another 50,000 jobs
articles.summary: The group - which includes Audi, Porsche, Skoda as well as the VW brand - plans to cut a total of 100,000 by 2030.

blocks.text: The board of German car giant Volkswagen has approved a plan to cut another 50,000 jobs as part of a sweeping turnaround programme. It brings the total number of roles the company plans to shed by 2030 to 100,000.
The group - which includes Audi, Porsche, Skoda as well as the VW brand - said in March that it would cut 50,000 roles by the end of the decade.
The move is a "strong signal" for the future of the firm, which is "taking responsibility for our entire workforce", VW's chief executive Oliver Blume said in a statement on Thursday.
Blume said in July that the firm was looking to make the additional cuts.
The Beetle-maker has been hit by a drop in profits due to falling sales and fierce competition, especially from Chinese brands.
VW will also prioritise the "most compelling vehicles" and make more of each model, which will help lower costs, it said.
A "fundamental adjustment of the global workforce capability is necessary" to safeguard the competitiveness of the company, which faces shifting demand and technological change.
It added "a Group-wide workforce adjustment of approximately 50,000 positions - including management roles - will be necessary."
The company is also considering the future of its Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and Neckarsulm plants, where it has said production capacity exceeds demand.
"Alternative uses for these plants are being assessed," it said.
The restructuring marks the biggest in VW's almost nine-decade history.
As of 2025, VW employed more than 660,000 people worldwide. Its brands also include Seat, Bentley and Lamborghini.

Christianne Benner - the president of Europe's largest industrial union IG Metall and deputy chair of VW's Supervisory Board - said the carmaker had "fought hard for good solutions" to address a "crisis situation".
VW's profits have fallen sharply in recent years, hit by falling sales in China, which was once one of its biggest markets.
Sales have also fallen in the US, partly due to the impact of tariffs on car imports that were introduced by President Donald Trump's administration.
Chinese carmakers have been expanding aggressively as they roll out new technologies while benefiting from lower production costs than their rivals.
In recent years, firms like BYD have seen their sales rise sharply in markets including the UK, European Union and South East Asia.

articles.title: Missouri state legislative candidate accused of trying to plant cocaine on opponent
articles.summary:
Republican candidate Thomas Ross and his former campaign manager devised a plan to stash drugs in their opponent Louise Secker’s purse or vehicle

A Missouri House race has been rocked by the…

blocks.text: A Missouri House race has been rocked by the Wednesday arrest of Republican candidate Thomas Ross, whom prosecutors accuse of attempting to frame his primary opponent Louise Secker for cocaine possession.

In June, Ross allegedly gave his former campaign manager, identified by the initials “CS” in court documents, a bag of cocaine and Adderall. The two devised a plan for the former manager to stash the drugs in Secker’s purse or vehicle.
On 21 June, Ross asked for an update on the plot.
“Taking it no luck with the substance of it all?” he wrote in a text to his staffer. “Substance” was a euphemism for the narcotics, authorities say.

“I am actually creeping down to the car show right now and seeing if I can see your car. I have had it on me for a couple days in order to be able to take full advantage of any opportunity that arises,” the former manager replied, according to court documents.
“I thought I had it at the forum Walter went to, but never got close [and] car was locked.”

The Joplin police department in Missouri alerted the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on 30 July to a public corruption matter. (It’s unclear how the police were alerted to the alleged scheme.) The next day, the federal agency gave the former manager a covert recording device, which he used to tape a conversation with Ross.
The former manager offered to call in an anonymous tip about Secker’s car containing drugs and asked if Ross wanted it done.
“If you can pull it off … pull it off,” Ross replied.
Ross has been charged with conspiring to distribute a controlled substance. It’s unclear if the former manager will also face criminal charges.
Secker did not immediately respond to a phone call.

Ross defeated Secker in August by a razor-thin margin of just 33 votes in the Republican primary for House District 161. The district includes Joplin, a city about 70 miles (112 km) west of Springfield.
The incumbent state representative, Republican Lane Roberts, is not running for reelection.
Missouri Republican party chair Peter Kinder called on Ross to withdraw from the race.

“While Mr. Ross is entitled to due process and the facts surrounding this matter must be allowed to come to light, the circumstances of his arrest are serious and deeply troubling,” Kinder said in a statement.
“The people of the 161st District deserve a nominee who can devote his full attention to earning their trust and representing their interests in Jefferson City.”

articles.title: Canadians should prepare for a 5 C hotter future, report warns
articles.summary: The federal government's new report summarizing the latest science on climate change warns that under current climate policies, the impact on Canadians will likely be "far from benign."

image.caption: A woman bikes along the waterfront in Toronto as wildfire smoke fills the city in July. A report from the federal government suggests that under current global climate policies, Canadians should expect fire season to continue to lengthen. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The federal government's new report summarizing the latest science on climate change warns that under current climate policies, the impact on Canadians will likely be "far from benign."
In Nunavut, warming in winter could exceed 10 C
Canadians will have to prepare for a future that's 5 C hotter, according to a new report summarizing the latest science on climate change.

The second edition of Canada's Changing Climate Report, a synthesis of the science on the impact of a warming planet on Canadians, confirms with greater confidence that burning fossil fuels, or what the report calls "human activities," are responsible for climate change.
On Thursday, the federal government released a summary of the report's findings.
The report is forward-looking, assessing what Canada would look like under different scenarios depending on whether countries fulfil their climate commitments.

"We do still have some agency," said Nathan Gillett, one of the report's authors and a research scientist with Environment and Climate Change Canada. "Where emissions go from here will affect how temperatures evolve through the century and whether we can stabilize temperature or whether it just keeps increasing."

items: Carney government asks court to strike down climate litigation
These may be the UN climate panel's last words before we hit 1.5 C limit

blocks.text: The report finds that if global governments keep pursuing their current climate policies, Canada will still see intensified warming, which "corresponds to a future climate for Canada that is far from benign," the report states.
Glaciers could 'largely disappear'
Under such a scenario, Canada is projected to warm through this century with an estimated temperature increase of 5 C. In Nunavut, warming in winter could exceed 10 C.

Glaciers in western Canada are projected to lose more than 75 per cent of their ice, it finds, and there's a more than 60 per cent likelihood that the central Arctic Ocean will be ice-free most Septembers.
"Iconic landscapes are changing across Canada as snow and ice disappear," the report states. "Glaciers in western Canada will largely disappear by the end of this century."
Satellite images show glacier collapse that triggered flooding at Nepal-China border
Beyond considerable warming in the North, the report paints a difficult future in southern Canada, where most of the country lives.
Summer droughts are projected to become longer, more intense, and more frequent in central and southern Canada, the report states.
Canadians should also brace for an increase in the frequency and intensity of flash flooding and atmospheric rivers.

items: Climate change made Canadian wildfires in N.W.T. and Ontario roughly twice as likely, analysis finds
Is Canada flunking climate? The picture isn’t great, but there might be a way out

blocks.text: "Multiple lines of evidence support the finding that the length of the fire season has increased in most parts of Canada and is projected to continue to lengthen as global temperature rises," the report states.
Things would look even worse for Canada if countries abandoned their climate policies, with average temperatures projected to increase 6.9 C this century.
If the world, however, dramatically reduces greenhouse gases and achieves net-zero around 2075, Canada's climate is projected to stabilize and average warming would increase by 3.5 C.
Report is 'physics, not fate'

Despite the grim picture the report paints, 5 C of warming is not locked in, and there's still time for Canada to avoid a hotter future, independent policy research organization the Canadian Climate Institute says.
"This report describes physics, not fate," the group said in a statement.
Cutting emissions in Canada and around the globe, the institute says, will determine "whether Canadians have to live with the consequences of more than 5 C of warming or 3.5 C."

The institute says each degree of warming that's avoided will save lives and prevent homes, communities and livelihoods from being destroyed. It will also save the Canadian economy billions of dollars, the statement says.
In a statement responding to the federal report, a climate advocacy group called for greater action to reduce emissions, linking Toronto's flash flooding on Wednesday to climate change.

"As the climate breakdown accelerates, more than 65,000 Torontonians lost power in yesterday's severe storm, often for many hours," said Toronto city Coun. Dianne Saxe, writing for Climate Caucus, a network of municipal leaders from across the country. "There was also extensive disruption to traffic and to transit, and expensive flood and wind damage to homes."
"Our communities cannot afford the frequent human and economic blows that oil and gas use are causing."
Responding to the report, a statement from Canada's environment minister said Canada remains committed to reducing its emissions and achieving net-zero by 2050.

"Our government is moving with urgency to fight climate change, while working together to build the energy security, industrial capacity, and strategic autonomy that will define this century for Canada," said Chris Zhou, the director of communications for the environment and climate change minister.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

blocks.text: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is holding its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026, after being postponed at least four times: first in May 2022, then in May 2025, October 2025, and again in March 2026.

The historic polls are seen as a pivotal moment in the decades-long peace process in a region that was mired in conflict and socioeconomic and political challenges. The upcoming elections are also a test for the Bangsamoro transition and the institutions and systems established in the last seven years.

articles.title: From leaves to loom, Abra brings indigenous knowledge into classrooms
articles.summary: At Peñarrubia Integrated School in Abra, students learn natural dyeing, weaving, and embroidery through a specialized senior high school curriculum rooted in indigenous knowledge

items: Peñarrubia Integrated School has introduced a specialized curriculum called Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Practices (IKSP), which includes a Natural Dyeing subject aimed at preserving local indigenous knowledge.

The curriculum was developed through community research and collaboration, involving teachers and local government support, and focuses on hands-on learning experiences for students using plant materials for dyeing.

Future stages of the curriculum will expand to include Loom Weaving and Indigenous Embroidery, emphasizing the importance of community engagement and the cultural significance of the practices being taught.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – Students at Peñarrubia Integrated School learn chemistry from leaves, culture from thread, and indigenous history with their own hands.
They gather plant materials, chop and weigh them, extract their color, and watch plain fibers take on shades of beige, brown, and rust.
This is not an extracurricular activity. Natural Dyeing is now part of senior high school.

The subject is the first offering under Peñarrubia Integrated School’s specialized Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Practices curriculum (IKSP) developed to help document, teach, and sustain local knowledge that educators feared was slowly fading from everyday use.

blocks.caption: Students tend plants that can serve as sources of natural dyes, part of a curriculum that teaches them to recognize and work with materials found in their environment. All photos courtesy of Peñarrubia Integrated School

blocks.text: The first batch of 28 Grade 11 learners took Natural Dyeing during the second semester of the 2025-2026 school year.

Sherwin Zapatero, master teacher III, senior high school coordinator, and focal person for specialized subjects in DepEd Abra, said the curriculum grew from the initiative of Adelaida Bogayao, education program supervisor and Indigenous Peoples Education focal person of the Schools Division Office of Abra.
“Many indigenous traditions and practices were steadily fading from everyday life,” Zapatero said, explaining why Bogayao pushed for IKSP to be integrated into the senior high school curriculum.
The aim, he said, was “to help preserve and pass on this cultural heritage to younger generations.”
Peñarrubia Integrated School was chosen as the pilot site because it already had an established senior high school program.
Before the lessons reached students, however, teachers and other personnel first went back to the community.

Four research teams were formed to document natural dye sources, traditional dyeing processes, weaving patterns and designs, and indigenous embroidery. The teams included teaching and non-teaching personnel from Peñarrubia Integrated School and the Schools Division Office of Abra.
Zapatero said the research and curriculum development were carried out through trainings, workshops, and collaborative sessions funded under DepEd’s Indigenous Peoples Education Program.
“The findings from these community-based studies became the cornerstone of the curriculum,” he said.
Teachers then translated the documented knowledge into learning competencies, lessons, and instructional materials aligned with DepEd standards.
According to Zapatero, the curriculum went through technical review, validation, and quality assurance before it was approved by the DepEd Cordillera Administrative Region on January 3, 2025.

Zapatero worked with then school principal Pepito Trinidad and his fellow senior high school teachers in preparing the documents needed for implementation, including the feasibility study, strategic plan, and implementation framework.
The teachers also helped translate the research into classroom-ready lessons and materials, while Zapatero developed the curriculum framework and coordinated the submission and review process.

blocks.caption: Teacher Sherwin Zapatero shows students dyed fibers during a Natural Dyeing class at Peñarrubia Integrated School in Abra.

blocks.text: The municipal government later joined the effort. Zapatero said the Sangguniang Bayan, under then mayor Jane Cecilia and then vice mayor Geraldine Balbuena, authorized a memorandum of agreement between the municipality and DepEd Abra through Peñarrubia Integrated School.
Under the agreement, the municipality committed support for an LGU-funded teacher, as well as tools, equipment, and materials needed for the hands-on electives.
Zapatero said the total commitment amounted to P288,940, including three years of salary for the designated teacher. The support has continued under Balbuena, now the municipal mayor.
For a subject built around making things by hand, that support matters. Students cannot learn dyeing, weaving, and embroidery from lectures alone.
Zapatero underwent specialized training in natural dyeing through the Department of Science and Technology Philippine Textile Research Institute in partnership with the University of Abra.
That training allows him to teach both the cultural and scientific sides of the process.
Students learn which plant materials can produce color and how these are prepared. They also observe how extraction, measurement, and treatment affect the final shade.

blocks.caption: Skeins of fiber show different shades produced during the students’ natural dyeing activities. The colors vary depending on the plant material and the dyeing process used.

blocks.text: In class and during outdoor learning sessions, plant materials are sorted, cut, weighed, and processed before being used on fibers.
Finished skeins show the results. Some come out pale and earthy. Others turn warmer shades of brown and rust.
Something growing nearby becomes pigment. Pigment becomes thread. Thread will eventually become textile.

The process also gives students a practical way of seeing how indigenous knowledge and science meet. They are not only told that certain plants can produce dye. They test them, compare results, and work with the materials themselves.
The next stage of the curriculum will move from dyeing to textile making.
Loom Weaving and Indigenous Embroidery are scheduled for implementation in the third term of the 2026-2027 school year for Grade 12 learners who previously completed Natural Dyeing in Grade 11.

“This progression allows students to deepen their understanding of indigenous craftsmanship while developing practical skills that contribute to the preservation and continued practice of Abra’s rich cultural traditions,” Zapatero said.
Students first learn where color comes from, then how that color becomes part of something woven or embroidered.
Bringing indigenous knowledge into formal education also comes with responsibility.
The designs and practices being taught are not simply classroom materials. They carry histories, meanings, and identities rooted in communities.
The knowledge did not begin in school. It came from people who practiced it and passed it on long before it became part of a curriculum.
That makes continued engagement with the community important as the program grows.
Current school principal Maria Lorena Bisares is overseeing the continued implementation and development of the specialized curriculum.

For the 28 students in the first batch, the lessons are practical. They learn which plants can produce color, how fibers respond to treatment, and how those fibers can eventually become woven or embroidered pieces.
But they are also learning something harder to measure. The knowledge behind those processes came from communities that practiced and passed them on across generations.
Peñarrubia Integrated School is now trying to make sure another generation gets the chance to learn them. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Tensions flare as judge declines to remove juror in Lindsay Clancy trial
articles.summary: The defence lawyer is upset after the judge decides not to remove a holdout in the triple murder case.

blocks.text: A judge has again told the deadlocked jury in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial to keep trying to reach a verdict after a dramatic sixth day of deliberations in a case that has gripped America.
Tensions flared in court after the jury forewoman sent the judge a note saying one juror would not follow the judge's instructions on reasonable doubt.
There was audible shock in the room when the defence team asked for the juror to be removed, a request that was denied by the judge.

Clancy, 36, is charged with three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan - at her Massachusetts family home on 24 January 2023.
Warning: This article contains distressing details
The former labour and delivery nurse does not deny strangling her two sons and daughter in the basement of their house.
But her lawyer argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, and could not distinguish right from wrong.
The jury of nine women and three men in Plymouth has deliberated for some 35 hours without a verdict, following nearly six weeks of trial proceedings.
The panel has twice previously sent the judge notes saying it could not come to a unanimous decision, but Thursday was the first hint of rancour in the deliberation room.

Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said in court that the jury forewoman had sent another note, this one complaining to Judge William Sullivan that a juror was refusing to listen to the law on reasonable doubt.
Reddington and prosecutor Jennifer Sprague had an animated discussion with the judge in court.
Reporters in the room could not hear the exchange, but the BBC saw exasperated facial expressions and gestures from Clancy's lawyer.
Reddington then went over to Clancy to explain what had just happened, in what seemed to be a tense conversation.
Clancy, who was paralysed from the waist down when she jumped out of a second-floor window after killing her children, was pushed in her wheelchair by her lawyer to join a discussion with the judge.
Afterwards, Judge Sullivan brought in each juror individually and questioned them.

He reminded the panel they must unanimously believe beyond reasonable doubt that the defendant is guilty in order to convict her of a crime. As each juror came up, some looked at Clancy, while others did not.
When the defence lawyer told the court about his request to have a juror removed, there were gasps and reporters quickly began typing.
Clancy bowed her head as the media begin to exit the room.
Reddington, looking upset, could be seen consoling his client, holding her in a side hug and rubbing her back as journalists left court.

The defence lawyer told reporters afterwards that the forewoman's note to the judge stated that there was one holdout in the jury who, as he described it, "refuses to listen to the law... on reasonable doubt".
Reddington said he had suggested to the judge "a motion to remove the juror who refuses to accept your instructions on the law on a reasonable doubt".
The defence lawyer said he had no indication of what this lone juror was thinking and he did not confirm the 11-1 split the jury forewoman reported earlier.
The issue with the juror is expected to be addressed again when court convenes at 09:00 EST (14:00 BST) on Friday.
If the jury does not reach a verdict and Judge Sullivan declares a mistrial, prosecutors would need to decide whether to retry the case.
Clancy faces life in prison without parole if convicted of first-degree murder.
If found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, or reason of insanity, she could be committed to a state psychiatric hospital.
Under US law, a jury must unanimously believe "beyond a reasonable doubt" that someone is guilty in order to convict them of a crime.
The designation is the strictest standard in the US legal system. It places the burden on the government to prove that the accused is guilty, and not the accused to prove their innocence.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.
In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

articles.title: U.S. aims 'to really tighten the screws' on Cuba with newest sanctions: analyst
articles.summary: The U.S. government on Thursday slapped new sanctions on Cuba in a fresh push to strangle the island's economy and deepen its multiple crises.

image.caption: A man pulls a cart carrying drinking water along a street in Havana last month. On Thursday, the U.S. government slapped new sanctions on Cuba in a fresh push to strangle the island's economy and deepen its multiple crises. (Ramon Espinosa/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
The U.S. government on Thursday slapped new sanctions on Cuba in a fresh push to strangle the island's economy and deepen its multiple crises.
Company that imports parts needed to maintain Cuba's power grid among those hit with sanctions

Among those hit with sanctions are Fidel Ernesto Castro, grandson of former president Raúl Castro, and Cuba's Oil Industry Supply Import Co., known as Abapet. The company is responsible for importing special equipment and spare parts needed to sustain Cuba's crumbling power grid.

The sanctions aim to push Cuba's critical machinery offline and exacerbate its energy crisis, said Brett Erickson, a sanctions expert and managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors, a consulting firm.
"The U.S. is trying to really tighten the screws as much as possible," he said.

"The Trump administration seems to have no seriousness to accept any change from Cuba other than a toppling of regime. Marco is not going to let that go," he added, referring to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Erickson anticipated that Cuba's government would try to circumvent the sanctions "because they have to."
"They'll get creative in how they try to procure these maintenance parts," he said, warning it would be a costlier alternative, which in turn would raise inflation and further hurt Cuba's economy.
Frequent outages, fuel reserves dwindling

Islandwide blackouts have become increasingly common, while daily outages in Cuba now surpass 24 hours as the aging grid fails and fuel reserves dwindle ever since U.S. President Donald Trump in late January threatened tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to the island.

"The goal in theory is to create so much civilian hardship and suffering that they have no option but to essentially rise up and topple their government," Erickson said. "It is an attempt to cause a humanitarian crisis."
Talks earlier this year between the U.S. and Cuba have since halted, while sanctions have increased in recent months.

Erickson said he expects the U.S. to keep targeting smaller and smaller state companies to try to push them "into a death spiral." The U.S. has previously sanctioned entities including Cuba's state-owned oil and gas company.
LISTEN | Cuba and fears of a U.S. invasion:
Front Burner32:39Will the U.S. invade Cuba?
The U.S. State Department made the announcement just hours after Cuban officials held a press conference to share more details on the historic economic reforms approved in June.
When asked about the current situation in Cuba, Oscar Pérez-Oliva Fraga, Cuba's deputy prime minister and minister of foreign investment, blamed the U.S. government.
"This past year has been very complex, and we know why," he said. "The blockade is a genocide."
He spoke before the sanctions were announced.
No sense of 'what's going to happen to you'

Among the Cubans exhausted by the ongoing outages is 49-year-old Yaqueline Bernal. She said Thursday that she hasn't had electricity since Sunday and worries most about the consequences for her eight young grandchildren.
"If we don't have power, we don't have water," she said. "You really don't know what's going to happen to you."
Bruno Rodríguez, Cuba's foreign affairs minister, decried the latest sanctions on X.

"Collective punishment is a crime. So, too, is inflicting suffering on an entire population through measures coldly calculated to trigger a humanitarian crisis," he said. "Enough with the abuse. Put an end to the blockade once and for all and allow Cuba to live in peace."
Eugenio Martínez Enríquez, Cuba's ambassador in Mexico, called Rubio "a liar without scruples."
"We will not forget his crimes," he wrote on X.
Meanwhile, Rubio asserted on X that those sanctioned "are part of the corrupt Castro financial and intelligence network."

"Cuba's Communist regime elites preside over a failed state where ordinary Cubans go hungry while the Castro family and other insiders enrich themselves through sanctions evasion and other illicit schemes — and seek to export subversive Marxist ideology to the United States and other states in the Western Hemisphere," he wrote.
"Trump and I are unwavering in our commitment that Cuba will be free."

articles.title: 8 years on, Philippines yet to claim Filipino seafarer's remains from Somalia
articles.summary: The Department of Foreign Affairs has vowed to send fresh instructions to the Philippine embassy in Nairobi, Kenya, to press Somali authorities to return the remains of a Filipino seafarer who died…

blocks.text: September 4, 2026 | 8:49am
Rep. Brian Poe Llamanzares (FPJ Panday Bayanihan party-list) addresses Department of Foreign Affairs officials during a budget hearing at the House of Representatives on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026.
Llamanzares' office via FB

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Foreign Affairs has vowed to send fresh instructions to the Philippine embassy in Nairobi, Kenya, to press Somali authorities to return the remains of a Filipino seafarer who died more than eight years ago, after its latest request went unanswered.

Sam Dela Cruz, a 25-year-old seafarer registered with manning agency GMM Global Maritime, died of cardiopulmonary arrest in Somalia on July 28, 2018. His remains have yet to be brought back to the Philippines.

The issue was brought up during Thursday's House deliberations on the DFA's proposed 2027 budget, when Rep. Brian Poe Llamanzares (FPJ Panday Bayanihan), vice chair of the House appropriations committee, asked the department what progress had been made to repatriate Dela Cruz' remains.
The DFA said its attempts since 2018 to return Dela Cruz' remains have stalled in the absence of a Philippine mission in Somalia and the COVID-19 pandemic.
Dela Cruz' burial was carried out immediately under Somalia's Islamic Sharia law before the family could weigh in.

Context reported in 2025 that a burial request was filed with a Somali court the day after Dela Cruz's death. The agency he was under, GMM Global maritime, no longer appears in a Singapore online business directory, "which can mean it has ceased operations or changed names," the report stated.

"We understand the immense difficulty and emotional pain the family continues to endure during this prolonged process," Undersecretary Ezzedin Tago, DFA's officer in charge of migrant affairs told House lawmakers. "The DFA remains committed to supporting the Dela Cruz family."
Because the Philippines has no mission in Somalia, the case has been handled through the Philippine embassy in Nairobi, which holds jurisdiction over the country.
The DFA official said the embassy has a record of diplomatic notes sent to the Somali government since 2018, none of which drew an official reply.
GMM Global Maritime reached out to Somali authorities in November 2018 and located Dela Cruz's burial site in Bosaso, roughly 1,000 kilometers from the capital, Mogadishu, according to the DFA.
The manning agency secured permits and funding for exhumation and reached a "preliminary agreement with local officials," but negotiations stalled and the exhumation never happened.

In 2025, the DFA asked the Nairobi embassy to raise the case again with the Somali embassy there, to relay the department's and family's request to the Somalian government. That, too, went unanswered, Tago said.
"With that update, we will reinstruct or send the instructions again to our embassy in Nairobi to meet with the Somali embassy in Nairobi to revive this issue," the DFA official said.
Poa said Somalia's non-response was "not our fault," but said the government should continue to "try its best to bring home the body of our kababayan."
"We should not stop knocking at their door to ask for the body back," Poe said.

articles.title: Kenya's chai tea lovers are not happy as the nation's cows run dry
articles.summary: Supermarket shelves are emptying, sellers are rationing supplies and prices are rising.

blocks.text: Kenya's chai tea lovers are not happy as the nation's cows run dry
Image source, Getty Images
Chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts of milk, is sometimes flavoured with ginger and spices
ByBasillioh Rukanga
Reporting fromNairobi
Kenyans love their milky tea, or chai, but some are facing the worrying possibility of doing without as the country has been hit by a milk shortage.

A breakfast here is often incomplete without a cup of chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts of milk, sometimes flavoured with ginger and spices. It is often served at meetings and during social visits, with many people taking the hot brew several times a day.
But now some may have to do without as supermarket chilled sections are nearly empty. Retailers have upped the price and are limiting how much shoppers can take home.
The government has put the dearth of milk in recent months down to drought, which has significantly reduced pasture and hampered production.
But the recent shortages are unusual, with the country's industry regulator itself admitting to "supply constraints" and "low stock levels" across the country.
Muthoni Macharia, who runs a restaurant in the capital, Nairobi, usually buys more than 70 packets of fresh milk - and is desperate and puzzled by the scarcity.
"Where has the milk gone?" she asked when the BBC spoke to her as she was out searching for at least a few packets to quench her customers thirst for chai.

blocks.caption: Image caption, For restaurant owner Muthoni Macharia, the milk shortage means a loss of business

blocks.text: For restaurant owner Muthoni Macharia, the milk shortage means a loss of business
Macharia says there have been shortages for about a week - and it was especially affecting her morning rush hour. Her regulars are not happy: some opting to take their tea black - but many will not.
"If they come in groups, and there's no milk tea, you see that's a loss for me," she said.
Kenya is one of the leading milk producers on the continent.

A long-established commercial dairy industry has led to pasteurised milk being very popular, particularly in urban areas, with Kenyans ranked among Africa's highest consumers, according to industry data.
Raw and fermented milk is more widely drunk in rural areas.
The milk shortage has sparked widespread public concern with some people promoting unfounded conspiracy theories about supermarkets deliberately trying to profit.

According to the Kenya Dairy Board (KDB), the government body that oversees the dairy sector, formal milk deliveries to processors fell by 3.7% from 84.4 million litres in June to 81.3 million litres in July, while preliminary investigations suggest deliveries declined further in August.
The Consumer Federation of Kenya (Cofek) says there has been a downward trend of supply since the beginning of the year.
It attributes this to a delay in the seasonal rains, which has reduced the grazing ground available, coupled with a 45% rise in the cost of animal feed.
Cofek has expressed concern over the rationing as well as the increasing cost, saying fresh milk prices have risen from 70 to 80 Kenyan shillings ($0.54 to $0.62; £0.40 to £0.46) a litre.
"This shortage was foreseeable, and in material part, avoidable," it says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Normally fresh milk is in plentiful supply on supermarket shelves

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Normally fresh milk is in plentiful supply on supermarket shelves

The consumer body says dairy processor New KCC, a state-owned company, and the KDB did not adequately absorb the milk surplus last year, adding that powder processed from the excess milk would have helped resolve the current crisis.
Some of the milk processors in Kenya often reconvert the powder into the more-preferred liquid milk during dry seasons when the supply of fresh milk goes down.
"Had these buffers been in place, today's supply shock would have been substantially cushioned," Cofek says.
It has demanded a recovery plan to include fodder and subsidy support for farmers.
This would include waiving of taxes on animal feed inputs, as well as "active retail price monitoring to deter opportunity price gouging and rationing".
In response to media enquiries, the dairy board's managing director William Maritim assured that despite the "temporary supply constraint", milk continued to be available.
Fresh pasteurised milk, which has a shorter shelf life, had been more affected than the more long-life UHT milk, he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dairy cows need to eat well to produce milk

blocks.text: Dairy cows need to eat well to produce milk
Customers at Nairobi supermarkets on the hunt for milk told the BBC they were worried about rising costs.

"Sometimes when I go to the supermarket I find there is none. When I do find some, the price has gone up. Today it is this price, tomorrow it has gone up again," said Bernard Abok, who does his shopping after finishing work.
Patricia Gathoni said if the prices kept going up she would have to rethink what she gave her children, saying she had resorted to adding water to the milk that she managed to buy.

On Thursday, agriculture ministry officials held a meeting with the association of dairy processors about the problem, with the ministry committing to support farmers, stabilise milk supply and protect consumers.
The ministry's top official in charge of livestock development, Jonathan Mueke, said the immediate focus was to get more feed for farmers, including through duty-free importation of yellow maize.
He said they were also looking at longer-term solutions that would manage stability across periods when there was surplus milk and when there were shortages.

Reports of milk going to waste are not uncommon during periods of a dairy glut. Farmers have often complained about how little they are paid for their perishable produce at such times - but they have few options because of limited processing or storage capacity.
According to Mueke, the government is considering setting up a fund to help support the preservation of milk during such periods.
In the meantime, the government is also considering temporarily importing milk from the neighbouring countries to ease the shortage.
For the devoted Kenyan chai lover, that may offer some respite.
Additional reporting by Ahmed Bahajj

articles.title: Global Affairs collecting DNA from families of Canadians missing in Nepal
articles.summary: Federal government officials said Global Affairs Canada is working to collect DNA from the families of Canadians still missing in Nepal and China after a flash flood ripped through the border region…

image.caption: An aerial view shows houses standing amid debris during a helicopter flight from Nuwakot to Rasuwa following the deadly flash floods and mudslides in Nepal. Officials are searching for hundreds of missing people, including 29 Canadians. (Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters)

blocks.text: Canada

Federal government officials said Global Affairs Canada is working to collect DNA from the families of Canadians still missing in Nepal and China after a flash flood ripped through the border region last week.
There are 29 Canadians unaccounted for following flash flooding last week

Senior government officials, briefing reporters on background, said they are starting to collect the samples from the families of 29 people still considered missing, with assistance from the RCMP and police forces in Nepal and China.
The flooding on Aug. 26 killed more than 1,100 people and left roughly 4,400 missing after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.
In Kathmandu, police have buried dozens of unidentified bodies in trenches because there are too many to keep or identify individually.
Canadian located safe
One Canadian was found safe, while the remaining 29 are believed to have been in the region where the flash flood occurred.
The Nepal Tourism Board reported on Sept. 1 that more than 580 foreign nationals and tourists were still unaccounted for, while another 330 had been rescued.
Federal officials said the situation is changing by the day and they continue to work with local authorities and the families of the missing.
Global Affairs has 10 officials in Kathmandu and has established points of contact with the families of the missing Canadians.
Search, recovery and identification efforts are being led by Nepali and Chinese authorities and Canada has offered assistance, the federal officials said.
