articles.title: PNP: Bonoan may not be released Thursday night pending records check
articles.summary: Despite the Sandiganbayan ordering the release of former Public Works chief Manuel Bonoan, the Philippine National Police (PNP) may still hold him temporarily on Thursday night.

blocks.text: Published September 3, 2026 10:10pm
Despite the Sandiganbayan ordering the release of former Public Works chief Manuel Bonoan, the Philippine National Police (PNP) may still hold him temporarily on Thursday night.
PNP spokesperson Col. Allen Rae Co said that they have already received a copy of the order from the Sandiganbayan and it is being processed by the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG).

“Makikita naman po natin sa order ang last sentence doon ‘unless he's being detained for any other lawful reason’, so ang ating CIDG will be doing their due diligence na titingnan po natin kung mayroon pang ibang outstanding warrant against him or if he's facing any other cases sa ibang division,” Co told reporters.

(You can see it in the order that the last sentence there is 'unless he's being detained for any other lawful reason', so the CIDG will be doing their due dilligence that; we will check if there is any other outstanding warrant against him or if he's facing any other cases in other divisions.)
Asked if it is possible that Bonoan will not be released tonight, Co answered in the affirmative.
Co said that after checking Bonoan's records, they will follow the court's orders and release him. The process should be done by Friday morning.

Bonoan has been detained at the PNP General Hospital due to his old age and medical conditions. Co said that they will do final medical checks on him but he would also be free to seek treatment wherever he wants.
“Based on the reports, nasa stable condition naman ang kanyang health,” Co said. (Based on reports, his health is in stable condition.)
Co said that since Bonoan is a free man, there would be no reason for the police to escort him anywhere.

The anti-graft court dropped Bonoan after he was removed from the plunder case against Sen. Jinggoy Estrada, in relation to the flood control scam. Bonoan, in turn, will serve as a government witness. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Impeachment prosecutors evaluating not just bribery article but witnesses list --Luistro
articles.summary: The House prosecution team is discussing ways to expedite proceedings at the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, including possibly dropping the Article on bribery.

blocks.text: Published September 3, 2026 10:09pm

The House prosecution team is discussing ways to expedite proceedings at the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, including possibly dropping the Article on alleged bribery in the Department of Education, and evaluating the list of succeeding witnesses.

“The many discussions that the impeachment team is holding, as a matter of fact, hindi lang yung [is not just the] concern about whether to present or not the article on bribery. Even the list of witnesses in the remaining articles are being re-evaluated,” lead prosecutor Representative Gerville Luistro of Batangas told reporters in an ambush interview on Thursday.
She added that they have not reached a final decision.
“So, concerning that article on bribery, I can only confirm that's part of our discussions. But no official stand yet kung ida-drop ba o hindi [whether to drop it or not],” she said.

Asked what factors the prosecution team will consider in arriving at a decision, Luistro replied, “Well, tinitingnan din natin yung nauna nating nai-present, kung satisfied ba tayo, na-establish ba yung mga facts which we want to be established. Ganundin yung importance noong articles.”
(We will look at what we have already presented, if we are satisfied, if we have established the facts which we want to be established. And the importance of the articles.)
Luistro emphasized that all four Articles of Impeachment are “equally strong.”

“So lahat sila ay malakas, lahat sila ay strong, but we have this confidential fund already na pertaining to both the OVP [Office of the Vice President] and the DepEd. Siguro we focus on something else,” she stated.
Luistro also said they are considering the timeline.

“We do not want to drag this impeachment trial too much because we understand that somehow, naapektuhan yung buhay ng mga Pilipino [it is affecting Filipinos' lives] and even the focus of the parties concerned. As for one, the prosecutors, the senator-judges, and even the defense,” she said.

“Narinig natin yung manifestation ni presiding officer na talagang medyo challenge na sila [We heard the presiding officer when he waid they are challenged] considering that three important functions are being addressed by the Senate at the same time: yung kanilang regular legislation, yung budget hearing for next year of course, and itong impeachment trial. So, kino-consider din natin yun [we are considering that] as part of the government. We do not want to spend too much time on this impeachment trial,” she added.
One way to expedite the proceedings, Luistro said, was for the defense to accept the prosecution’s stipulations.

“Pinipilit natin mag-offer lagi ng stipulation to shorten the presentation of witnesses for the prosecution. Yun nga lang, minsan ay they refuse to agree even to common exhibits. Kaya natatagalan,” she explained.

(We are always offering stipulations to shorten the presentation of witnesses for the prosecution. Only they sometimes refuse to agree even to common exhibits. That's why it's taking longer.) — BM, GMA News

articles.title: DFA reports fewer incidents in Ayungin Shoal due to provisional PH-China arrangement
articles.summary: A provisional agreement between the Philippines and China on resupply missions to Ayungin Shoal has led to fewer confrontations between the two sides in the area, the Department of Foreign Affairs…

blocks.text: Published September 3, 2026 10:03pm

A provisional agreement between the Philippines and China on resupply missions to Ayungin Shoal has led to fewer confrontations between the two sides in the area, the Department of Foreign Affairs said on Thursday.

According to Tina Panganiban-Perez's report on "24 Oras," House members asked DFA officials about its response to confrontations between Chinese and Filipino vessels in the West Philippine Sea during the Committee on Appropriations hearing on its proposed P35.17-billion budget for 2027.

“One of the important provisions is not to prejudice the positions that we have had. That means UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea) and the 2016 Arbitral Award," Foreign Affairs Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said.
"This is a provisional arrangement only in this particular shoal, the Ayungin Shoal, because this is with particular reference only to the Sierra Madre ship,” she added.
The BRP Sierra Madre has been run aground at the Ayungin Shoal and serves as a Philippine outpost in the area.
Philippine authorities conduct rotation and resupply missions to the shoal to relieve personnel of duty and bring fresh supplies.
The DFA said there were 16 rotation and resupply missions that were implemented without incident in the past two years.
The DFA also said that it was correcting the false information that China was spreading.

“Meron din po kaming pagkakataon para mag-issue ng formal protests when it comes to very specific statements of the foreign ministry and the Chinese government,” DFA Assistant Secretary Robespierre Bolivar said.
(We have moments to issue formal protests when it comes to very specific statements of the Foreign Ministry and the Chinese government.) —Jean Mangaluz/NB, GMA News

articles.title: Anthony Joshua's driver attempted overtake before fatal crash, trial hears
articles.summary: Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode, 46, is charged with offences including causing death by dangerous driving and reckless driving.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
BySimi Jolaoso
Africa Correspondent
The driver of a car carrying Anthony Joshua was attempting to overtake another vehicle when it crashed, killing two of the boxer's friends, a court has heard.
Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode, 46, faces charges including causing death by dangerous driving and driving without a valid national driver's licence. He denies the charges.

The court was told that the group - who had been travelling to visit Joshua's father in Ogun State, near Lagos in Nigeria, last December - were asleep when Kayode lost control of his Lexus SUV while he overtook a moving truck and collided with a parked lorry.
Joshua's personal trainer, Latif Ayodele, and strength coach, Sina Ghami, died in the crash.
A second defendant Abubakar Adamu, 35, the driver of the stationary lorry the car collided with, denies a charge against him of obstructing the free flow of traffic.
Inspector Christopher Ajayi Taiwo of the Ogun State Motor Traffic Division told the court that by the time he arrived at the scene, both the damaged Lexus and the stationary lorry had been removed.
But debris from the crash and soya beans scattered on the road from the lorry's load were found by officers, he added.
The only items recovered from the Lexus were a logbook, painkillers and an energy drink, which were found near the driver's side, Ajayi said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The former heavyweight champion was a passenger in the crash, which killed his team members Latif Ayodele (left) and Sina Ghami (right)

blocks.text: Image source, Social Media
The former heavyweight champion was a passenger in the crash, which killed his team members Latif Ayodele (left) and Sina Ghami (right)
The court heard police had yet to take a statement from Joshua following the crash.

During cross-examination, Kayode's lawyer questioned Ajayi over the lack of statement, to which he replied that "efforts are ongoing" and that he had not contacted Joshua because he "didn't have his number".
The trial was adjourned until 10 September.
Joshua, who was born in Watford, has family roots in Sagamu - a town in Ogun state, near the crash site.
After the collision, the boxer posted a tribute to Ghami and Ayodele on social media.
"I didn't even realise how special they are," he wrote.
"I'll just be walking with them and cracking jokes with them, not even knowing God kept me in the presence of great men.
"100% it's tough for me, but I know it's even tougher for their parents."

articles.title: Senate may revisit impeachment voting threshold amid changes in composition --Zubiri
articles.summary: Senator Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri said some senators are seeking to revisit the voting threshold for the impeachment case, citing changes in the composition of the Senate since the required vote was…

blocks.text: Published September 3, 2026 9:51pm

Senator Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri said some senators are seeking to revisit the voting threshold for the impeachment case, citing changes in the composition of the Senate since the required vote was set.

“There were some colleagues who want to revisit because at that time wala pa yung mga nawawalang senador ngayon kasi may nasa kulungan, isa at large. I think that is the issue,” Zubiri told reporters in a press conference on Thursday.
(There were some colleagues who want to revisit it because at that time, the senators who are now absent were still there—one is detained and one is at large. I think that is the issue.)
Asked if there were proposals to lower the threshold, Zubiri answered:
“Yes,” he said, noting some senators have concerns about the threshold, but when asked when it would be debated, he deferred to the presiding officer.
“Best person to answer is PO (presiding officer)," he said.
He also said he expects the issue could eventually be brought before the Supreme Court
“I’m sure someone will take it to the Supreme Court,” he added.
He further stressed that the matter should be debated publicly.

Meanwhile, Zubiri also defended the Senate’s decision to allow budget hearings to run alongside plenary sessions, saying the chamber would not be able to complete its workload if the proceedings were kept to the usual schedule.
The Senate is currently juggling three major activities: the impeachment trial, the 2027 budget process and its legislative agenda.

He said the Senate amended its rules to allow senators attending budget hearings during plenary hours to be recognized as present. The arrangement is intended to maximize the chamber’s working time and prevent delays in the approval of the national budget.
He noted that the Senate is targeting completion of the budget deliberations by October so that plenary action can proceed in November and the country can avoid a reenacted budget.
Zubiri said that without the simultaneous budget hearings and plenary work, the Senate could still have 12 departments left to tackle by October 23, based on Senator Joel Villanueva's estimate.
“Pagod na pagod”
Zubiri also acknowledged the strain of the Senate’s unusually heavy workload.
“I’m very candid so I just tell them how I feel. I’m just being honest. It doesn’t matter kung pagod na pagod na ako. If we have to work 24/7, we will work.”
(It doesn’t matter if I’m extremely tired. If we have to work 24/7, we will work.)

He said the remark reflected his candid assessment of the workload, noting that it is the first time the Senate has had to handle the impeachment proceedings, budget deliberations and legislative agenda simultaneously. He added that senators may not get their usual October break as they work to meet the demands of the impeachment case and the budget. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Vance's Antichrist comments are a 'common belief', his friend tells BBC
articles.summary: The US vice-president recently mused with a Christian podcast host on whether the end of the world was nigh.

blocks.text: Recent remarks by US Vice-President JD Vance about the Antichrist and "the end times" are a "very, very common belief", one of his friends says.

Vance recently mused on his religious views while responding to a question on a Christian podcast. He said he would "not [be] shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us" and speculated on whether the end of the world was nigh.

His friend Rod Dreher, a conservative writer, rejected any suggestion that the comments would harm the vice-president. He told the BBC's Today programme: "Most Americans who are inclined to vote Republican already believe this stuff."
In his podcast comments, Vance also clarified that such thoughts did not preoccupy him.
In Christianity, the "end times" phrase refers to theories about what will happen at the end of the world. Many churches believe God has a divine plan for the end of everything.
Meanwhile, the Antichrist is seen as the enemy of God who appears during the final phase of the world's existence and takes it over.
Vance, who became a Catholic as an adult, reflected on these topics during a recent podcast discussion with Bryce Crawford, a US Christian podcaster.

"Do I think that we're in the end times? I don't know," he said in response to a Crawford question on the subject. "And I think that it's probably bad for me spiritually to focus too much on it, because there are, like, things you gotta do.
"I gotta be good to my wife. I gotta be good to my kids. I have to be as good of a leader as I can for the United States of America."
The vice-president continued by saying: "I think that there are, like, things about the world that make me feel, like, not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us."
But Vance reiterated that he was preoccupied with being vice-president, explaining: "What I'm trying to focus on is doing as much of God's work as possible right now."
Reacting to Vance's comments about the Antichrist, Dreher said: "This might sound bonkers to someone who is outside the Christian religion, but it is a very, very common belief within Christianity."
He said his friend was simply reflecting that the world appeared to be going "crazy" through the rapid development of AI and ongoing conflicts.

Dreher, who was present when Vance was received into the Catholic Church, said Ronald Reagan had made similar comments when he was the US president, and that this was seen as "perfectly normal" by his voters.
Vance converted to Catholicism in 2019, then in his mid-30s, and has described how the Church resonated with his family and social values and his conservative politics.
Since becoming vice-president, he has occasionally tangled with Pope Leo and his papal predecessor Francis, on issues including the Trump administration's immigration policy.
Vance is due to appear behind the lectern on Thursday afternoon to deliver the first White House press briefing since the departure of Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt.

articles.title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach
articles.summary: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border

blocks.text: Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.

The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.

“I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.

Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.

blocks.caption: A protest against the Spanish government’s handling of the recent border breach at Ceuta. Photograph: Francesco Militello Mirto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.

But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.
Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.
Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.

In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”

blocks.caption: People who entered Ceuta from Morocco in late July on hunger strike last month to demand asylum.  Photograph: Laura Rincon/EPA

blocks.text: As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.
Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.

Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.

In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”

It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.
There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.

However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.
“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.
Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

articles.title: Can Hichilema heal Zambia's political divide?
articles.summary: The Zambian president starts a second term after a contested election exposed deep political divisions. His challenge now is to unite the country while addressing concerns over political freedoms.

image.caption: Hichilema was sworn in at an event at the National Heroes Stadium in the capital Lusaka in front of thousands of supportersImage: Jean Mandela/REUTERS

blocks.text: Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema was sworn in for a second five-year term on Tuesday.

For decades, Zambia has worn its peaceful transfers of power almost like a badge of honor in a region where elections have too often ended in disputed results, violence or leaders refusing to leave. Hichilema's own victory in 2021 appeared to strengthen that reputation.
Five years later, the picture is more complicated.

Hichilema begins his second term after a disputed election, with his main challenger facing treason charges, opposition supporters questioning the credibility of the vote and controversy surrounding the closure of courts during the crucial window for election petitions.

Hichilema has promised reconciliation. But for a president who once sat on the other side of power as an opposition leader and treason suspect himself, the test now is whether those words will be matched by the political space he gives his opponents.
Ngobola Cengelo Muyembe, a political, business and social analyst, told DW that reconciliation must begin by recognizing that a significant part of the electorate backed someone else.

"You have to remember that in every 10 people that voted, four people voted for the other side," Muyembe said, noting that during the president's inaugural address, he spoke about reconciliation and uniting people. "But that message can only resonate if what is on the ground reflects what is being spoken about."
Can Hichilema reunite a divided country?

Raymond, a self-employed Zambian who asked that his full name not be used, told DW that Hichilema should look beyond who supported him at the ballot box and govern across Zambia's political and ethnic divisions.

"The president, congratulations! Don't think about people who voted for you, didn't vote for you. One Zambia, one nation, one city," Raymond said. "Real change in mines and agriculture. The mines want us Zambians to be benefiting. Even your Tonga, your Bemba, you are all Zambians."

blocks.caption: The southern African nation has held largely peaceful elections since it returned to multiparty democracy in 1991Image: Jean Mandela/REUTERS

blocks.text: Artist Mazuba Nzabuka told DW he also wants Hichilema to govern those who supported him and those who did not, while giving young people a greater voice.

"Going forward, he is going to do the promises left behind. He is a president for all people," said Nzabuka. "Those who did not vote for him, those who voted for him. We are the same people. The five years going forward, our voices can be heard. Look after the youths."
But reconciliation will have to contend with the political fallout from the election.

Zambia returned to multiparty democracy in 1991 and has since witnessed several changes of governing parties through elections. Hichilema himself benefited from that tradition when he defeated incumbent President Edgar Lungu in 2021.
The latest election prompted debate about whether that image remains intact.
Democracy faces a new test
The independence of Zambia's institutions may feature prominently during Hichilema's second term.

Critics said their concerns intensified after courts were closed on the final day available for presidential election petitions. Interruptions during the announcement of election results prompted some opposition supporters to question the process.
Can Zambia trust election referee?
Analyst Muyembe said that protecting political speech and allowing opponents to openly challenge the government will be crucial to rebuilding confidence.

"If you really respect the people that voted against you, allow them to speak, engage them in a debate, not where you just have to bring in only the people that agree with you and the ones that are talking to themselves on TV, and encourage this national dialogue," Muyembe told DW.

"Allow the opposition who lost to complain about it the way they want, and then from there you can chart a way forward. But to stifle debate and fudge facts, this is not really helping our democracy."

The arrest of Hichilema's main challenger, Brian Mundubile, and his running mate on treason charges linked to allegations of plotting an armed uprising has become another point of political controversy.
Authorities maintain that the case concerns national security, while opposition supporters have questioned the timing of the arrests.
The situation has drawn attention because Hichilema himself once faced a treason charge while in opposition.

The question of whether the institutions that once wielded enormous power over him can operate independently when dealing with his own political opponents is likely to remain part of the debate surrounding his second term.
From economic stability to household relief
Political freedoms are not the only test.
Hichilema enters his second term pointing to progress in stabilizing Zambia's economy, including lower inflation and the restructuring of the country's external debt.
But many Zambians are waiting for those gains to reach their homes.
Mutinta Mushabati, who attended the inauguration at Heroes Stadium in the capital Lusaka, told DW that she was encouraged by what she heard from Hichilema.

"That he is going to increase everything, new allowances for school-going children, social cash transfer, CDF," she said, refering to Zambia's expanded Constituency Development Fund, which allocates public money directly to each of the country's constituencies to finance community-driven local development projects and infrastructure.
"I'm very excited right now. I don't even know what I can say. I'm very happy."
Muyembe told DW that the gap between positive national economic indicators and the experience of ordinary households represents a key challenge for Hichilema's second term.
He compared the economy to a reservoir that may be full while the pipes carrying water to individual homes remain blocked.
"Imagine that you got a giant command reservoir that distributes water to houses in the village," the analyst said.

"When the reservoir is full, you have stabilized your macroeconomic arrangement. But if the pipes that take water to the small little villages, the small little houses in these villages, are clogged and blocked, then you haven't really solved the issue because the people need to have the water in their individual houses."
Making Zambia's minerals work for Zambians
Copper and mining remain central to Zambia's economy and could provide one route for translating economic growth into household gains.

Muyembe told DW that Hichilema's government should focus not simply on attracting billions of dollars in investment but also on ensuring Zambian businesses participate in the supply chains created by that investment.
"If a mine is going to spend $2 billion or $3 billion [€1.7 billion to €2.6 billion] to expand that mine, that $3 billion has to go to the people, the people that are small businesses."
Greater local participation, Muyembe argues, could help create businesses and employment while allowing Zambia to retain more of the wealth generated from its natural resources.
The challenge is particularly important for young Zambians, whose expectations extend beyond political stability to jobs and opportunities.
Five years to shape a legacy

Despite his criticism of the political environment surrounding the election, Muyembe told DW that Hichilema still has an opportunity to determine how his second presidency will ultimately be remembered.
He pointed to former Zambian President Levy Mwanawasa, whose disputed 2001 election was followed by a presidency that later gained broader respect.

"I think he has a chance, basically, to redeem himself from the dent of these elections because it also happened with Mwanawasa. I think Mwanawasa's elections were also looked at funny, but he redeemed himself in the way he governed the following year."
That leaves Hichilema with two closely connected tests over the next five years.
One is economic: whether improving headline indicators can translate into jobs, stronger local businesses and better living standards.

The other is democratic: whether opposition voices can operate freely, institutions can command public trust and political competition can take place without eroding Zambia's long-standing tradition of peaceful transfers of power.

The crowds celebrating at Heroes Stadium showed the hope that still surrounds Hichilema among his supporters. The disputed election and its aftermath revealed the mistrust that exists among many other Zambians.
How he governs both groups may ultimately determine not only Hichilema's legacy, but the kind of democracy Zambia carries into its next political chapter.
This article has been adapted from an episode of DW's AfricaLink podcast.

articles.title: Senate asks COA for list of fraudulent, substandard flood control projects
articles.summary: Senator JV Ejercito said the Senate has asked the Commission on Audit (COA) to provide a list of flood control projects that its ongoing fraud audits have found to be fraudulent or substandard.

blocks.text: Published September 3, 2026 8:49pm
Senator JV Ejercito said the Senate has asked the Commission on Audit (COA) to provide a list of flood control projects that its ongoing fraud audits have found to be fraudulent or substandard.
In an ambush interview on Thursday, Ejercito, chairperson of the Senate Finance Committee, said the list would help lawmakers determine which projects should proceed and which should be scrapped.
“We asked them for their cooperation as we resumed the flood control projects," he said.
“We would need a list of projects sa investigation nila that are fraudulent or substandard para at least alam natin kung which projects can be completed, yung pwede ituloy at hindi pwede ituloy."
(We would need a list of projects from their investigation that are fraudulent or substandard so that we know which projects can be completed, which can proceed and which cannot.)

Meanwhile, Ejercito said the Senate has asked concerned agencies to clarify the joint circular governing confidential and intelligence funds and consider issuing clearer guidelines and safeguards following controversies over their use.

On the Senate’s plan to hold budget hearings alongside plenary sessions, Ejercito said the arrangement may begin next week, as agencies still need to be informed and are simultaneously attending House budget hearings.
He described the scheduling as a major challenge given the simultaneous impeachment proceedings, plenary sessions, and budget deliberations.
“Very, it’s really a challenge,” he said.
“Extraordinary talaga itong time na ito because of the impeachment and the plenary and the ongoing budget hearings.”
(This is really an extraordinary time because of the impeachment, plenary sessions, and ongoing budget hearings.)

Ejercito said he had appealed to committee vice chairs to follow, as much as possible, the schedules to be published by the Legislative Budget Research and Monitoring Office (LBRMO) or the Finance Committee.
He acknowledged that senators may have to move quickly between budget hearings and plenary sessions if a vote is suddenly required.

Ejercito also clarified that the arrangement would apply to the Finance Committee given the exceptional circumstances. He said he had raised concerns that the proposed nearly two-week marathon schedule for the impeachment proceedings could significantly affect the budget hearings.
“Dalawa yung choice natin, tapusin yung impeachment or magka-reenacted budget tayo," he said.
(We have two choices: finish the impeachment proceedings or have a reenacted budget.)
He said the Senate is discussing how to fit the budget hearings into the impeachment and plenary session schedules.
“We do not want a reenacted budget as well,” Ejercito said. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Nvidia to buy Hugging Face in $12.93 billion deal
articles.summary: The acquisition of the AI software platform will keep it as an open platform, Nvidia said.

image.caption: The chipmaking giant is seeking to diversify its hold on the AI sector [FILE: Jul 16, 2025]Image: Kyodo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nvidia will acquire artificial intelligence software platform Hugging Face for $12.93 billion (roughly €11.13 billion), the AI chipmaking giant announced on Thursday.

"Together, we will scale Hugging Face's platform, strengthen its infrastructure and expand access to AI for developers and institutions worldwide," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a post on the company's website.
What is Hugging Face and why does its open model stand out?
Hugging Face was founded in 2016 by three French entrepreneurs in New York. The company describes itself as "the AI community building the future."
It touts open models that can be downloaded and modified, in contrast to closed models such as rivals OpenAi or Anthropic.

"Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem. Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want and the computing platforms they want," Huang wrote when announcing the acquisition. "Nvidia compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face."
Nvidia, best known for its GPUs, specialized chips originally designed to render gaming graphics at high speed, has released over 500 models on Hugging Face and more than 250 open datasets.

articles.title: South Africa airline behind viral stadium flyby scraps repeat display
articles.summary: Two passenger jets passed close to Cape Town's DHL Stadium during a flyover last weekend. The carrier said it has shelved plans to repeat the display as South Africa's aviation authority investigates…

image.caption: About 56,000 people were in Cape Town's DHL stadium when the jets flew overheadImage: Stringer/REUTERS

blocks.text: South African aviation authorities are reviewing a low-altitude flyover by two Airlink passenger planes at an international rugby match in Cape Town last weekend.

The regional airline, meanwhile, said it had canceled another flypast scheduled for Saturday's rugby test between South Africa and New Zealand in Johannesburg this weekend, citing unfavorable weather.

In a statement, the South African Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) said it was carrying out a "compliance verification" of the August 29 flyover at Cape Town's DHL stadium to ensure "all safety protocols were adhered to by the crew."
Footage of the flyby, showing two planes in formation passing over the crowd, was widely shared on social media and prompted discussion about potential safety risks.
According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, the lead aircraft passed less than 15 meters (50 ​feet) above the top of the packed stadium.
What did SACAA and Airlink say?
The SACAA said it was analyzing flight data provided by Airlink and would go over additional information requested from the carrier before issuing a report.
The regulator said the airline had made applications for the flyovers, which were approved in line with the requirements for special air events.
Airlink, for its part, said the maneuver had been carefully planned and rehearsed, with safety being "the first consideration at every stage of the process."
It said each aircraft had three senior captains on board with a combined 75,000 hours of flying experience.
Nevertheless, it also recognized what it described as the "valid questions and concerns."

Airlink Chief Executive de Villiers Engelbrecht said the decision had been made to withdraw plans for this weekend's stadium flypast in Johannesburg because "the forecast weather points to unfavorable ⁠conditions for a ​safe formation flyby."
A history of flybys in rugby

Stadium flybys have long been tradition at major rugby matches in South Africa, dating back to the 1995 Rugby World Cup final in Johannesburg, when a Boeing 747 swept overhead before the Springboks faced the All Blacks.
The SACAA said in a statement that South Africa "is ranked seventh globally and first in Africa for our aviation safety standards by the International Civil Aviation Organization."
There have been no fatal accidents in its commercial airline operations space for over four decades, it added.

articles.title: Australian science prize awarded to researcher studying memory accuracy of domestic violence survivors
articles.summary:
Helen Paterson’s work on advancing how police and courts understand memory is recognised in prestigious Eureka prizes

  • Get our

blocks.text: Memory is an imperfect thing: research shows that recollections of single events – a purse being snatched, say – differ to those about repeated or ongoing events, such as incidents of domestic and family violence.

“What our research shows is that compared to a single-event witness, a repeated-event witness tends to report more gist-like details, the overall details of what typically would happen, and the things that remain constant between the episodes,” said Helen Paterson, an associate professor in forensic psychology at the University of Sydney.
“Sometimes they confuse one episode with another,” she said. Paterson’s work has important implications for victim-survivors of domestic and family violence and how their testimony is received.

“If they’re saying this in trial, it’s defence 101 to say … they’ve made this inconsistency, therefore their whole memory is unreliable,” she said. “But we do know what they do report tends to be highly accurate in that it did happen to them. It’s just they might mix up the episode in which it happened.”

Paterson’s work has also found that repeated-event witnesses are perceived to be “less honest, less cognitively competent, and less overall credible than the single-event witnesses – which is pretty concerning that the more repeatedly you are victimised, the less credible you appear to others”.
In recognition of her work in advancing how police and courts understand victim-survivor testimony in such cases, Paterson was awarded a prestigious Eureka prize on Thursday night.
Established in 1990, the Australian Museum Eureka prizes recognise the work of Australian scientists and science communicators.
Paterson was recognised for excellence in forensic science – one of 19 categories – at an event at Sydney town hall.
She hopes the award will help elevate the voices of victim-survivors. “Often we don’t give them the support and encouragement, and we don’t believe them and see them as credible as we should.”

blocks.caption: Assoc Prof Jane Tiller was recognised at the Eureka prizes for driving national legislative change that bans life insurers from discriminating against people due to genetic test results. Photograph: Michelle McFarlane/Australian Museum

blocks.text: Also among the winners was Assoc Prof Jane Tiller of Monash University, recognised for driving national legislative change that bans life insurers from discriminating against people due to genetic test results.

Passed into law in April, the ban will come into effect on 8 October. The legal change will enable scientists to use genomics more effectively to prevent conditions such as cancer and heart disease, Tiller said.
“The biggest reason that people don’t want this testing is because of fear of insurance discrimination,” she said. The legal change was a “critical barrier that we needed to remove”.

“We want to … start finding young people who we know have very high risks of diseases that we can prevent, and give them the screening, the surveillance, the health tools available to them to prevent or treat those diseases early.”

Prof Georgina Long, who alongside the late Prof Richard Scolyer was named Australian of the Year in 2024, won the Eureka prize for scientific research, for her pioneering melanoma work. Four other Australians of the Year have previously received Eureka prizes: Prof Tim Flannery, Prof Ian Frazer, Prof Michelle Simmons, and the late Prof Alan Mackay-Sim.

Also among Thursday night’s winners were Australia’s marine heatwaves forecasting tool, developed by the CSIRO and Bureau of Meteorology; the Women’s Microbiome Innovation Group, a Melbourne-based research collaboration that discovered that bacterial vaginosis is sexually transmitted between partners; and Prof Yansong Shen at the University of New South Wales, who developed a scalable low-cost process to recover valuable metals and silicon from used solar panels.

Kim McKay, Australian Museum director and chief executive, said: “This year’s winners are tackling some of our greatest challenges: protecting our environment, advancing healthcare, informing public policy and inspiring the next generation of scientists.
“World-changing discoveries do not happen overnight. They are built on years of dedication, collaboration and sustained investment.”

articles.title: Is Germany's economic slump finally over?
articles.summary: Despite a slew of negative headlines, the German economy has posted its best figures in years. There are reasons for optimism but structural issues remain.

image.caption: There are signs that Germany's economy may have bottomed outImage: Gregor Fischer/Getty Images

blocks.text: The German economy is showing tentative signs of recovery after a prolonged period of gloom. Europe's largest economy is on track for its strongest GDP growth since 2022, while business sentiment is finally trending upwards again after a lengthy spell in the doldrums.

The country's official statistics office reported last week that the economy grew by 0.3% in the second quarter of 2026, beating estimates and building on robust figures for the previous two quarters.

Several others have revised their forecasts upwards. The Ifo Institute, Kiel Institute for the World Economy and the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research are all now predicting growth of 1.3% or more for 2026.
Meanwhile, the Ifo business climate index — a key barometer of the country's corporate mood — returned its highest reading in a year for August.
"It's more than a flash in the pan," Clemens Fuest, President of the Ifo Institute, told DW. "It could be a recovery."
"The momentum is positive and the economy has shown a better-than-feared level of resilience," Carsten Brzeski, ING's global head of macro, told DW.

However, he cautioned against too much cheer, saying some of the economy's fundamental problems remain. "In order to really transform this into a longer-term recovery story, we still need more," he said.
Where has the good news come from?
The positive figures come as negative headlines related to Germany's economy continue to stack up.

Volkswagen, one of the country's most iconic companies, is in the midst of a bitter downsizing — reflecting a wider restructuring across the country in the face of competition from China and other global headwinds.

This summer, record low water levels on key German waterways such as the Rhine and Danube significantly disrupted trade and economic activity while the war in Iran continues to drive energy prices upwards.

blocks.caption: Low water levels on the Rhine hit economic activity this summerImage: Dominik Bund/IMAGO

blocks.text: Yet part of the reason for the upturn relates to how the German economy has handled some of those challenges, notably the closure of the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the Iran war.

Germany's exports and industrial base have powered GDP growth, with new orders increasing for the third month in a row, leading to the strongest production growth since early 2022. The VDMA, which represents the German mechanical and plant engineering sector, reported a 2% increase in foreign orders for July year-on-year.

Brzeski says many German manufacturing firms, especially in energy-intensive sectors such as chemicals, have benefitted from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. They have increased orders and taken some market share from Asian suppliers who were more severely dependent on Middle Eastern oil.
"There was a bit of a re-channeling of industrial orders away from Asia to Europe and Germany," he says.

The German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action itself identifies this factor in its August statement, saying Asian rivals "were more affected by price increases and supply bottlenecks."
It says that the multiple shocks of recent years have led German companies to diversify supply chains.

"Many companies have altered their transport logistics in recent years, are maintaining larger stocks, and are using a variety of transport routes in order to make their supply chains more resilient," it added.
Can the German government take some credit?
Analysts also think Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government deserves some credit for the turnaround, despite it hitting historic levels of unpopularity in 2026.
"It's driven by government demand and debt-financed spending, particularly in defense," says Fuest.
German industry shifts to defense production amid job losses

The government's economic plans are built around a €500 billion ($580 billion) infrastructure investment drive, a massive increase in defense spending and a major reform proposal aimed at boosting competitiveness.

It has also introduced some energy price relief measures and a €10 billion tax relief plan for lower-income households. "Companies are more optimistic and a big part has to be the stimulus," says Brzeski. "It is gradually reaching the economy."
Germany's structural problems remain
Despite the positive data, many of the issues which have dogged the German economy in recent years remain.

The recent uptick is driven by export demand, with practically no increase in domestic demand. According to the Federal Statistical Office, public and private consumption spending was flat, while investment declined.

"Even though everyone is happy that we have some positive news, we need to watch out and not fall into the trap of thinking that now 'everything is fine,'" says Brzeski, noting that the factors undermining German competitiveness persist.

"Chinese competition is still there," he says. "The long loss in international competitiveness in the automotive industry and other industries is still here," he added, stressing that these structural challenges would be difficult to alter or reverse.
Tentative optimism among Germany's businesses

Yet the positive sentiment remains. Indicators for the third quarter of 2026 suggest significant optimism among business leaders about the future, while overall German growth is now on track for a 1.2% increase for 2026. That puts it ahead of other European countries such as France, the UK and the Netherlands.

In the wake of the war in Ukraine, Germany's economy fell into a sustained slump from which it has struggled to emerge since 2022. While other economies showed signs of recovery, Germany remained in the doldrums.
For some analysts, the recent positive data reflects a sense that things had reached a natural "bottoming out" and that a return to growth was inevitable.

blocks.caption: Germany's industrial backbone remains intactImage: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "It could hardly have gotten much worse," says Brzeski. "We're bouncing back from low levels. This is not wirtschaftswunder 3.0, we have to keep that in mind."

He also thinks part of the optimism is related to corporate Germany finally accepting some harsh truths about how it had fallen behind in key areas such as innovation and digitalization, and belatedly trying to improve.

"They realize they simply have to embrace technological change, AI and so on, and have to start investing," he says. "They are no longer waiting for what's happening in Berlin in terms of reform packages; it's a question of survival."

For Fuest, the data suggests Germany's "industrial core" remains intact. He says that three-quarters of German manufacturing companies are still expanding, but warns that the recovery will be short-lived unless bigger change follows.
"It is urgent to allow for structural change and to find new areas where German companies have competitive advantages," he says.

articles.title: DepEd to propose new rules on class suspensions, resumptions
articles.summary: Education Secretary Sonny Angara will submit to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. a proposed executive order (EO) that would overhaul the rules on class suspensions and resumptions, after the measure…

blocks.text: Published September 3, 2026 8:24pm

Education Secretary Sonny Angara will submit to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. a proposed executive order (EO) that would overhaul the rules on class suspensions and resumptions, after the measure was approved by the Social Development Committee Cabinet Cluster on Thursday.

The proposed EO seeks to update the framework under Executive Order No. 66, series of 2012, by giving local officials and school heads greater authority to make site-specific decisions while preserving learner safety and minimizing unnecessary learning disruptions.
The proposed policy comes amid significant instructional losses caused by weather disturbances and disasters.

According to data presented to the Cabinet Cluster, basic education institutions lost up to 53 of 180 school days during School Year 2023-2024 because of weather-related and disaster-related class cancellations.
From June 8 to August 31, 2026, some schools also recorded 20 to 40 days of instructional loss, highlighting the need for a more flexible approach to suspensions and resumptions.
Angara said learner safety would remain the government’s priority, but learning continuity must also be protected.

“When a hazard strikes, the safety of our students, teachers, and school personnel is non-negotiable. However, every unnecessary day a classroom stays closed costs our learners their potential and compromises our long-term economic productivity.”
Three-tiered system proposed
The proposed EO would establish three decision-making mechanisms:

items: Automatic suspensions based on national technical thresholds;
Localized suspensions determined by local chief executives; and
Granular, school-level suspensions and resumptions, allowing school heads to make site-specific decisions based on actual conditions, subject to the required coordination and concurrence.

blocks.text: The policy would also expand the hazards covered beyond typhoons to include heavy rainfall, flooding, earthquakes, storm surges, poor air quality, volcanic smog, volcanic hazards, and extreme heat reaching a heat index of 40°C or higher.
Under the proposal, school heads would retain authority to suspend in-person classes based on documented site-specific assessments, with the concurrence of their Schools Division Superintendent.

The measure would also allow schools to resume in-person classes based on site-specific assessments once hazards have cleared. For public schools, the school head would need concurrence from the local chief executive; private basic education schools may declare resumptions in prompt coordination with the local chief executive.
Learning continuity to continue during disruptions

The proposed policy would also formally institutionalize alternative ways of delivering instruction when in-person classes are disrupted, including alternative learning delivery modalities, flexible learning options, self-learning resources, and temporary learning spaces.
Angara said the proposed framework would give local officials and school heads greater flexibility to respond to actual conditions on the ground.
“Under President Marcos’ leadership, we are reframing our approach: we are not merely suspending classes; we are safeguarding learning continuity.”

“By institutionalizing granular suspensions and resumptions, we give our local executives and school heads the legal backing and flexibility to make science-backed decisions tailored to real-time, ground conditions.”

The proposed EO will provide the overarching policy framework, while specific technical thresholds and operational guidelines will be contained in a separate Joint Memorandum Circular to be jointly issued with the Commission on Higher Education, Technical Education and Skills Development Authority, Department of the Interior and Local Government, and Department of Science and Technology. The policy was formulated following consultations with local chief executives, school heads, teachers, parents, and learners. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?
articles.summary:
Relocation coincides with proposed laws that opponents say would entrench power of US tech billionaires in country

Dozens of protesters converged on Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires…

blocks.text: Dozens of protesters converged on Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week after a congressional session raised questions about the billionaire’s presence in the country.

In white masks, they held signs saying “Peter Thief” and “No to the Peter Thiel law” in front of the wrought-iron gates of the $12m (£8.9m) residence, which Thiel bought in April as he moved his family to Argentina.

There is broad unease at the tech magnate’s presence in the country. His move has been characterised as part of a plan to hedge against world war three: Argentina, agriculturally rich and deep in the southern hemisphere, might just be the ideal place for a tech billionaire to wait out the apocalypse.
But recent developments in the country suggest Thiel could have more pragmatic considerations.

blocks.caption: Protesters marched to the gates of the $12m residence Peter Thiel bought when he moved his family to Argentina in April.  Photograph: Tomás Cuesta/Reuters

blocks.text: Last week, Argentina’s chamber of deputies held a six-hour debate on a set of sweeping regulatory changes put forward by Javier Milei’s rightwing government shortly after Thiel moved to Buenos Aires. They invited Thiel, Milei and an official linked to Argentina’s intelligence services to answer questions.
“None of them answered, and none of them came to the meeting,” said Juan Marino, a member of the chamber of deputies and the leader of the Piquetero party.

Marino said the new laws amounted to a “technofascist legislative package” aimed at entrenching the power of US tech billionaires in the country. Thiel has not publicly advocated for them, but Marino and others have said that their timing was suggestive.

The meeting in the chamber of deputies came after Argentinian deputies from several parties made public requests to the government for information about Thiel, his meetings and his businesses. None have been answered.

blocks.caption: Peter Thiel held closed-door meetings with Javier Milei and key presidential advisers in the months after he moved to Argentina. Photograph: Gage Skidmore/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: One of the laws, the “super RIGI”, would put in place an investment regime offering foreign companies a minimal tax rate and a 30-year guarantee against regulatory change. It specifically names AI datacentres among investments it hopes to attract.

Another, which failed, aimed to eliminate most of the restrictions around foreigners buying land in Argentina. A final decree would require some civilian government departments to share vast amounts of personal data on Argentinian citizens with the state intelligence services.

There is no evidence that Thiel has advocated for these laws directly. But in the months after he moved to Buenos Aires, he held closed-door meetings with Milei and key presidential advisers. It is uncommon for a foreign investor to have this degree of access.
In the regulatory package, Marino and others see the footprint of Thiel’s larger techno-libertarian interests.

The decree that gives vast amounts of Argentinians’ personal data to state intelligence services comes as Argentinian deputies have asked increasingly pointed questions about whether Palantir, the company Thiel co-founded, has undisclosed contracts with the state, which have gone unanswered.

blocks.caption: One of the proposed laws protesters oppose would offer foreign companies a minimal tax rate and a 30-year guarantee against regulatory change.  Photograph: Tomás Cuesta/Reuters

blocks.text: The land law, said Marino, could have paved the way for semi-autonomous “startup cities” – such as the controversial Próspera development in Honduras – that Thiel has advocated as a way for libertarians to carve out zones outside state control.

“Argentina is kind of a laboratory,” said Cecilia Nicolini, who represents Argentina at the Mercosur regional parliament. US tech billionaires, she said, “are using Argentina as a laboratory, because they have a person in power, Milei, who is even more crazy than they are”.
Over the summer Milei wrote an article in the Financial Times advocating the creation of “non-human corporations” – “entities operated by AI agents or robots”.

It parallels a vision put forward by OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, who predicted in 2024 that the world could soon be run by AI-owned companies. It also raises dark, thorny questions about the legal liabilities of those entities.
Nicolini said: “It’s not just that [Thiel] chose Argentina in terms of, it’s a secure place to live in a world that is facing a number of wars, etcetera.
“But really, behind it, I think there is a clear plan. And it is related to reforms that Milei is trying to pass, with some success in some cases, and in others, backlash.”
Thiel was approached for comment.

articles.title: Malaysia's middle path between China and US faces new tests
articles.summary: The prime minister's comments on Taiwan and US-backed military facilities near Sabah have revived questions over Malaysia's non-aligned foreign policy.

image.caption: US President Trump visited Malaysia during a tour of Asia last year [FILE: October 26, 2025]Image: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP

blocks.text: Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has spent much of his time in office insisting that Kuala Lumpur will not be forced to choose between the United States and China.
But two sets of comments last month have raised questions about how sustainable that position is as rivalry between the two superpowers increasingly spills into Southeast Asia.
"I see Taiwan as part of China, period," he said in an interview with news outlet Al Jazeera that aired on August 16.

Beijing considers democratically governed Taiwan part of its territory. While Chinese leaders say they favor "peaceful reunification," they have never ruled out using force to bring the island under Beijing's control.
More controversially, Anwar appeared to accept Beijing's argument that force could be necessary.
"If one province decides to break away. Do we use force? I think I will, [to] protect the sanctity and unity of the nation," he said.
China's gray zone warfare in the Pacific
Regional concerns

The comments drew an enthusiastic response from Beijing, while Taiwan's Foreign Ministry accused Anwar of effectively legitimizing the use of force against the islandand warned that his "one-sided support for China could negatively impact Taiwanese businesses' confidence in investing in Malaysia," including in the country's strategically important semiconductor sector.

Two days after his comments on Taiwan aired, Anwar argued that Malaysiashould strengthen its defenses in Sabah, citing the expansion of US-backed military facilities on the nearby Philippine island of Balabac.
The Philippines is upgrading facilities on Balabac, roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the Malaysian islands of Banggi and Balambangan.

Balabac was one of four additional locations added in 2023 to the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement, which allows US forces to access designated Philippine military facilities, construct infrastructure and pre-position equipment.
Taken together, Anwar's comments raised concerns that Malaysia is growing warmer towards Beijing while becoming more suspicious of Washington's military footprint in the region.
A fundamental realignment?

Kuala Lumpur has also been one of the region's strongest critics of Israel's actions in Gaza. Anwar has repeatedly accused the United States and European governments of hypocrisy and double standards for championing democracy and international law while failing, in his view, to hold Israel sufficiently accountable.
But Malaysia experts warn against interpreting Anwar's rhetoric as evidence of a fundamental strategic realignment.
"Malaysia still maintains very good relations with the US and other Western countries," Ngeow Chow Bing, director of the Institute of China Studies at Universiti Malaya, told DW.
Those ties may sometimes be less visible than Anwar's increasingly warm public rhetoric towards Beijing, Bing said, but the underlying relationship remains strong.

"It is certainly true that the space for maintaining its traditional balancing act between China and the US is narrower than before, but that space remains, and Malaysia will continue to operate within it," Bing added.
Philippine island on edge amid fear of China-Taiwan conflict
A shift in tone, not strategy

Anwar's comments about the Philippine military build-up are much more about an ongoing territorial dispute between Kuala Lumpur and Manila, Chee Meng Tan, assistant professor at the University of Nottingham Malaysia, told DW.

The Philippines maintains a territorial claim over Sabah, which became part of Malaysia when the federation was formed in 1963. Malaysia rejects the claim and regards its sovereignty over the state as indisputable.
Those tensions resurface regularly, and last month Kuala Lumpur lodged a fresh objection with the United Nations over a Philippine submission about its continental shelf.
"A neighbor that claims part of your territory is building a military base 20 minutes offshore — any government would react," said Tan.
Anwar called for the strengthening of Malaysia's own defenses, not for Chinese help, "and he went out of his way to say relations with Manila remain good," Tan added.

Anwar also sought to lower the temperature over Taiwan after his initial comments. Speaking to Malaysian media after the event, he stressed that Kuala Lumpur wanted a peaceful resolution to cross-Strait tensions and insisted that Malaysia's position had not changed.
Malaysia has formally followed a "One China" policy since establishing diplomatic relations with Beijing in 1974.

Chinese state media quickly interpreted Anwar's remarks through Beijing's preferred terminology, with Xinhua reporting that the Malaysian leader had "reaffirmed the one-China principle," something Malaysian analysts said isn't true.

Malaysia has not abandoned its traditional position, but Anwar's rhetoric "has sometimes been more accommodating towards Beijing than necessary," Khoo Ying Hooi, associate professor of international relations at Universiti Malaya, told DW.
"That can create the perception of a tilt even when Malaysia's wider strategic behavior remains more hedged and pragmatic," she added.
Less room to hedge
The prime minister faces mounting political pressure after his Pakatan Harapan coalition suffered three consecutive setbacks in state elections.
The defeats have intensified tensions within Anwar's broad governing alliance and speculation that he could call a snap general election.
Yet beyond Anwar's rhetoric and domestic political calculations lies a more structural problem for Malaysia.

Its longstanding strategy of hedging between the United States and China is becoming more difficult as Beijing's economic and military weight grows and Washington takes an increasingly transactional approach to foreign relations.
How much leverage does the US have over its adversaries?
"Malaysia is not abandoning its traditional balancing strategy, but the space for ambiguity is narrowing," said Hooi

Anwar is expected to visit China in late September, his first trip there in more than a year. He is reportedly due to attend the Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou and hold talks with Chinese Premier Li Qiang as Kuala Lumpur seeks to deepen economic ties with its largest trading partner.
But closer relations with Beijing do not remove Malaysia's dependence on Western markets, investment and technology, or its own differences with China.
Despite warm political ties, Kuala Lumpur continues to reject Chinese maritime claims in the South China Sea that overlap with waters Malaysia considers its own.

In February, Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan reiterated that Malaysia would not recognize Chinese claims that conflict with its maritime boundaries in the South China Sea, while Anwar has recently insisted that Malaysian oil and gas exploration will continue in the waters despite objections from Beijing.
For Tan, Malaysia's ability to continue balancing the two powers ultimately depends less on Anwar's rhetoric than on Malaysia remaining valuable to both.
"China wants friendly neighbors to keep trading with, and America needs Malaysian factories, where a big share of the world's chips is tested and packaged," said Tan.
"Neither gains from pushing Malaysia toward the other."

articles.title: Iran bets on shadow networks to evade US sanctions
articles.summary: To circumvent US sanctions, Iran has spent decades building a complex network of businesspeople and companies. A billionaire once sentenced to death is now back at its center.

image.caption: Iran is seeking new ways to bypass increasingly stringent US sanctions [FILE: February 23, 2016]Image: Ahmad Halabisaz/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: With its toughest sanctions yet, the administration of US President Donald Trump is seeking to force Iran's leadership into submission.
The measures, dubbed "economic D-Day" sanctions, are intended to achieve what military pressure since February has failed to accomplish.

In addition to targeting Iran's key sources of revenue and trade, including oil, banking, gold, shipping, aviation and certain technology sectors, US authorities are increasingly focusing on cryptocurrencies.

Digital currencies such as bitcoin, which operate outside the traditional banking system and dollar-based financial networks, are being used by Iran for money transfers, trade transactions and, increasingly, oil-related business.
An opaque network to help Tehran bypass sanctions
Iran also appears to be exploring cryptocurrencies as a way to secure oil shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
According to the Fars News Agency, which is close to Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the idea was proposed by Babak Zanjani.
The 53-year-old billionaire was released from prison last year and remains one of the most prominent figures in a network that has grown over decades and helped Iran navigate international sanctions.

blocks.caption: In 2016, Zanjani became entangled in Iran's internal power struggles and was sentenced to deathImage: Tasnim News/AFP

blocks.text: Individuals within these networks enjoy support and protection from influential figures inside the Islamic Republic. In return, they are believed to share part of their profits with powerful patrons within the system.

"Among these people, Zanjani belongs to an economic elite with innovative ideas and has repeatedly demonstrated his capabilities in the past," said Behzad Ahmadinia, an Iran-born journalist based in Cyprus who specializes in the oil and energy sector.
"It appears that the regime has decided to overcome internal rivalries and rely on professionals and experts who can work more efficiently than others and take over key positions."
Selling oil barrels on the black market

Iran can draw on decades of experience in operating under sanctions. The system extends far beyond individual businessmen and includes a vast network of companies, financial channels and personal connections.

Corruption and a lack of transparency are widely regarded as structural problems within Iran's political and economic system. Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index 2025 gave Iran a score of 23 out of 100 and ranked it 153rd out of 182 countries, indicating a very high perceived level of public-sector corruption.
Zanjani reportedly controlled a business empire of around 60 companies, including entities in Malaysia, Tajikistan, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.

Many of these firms were later sanctioned by the United States. Through this network, Zanjani began selling billions of barrels of Iranian oil on the black market during the presidency of Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, while also importing a wide range of goods, including aircraft, into Iran.
Is Iran set to become an economic outcast?
In 2016, however, he became entangled in Iran's internal power struggles. Authorities accused him of failing to return around $2.6 billion (€2.24 billion) in oil revenues to the Iranian state.

After a highly publicized trial in one of the country's biggest corruption cases, he was sentenced to death. For years, he disputed claims over the missing funds and negotiated with Iranian authorities.
US gains insight into sanctions-evasion routes

A key link in this network was Turkish-Iranian businessman Reza Zarrab. He was arrested in the United States in 2016 while on vacation and accused of money laundering and violating US sanctions on Iran.
Zarrab had built an extensive network in Turkey and possessed detailed knowledge of the financial and trading mechanisms Iran used to bypass sanctions.

Cases such as his gave US authorities valuable insight into how Iranian sanctions-evasion networks operate, allowing Washington to target them more effectively. Zarrab later cooperated with US investigators and was released from custody. According to reports, he now lives in the United States under a new identity.
"People like Zarrab or Zanjani are cultivated within the system and maintain connections to different centers of power," France-based economist Jamshid Assadi told DW.
Can the US 'asphyxiate' Iran without taking on China?

According to reports, Zanjani's rise began some 30 years ago during his military service, when he worked as a driver for the governor of Iran's central bank. The position is said to have opened doors to influential circles and provided him with key business contacts. How many billions of dollars flowed through his network and companies, and how much he personally earned from those activities, remains unclear.

In February 2024, Iranian media reported that assets linked to Zanjani had been repatriated from abroad. His wealth, they said, had grown beyond the value of his outstanding liabilities. In 2025, he was released from prison and quickly returned to the business world. Through one of his companies, he signed a multibillion-dollar contract with Iran's state railway operator.

At the same time, Zanjani has sought to reinvent himself. In an open letter to US business magnate Elon Musk, he offered his company as a bridge for economic cooperation between Iran and the United States. He now presents himself as an entrepreneur, mediator and advocate of dialogue.

After the United States placed Zanjani back on its sanctions list in January 2026, Washington expanded its measures in July to target a broader network of companies and business associates linked to him.

Just one day before the new sanctions were announced, Zanjani opened a café and pastry shop in western Tehran and attended a celebratory launch event. The business was shut down by authorities the following day.
Allies to adversaries: US-Iran relations over the decades
Can the US cripple Iran's shadow networks?
The key question, however, is whether the latest US measures can truly reach the networks underpinning Iran's shadow economy.

According to Jamshid Assadi, many of the traditional sanctions-evasion routes are now well known and increasingly difficult for Tehran to use. The United States has warned numerous countries that their companies, banks and private-sector actors could face penalties if they help Iran bypass restrictions.

At the same time, Iran has spent decades adapting to economic pressure and finding new ways around it. Whether Washington's latest sanctions will significantly weaken those networks remains uncertain. But the return of Babak Zanjani suggests that Tehran is once again turning to the businessmen who helped it weather previous periods of economic isolation.
This article was originally written in German.
