articles.title: India news: Jaishankar offers help to end war in Ukraine
articles.summary: Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar says India is prepared to assist efforts to end the war in Ukraine, as the foreign minister visits Kyiv. DW has more.

image.caption: Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar met his Ukrainian counterpart Andriiy Sybiha in KyivImage: Efrem Lukatsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 3, 2026
India ready to help end Ukraine war, Jaishankar says during Kyiv visit
India is ready to help end the war in Ukraine, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar said as he arrived in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Thursday.
"If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there," Jaishankar said as he addressed the media alongside Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
Sybiha welcomed Jaishankar for what he described as the "first-ever dedicated bilateral visit" of an Indian foreign minister to Ukraine.

"India is a global power and we welcome Prime Minister Modi's call to move from an endless war towards an end to the war. Ukraine stands ready for diplomacy," Sybiha wrote on X, referring to comments the Indian leader made during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan earlier in the week.

Jaishankar's trip to Ukraine comes more than a week after he attended the 27th session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation in Moscow with his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
The Indian foreign minister also met Putin during the Russia visit.
Since the start of Russia's war in Ukraine, New Delhi has been under pressure from Kyiv's Western partners over its cooperation with Moscow, India's decades-long ally.

"This historic moment takes place amid escalating Russian attacks against our cities, port infrastructure, and civil shipping. Our capital is constantly under attack and I appreciate my colleague's brave visit," Sybiha said as he talked about Jaishankar's Kyiv visit.
The Ukrainian minister added that he and Jaishankar discussed the need to restore freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, global food security, and bilateral cooperation.
"From infrastructure and pharmaceutical sector to technological innovation and digitalisation, we are ready to realise our full potential," Sybiha said.

articles.title: Yen soars as Bank of Japan tipped to raise interest rates
articles.summary: Jump lifts currency to highest level against dollar in a month, while global markets remain jittery

blocks.text: The Japanese yen has soared by more than 1.7% against the dollar amid speculation the Bank of Japan is set to raise interest rates.
The latest jump on Thursday lifted the yen to its highest level against the dollar in a month, at 155.85, and followed a 0.9% move the previous day.
Global markets remain jittery after this week’s dramatic government bond sell-off – caused by fears of a fresh inflation increase as a result of higher oil prices.
Investors have been reassessing their expectations for the future path of interest rates, in Japan and across other major economies.
Remarks by a Bank of Japan policymaker, Hajime Takata, suggesting it needs to move more “nimbly”, appeared to have heightened the prospects of a decisive move.

The chief executive of the financial adviser deVere, Nigel Green, said the scale of the yen appreciation over such a short time period underlined the febrile state of markets. “Markets this jumpy don’t need a shock to move hard, a rumour is enough,” he said.
Citi said in a note to clients: “(The) remarks are the strongest messaging we’ve heard from the board and reintroduces the idea of an expedited rate hike trajectory.”

The Bank of Japan has been incrementally raising rates for the past two years, after the economy finally shrugged off decades of deflation, or falling prices – but its main policy rate was left unchanged at 1% in July.
Markets now believe there is a 77% chance of a rate rise at the BoJ’s next meeting, which starts on 17 September.

Commenting on the latest market moves, Japan’s vice-finance minister for international affairs, Atsushi Mimura, said he was “neither satisfied nor reassured”, and policymakers “remain on a state of heightened alert”.
after newsletter promotion

The global bond market sell-off – pushing up the yield, or interest rate, on government borrowing – intensified earlier this week after the US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, used a speech last Friday to indicate that he was determined to bring inflation back to target.

Warsh had previously baffled some investors by withdrawing the Fed’s approach of signalling future rate moves, known as “forward guidance” – but in Friday’s speech at the central bankers’ conference in Jackson Hole, he said that if inflation did not move towards the 2% target the Fed would have “more to do”.

The bond sell-off appeared to have eased on Thursday, with yields on 10-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hovering at about 5.1% in morning trading – having touched the highest level since 2008, close to 5.3%, earlier this week.

articles.title: Dozens of trapped hydropower tunnel workers in Nepal could still be alive, official says
articles.summary: About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu

blocks.text: Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.
Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.

Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.
The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.
At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.

According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.

blocks.caption: A turquoise-green house stands tall amid sludge near Trishuli River in the aftermath of flash floods.  Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.

“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal ⁠electricity authority, told Reuters.

Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.

“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”
“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”

blocks.caption: The area around Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant before the flash flood.  Photograph: Maxar/DigitalGlobe/Getty Images

blocks.text: Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.

The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet, which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through ‌the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”

At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels ⁠because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we ​are told there is a ​dry space inside. We are ​trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.

The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology ​available in Nepal ‌right now, and we ​are taking help ​from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.

Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.

She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”

She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”

Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.
According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

articles.title: Toronto mayor to provide update as southern Ontario faces massive cleanup from destructive storm

image.caption: Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow in the city on Aug. 5. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Toronto mayor to speak after city hammered by powerful summer storm

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow is expected to speak Thursday morning after the city and surrounding areas were slammed by high winds and torrential rains that damaged buildings, flooded roads and left thousands without power.
The Latest

items: The Greater Toronto Area is cleaning up a day after a heavy thunderstorm damaged buildings, closed roads and knocked out power.
Toronto Hydro said early today roughly 8,300 customers were still without power. The province's Crown-owned power supplier, Hydro One, said more than 58,000 customers are without power.

Several major roads remain closed, including the Gardiner Expressway, Bayview Avenue and parts of the northbound Don Valley Parkway. In Vaughan, Ont., Huntington Road is closed indefinitely because of a large sinkhole.
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow is scheduled to provide an update on the storm response at 9:30 a.m. ET.

blocks.text: Pinned
Toronto mayor to provide update this morning
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow and city officials are scheduled to provide an update on the storm response at 9:30 a.m. ET at Toronto City Hall.
The City of Toronto says it has received more than 1,100 storm-related service requests and is assessing hazards across the city.
Though the southbound Don Valley Parkway is now open, the Gardiner/DVP connection from Jarvis to Bloor and a section of Bayview Avenue remain closed because of flooding and cleanup operations.
The TTC is running as scheduled, while Toronto Island ferry service has returned to normal.
The city says its 10 supervised beaches are expected to reopen at 10 a.m., although some have been affected by flooding.
All CampTO programs are operating, though activities may be adjusted on-site. Some drop-in programs may be limited or unavailable, and some park washrooms remain closed because of flooding.
Some outdoor pools and wading pools may also open late or remain closed today. Residents are being advised to check the city's website before heading out.

items: September 3Sinkhole in Vaughan, Ont.Hanna LeeA truck is seen in a sinkhole on a road in Vaughan, Ont. (CBC)A transport truck got stuck in a sinkhole on a road in Vaughan, Ont., just north of Toronto.It's not clear what caused the sinkhole, though it's likely that recent weather exacerbated the damage. No injuries have been reported, but two trucks were impacted, according to York Regional Police.We have reached out to York Region and the City of Vaughan for more information.

Chart: Nearly 50 mm of rain fell in Toronto in a narrow 2-hour windowGraeme BruceAccording to weather station data located in the Annex neighbourhood, nearly 50 mm of rain fell between 5 p.m. and 7 p.m.

6,000 customers still without power in TorontoVerity StevensonToronto Hydro says about 6,000 customers remain without power in the city after Wednesday's storm, down from a peak of 65,000.Crews worked through the night and have restored power to about 90 per cent of customers affected by the storm, the utility said in an update shortly before 8:30 a.m."Significant progress has been made and public safety remains our top priority," Toronto Hydro wrote on social media.Crews are continuing to deal with downed power lines and damage from fallen trees and branches. The utility is reminding residents to stay at least 10 metres away from any downed power line and to assume all wires are energized.

Toronto mayor to provide update this morningVerity StevensonToronto Mayor Olivia Chow in the city on Aug. 5. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow and city officials are scheduled to provide an update on the storm response at 9:30 a.m. ET at Toronto City Hall.The City of Toronto says it has received more than 1,100 storm-related service requests and is assessing hazards across the city.Though the southbound Don Valley Parkway is now open, the Gardiner/DVP connection from Jarvis to Bloor and a section of Bayview Avenue remain closed because of flooding and cleanup operations.The TTC is running as scheduled, while Toronto Island ferry service has returned to normal.The city says its 10 supervised beaches are expected to reopen at 10 a.m., although some have been affected by flooding.All CampTO programs are operating, though activities may be adjusted on-site. Some drop-in programs may be limited or unavailable, and some park washrooms remain closed because of flooding.Some outdoor pools and wading pools may also open late or remain closed today. Residents are being advised to check the city's website before heading out.

Transit updateHanna LeeFloodwater inundates a bus in Toronto yesterday. (@ea.eatss/Reuters)On the GO train, the Kitchener line is seeing significant delays, while Lakeshore West, Milton and Stouffville's are minor. Richmond Hill's service has been modified because of water levels around tracks near the Don River.All stops between Bloomington and Langstaff will be serviced, but the train will detour to Union Station. It will not stop around Oriole and Old Cummer — you're asked to take the TTC instead — and the route will take 30 minutes longer as a result.The TTC's subway system is up and running, though Line 2 will close at 11:59 p.m. tonight for planned track work. (Shuttle buses will run.) Museum Station's Queen's Park entrance, which had closed due to flooding, has been reopened. However, several buses are diverting their routes due to blocked roads, including the 82 Rosedale and 29 Dufferin. You can see more details here.

Pearson airport operational, but check your flightHanna LeeOperations at Toronto's Pearson International Airport are normal today, according to a post on X, which said 40 millimetres of rain fell on the airport in yesterday's storm.Still, travellers should check their flight status directly with their airline, it said, as some schedules were impacted by the downpour.On a cursory glance, more than 30 departing flights have been delayed, with 11 cancelled, including trips to Thunder Bay, Ont., Madrid and Islamabad.

DVP partially reopenedVerity StevensonThe Don Valley Parkway has reopened southbound lanes. The northbound lanes are still closed on the parkway from Bayview and Bloor to the Gardiner Expressway. Toronto police said the parkway would likely reopen after the morning rush hour.

Pelted with large hail and high windsHanna LeeA downed tree and power line during the storm in Toronto yesterday. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)Environment Canada sent three weather alerts to phones yesterday as the storm progressed. Toronto and Waterloo region residents got separate red alerts for a severe thunderstorm, warning of "golf-ball- to tennis-ball-sized hail."Parts of southwestern Ontario, including Clinton, Mitchell and Brucefield were under a tornado warning, as the storm at one point moved east at 75 kilometres per hour. Powerful winds reached up to 100 km/h in some areas, according to The Weather Network. The forecast hail also pelted certain regions, with one hail core exceeding five centimetres in some parts of the Greater Toronto Area.

Some Toronto watersheds floodingHanna LeeCars sit stranded on the flooded Don Valley Parkway in Toronto during a major storm on Wednesday. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)Meanwhile, some Toronto watersheds are already seeing major flooding, according to the Toronto and Region Conservational Authority (TRCA), including the Rouge River watershed in Markham, Ont., and the Don River watershed in Toronto. The authority said its watersheds have already received between three and 97 millimetres of rain, saturating their grounds and limiting their ability to absorb any more rain. "All rivers, streams, and shorelines should be considered dangerous due to flooding," it said. The TRCA remains under a flood warning until 9 a.m. today.

North and south lanes still closed on DVPVerity StevensonCrews were mopping up the Don Valley Parkway on Thursday, Sept. 3, in the aftermath of a powerful thunderstorm that flooded parts of the highway and downed power lines. (Paul Smith/CBC)Parts of the Don Valley Parkway — the highway that winds along the Don River through ravines and forests — were completely flooded with several metres of water. Images showed some people sitting on top of their submerged cars as they waited for help.Both northbound and southbound lanes are still closed on the parkway from Bayview and Bloor to the Gardiner Expressway. The Bay, Don Roadway, Eastern, Queen and Dundas on-ramps are also closed.Police say it's likely the road will reopen after the morning rush hour.-With files from Adam Carter

articles.title: DOJ careful in evaluating US extradition bid for Apollo Quiboloy
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The Department of Justice (DOJ) said it continues to assess the request by the United States to extradite jailed evangelist and alleged sex offender Apollo Quiboloy, as it does…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The Department of Justice (DOJ) said it continues to assess the request by the United States to extradite jailed evangelist and alleged sex offender Apollo Quiboloy, as it does not want to take the matter to the court “half-baked.”

Justice Undersecretary Ian Dato said in a news briefing on Thursday that the main factor in determining whether the DOJ should proceed with filing a petition for extradition in a local court is whether the request is “thorough enough” to stand in court.

“The department is conscious of the fact that it should not be filing anything half baked,” Dato stressed. “It will not bound itself to a timeline, but it will make sure that whatever case or petition it will file in court will stand scrutiny by the judge.”

The DOJ received on Aug. 7 the vast amount of documents from the US to boost its request for extradition of Quiboloy, who is facing charges of sex trafficking, visa fraud and cash smuggling in the US.

Chief state counsel Dennis Chan had noted that once the DOJ completes its evaluation and finds that the extradition request was in compliance with the 1994 treaty between the Philippines and the US, a petition would be formally filed before a regional trial court.
However, this could still be challenged by Quiboloy, but only up to the level of the Court of Appeals, based on the Supreme Court’s new extradition rules.
The DOJ also earlier maintained that it is serious in its commitment to international law as well as to a fair judgment of the case. /mr

articles.title: Gloria Steinem, leading U.S. feminist and author, dead at 92
articles.summary: Gloria Steinem, the celebrated U.S. author and activist who became one of the most potent voices of the feminist movement, has died. She was 92.

image.caption: Gloria Steinem speaks at The Creative Coalition's Spotlight Initiative Gala Awards Dinner in Park City, Utah, on Jan. 25, 2020. (Tibrina Hobson/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Gloria Steinem, the celebrated U.S. author and activist who became one of the most potent voices of the feminist movement, has died. She was 92.

Steinem, a co-founder of Ms. magazine, was a hugely recognizable presence wherever she went. And she went everywhere: Much of her life as an advocate was spent on the road, speaking at college campuses and community centres, at rallies and marches.
She died Wednesday at her home in New York City, according to her foundation's social media pages.

"Gloria's greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard," the posts said. "Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humour."

Steinem enjoyed writing and spending time in the community in recent years, the posts said. She also hosted talking circles for hundreds of people in her home. She died just before a planned memoir was to be released this fall.

In a 2019 interview with CBC News, Steinem said she had not seen as much grassroots activism in all of her years advocating for feminist issues as she had during U.S. President Donald Trump's first term.
My role is to listen to younger women and to say, 'What can I do to help?'" she said, when she was asked about the broader backlash from other activists amid a push for intersectional feminism.
"It's not to tell anybody what to do, that's ridiculous. It's to listen."
Feminist icon, author Gloria Steinem dead at 92

She began her career as a journalist, notably one who reported, in 1963, on degrading conditions in Hugh Hefner's Playboy empire, an undercover assignment she came to later regret. She credits a meeting six years later, where women spoke out boldly in favour of abortion rights, with changing her career path.

"That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me," Steinem, who had undergone a secret illegal abortion herself at age 22, told The Associated Press in an email in 2022, reflecting on the reversal of Roe v. Wade. "Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we're not living in a democracy."
'My friend and mentor'
Tributes to Steinem have begun pouring in from around the globe from leaders, cultural figures and women who were inspired by her.

Patti Smith shared a photo of Steinem, calling her "the greatest." Hillary Clinton highlighted Steinem's achievements in a post honouring her, pointing out that her activism helped society question misogynistic systems.
"She pushed open doors not just for herself, but for literally millions of women behind her," Clinton wrote in the post.

Meghan Markle, Duchess of Sussex, shared a lengthy post of her memories with Steinem. The two had appeared at multiple events together to encourage voting and advance women's rights, but Markle said her "friend and mentor" had also been over for Thanksgiving and gave "extraordinary advice and perspective with a cup of tea and an unrivaled cheekiness and wit."
Lena Dunham wrote in an Instagram post that she was honoured to have known Steinem and learned sides of her not everyone saw, like that Call The Midwife was her wind-down show after a party.

"You weren't just generous with your life force, your vision or your intellect: you were generous with your time, your laughter and even your jewelry (like the time I admired your silver vulva ring and you plucked it off your hand and placed it on mine.)," Dunham wrote.
PHOTOS | Steinem through the years:
Activism spanned decades

Though she soon became a known activist, those who watched Steinem denounce discrimination for so many years likely never suspected that she'd had to overcome a deep fear of public speaking. She would have simply stuck to writing, she said, if only editors at the time had been willing to let her write about the women's movement.
But they weren't interested, she told The Associated Press in 2015.
"So I ended up going out and speaking, which was my nightmare," she said. "I mean, I was terrified. But I'm grateful, even though I still get scared even now."

Time hardly slowed Steinem down; well into her 80s she was traveling the globe and speaking out on issues of importance to her. These included everything from genital mutilation to Korean reconciliation, but it was equality for women that took precedence.
"Being a feminist means that you see the world as whole instead of half," she once said. "It shouldn't need a name, and one day it won't."

A few days after her 85th birthday, she was leading a women's "talking circle" at an off-Broadway play celebrating her life, where one by one, women in the audience — many fighting tears — rose to thank her and tell their own stories of discrimination.
In 2020, her life was the subject of a feature film: The Glorias, A Life on the Road, based on her 2015 memoir and starring Julianne Moore.
Moore posted a set photo with Steinem on Thursday, writing that "the time I spent studying Gloria Steinem in order to play her was one of the most edifying of my life."

And at 91, Steinem collaborated on a picture book with Liberian peace activist and Nobel laureate Leymah Gbowee aimed at inspiring young people to change the world. Rise, Girl, Rise: Our Sister-Friend Journey. Together for All was published in February 2026.

The constant visibility came with a price. Even into her older years, Steinem expressed frustration that despite her accomplishments, she was often described as beautiful or glamorous (A 1992 Vanity Fair profile noted her "spectacular racehorse legs.") It was a label she said unfairly detracted from her message.

items: Solidarity sisters! Why Canadians are joining the Women's March on Washington
Gloria Steinem in Montreal: On feminism, abortion and online activism

blocks.text: "Nobody ever called me beautiful until I was publicly a feminist, and that was in my mid-30s," she said. "It was clear that label was being assigned to me. The most hurtful part is that you work very hard, and people say it's because of your looks."
Steinem also had to deal with hostility, which sometimes came from surprising places.

Appearing on Larry King's talk show on CNN in 1990, she was visibly stunned when a female caller greeted her cheerfully, then told her to "rot in hell" because she had ruined "the beautiful American family."

But by then, she noted, at least people were taking feminists seriously. That wasn't the case in 1972 when she co-founded Ms. magazine and many commentators — especially male — dismissed it as ridiculous, predicting an early demise. (The magazine continues to this day, published by the Feminist Majority Foundation.)

Among Steinem's detractors was then-president Richard Nixon, who was caught on an Oval Office tape ridiculing both her and the "Ms." title. The ridicule was mutual: In a 1972 National Press Club speech, Steinem called Nixon "the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon."
It was just one example of Steinem's trademark wit. Before she married at 66, she often explained her singlehood by saying "I can't mate in captivity."
Laughter, she wrote, was "the only free emotion — the only one that can't be compelled."

articles.title: Feminist activist and journalist Gloria Steinem dies at 92
articles.summary: Her foundation said she "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City, "surrounded by many who loved her".

blocks.text: Gloria Steinem, who became a face of the women's liberation movement in the US, has died, aged 92, her foundation says.
In a post on Instagram, it said she "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City, "surrounded by many who loved her".
Steinem, who was a writer and magazine editor, co-founded the Women's Action Alliance, a group dedicated to fighting sexism, more than 50 years ago.

She started her career as a journalist in New York in the 1970s and went on to co-found Ms. magazine, one of the first publications to focus on other women's issues than the perils of housekeeping and the mandates of the beauty industry.
During the 1970s, Steinem was one of the main voices campaigning for women's reproductive rights.

She celebrated the US Supreme Court's 1973 ruling in the case of Roe v Wade, which granted women the constitutional right to abortion. Nearly half a century later she witnessed the reversal of this decision.

articles.title: Gloria Steinem: An icon of American feminism
articles.summary: The trailblazing feminist was an iconic leader of women's rights in the US.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Gloria Steinem pictured in 1990 in her New York City apartment
Gloria Steinem was a powerful icon of America's feminist movement, and her career spanned a myriad of roles that changed the lives of generations of women.

With her iconic aviator sunglasses and long, blonde streaked hair - which she considered rebellious in the 1970s - Steinem was an internationally recognised activist in the fight for women's equality.
She spoke out for the legalisation of abortion, same-sex marriage, and equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.
Her activism was not without a backlash - from both men and women - and harassment that could be as vulgar as it was intimidating.
The early years
Born on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, Gloria Steinem did not have an easy childhood.
Her father Leo Steinem was a travelling salesman and, together with her mother Ruth and older sister Susanne, they lived in a caravan, crisscrossing the country.
Leo abandoned the family and moved to California when Steinem was 10 years old, leaving her to care for Ruth who had long suffered with mental illness and had terrifying hallucinations.
As a result, Steinem did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Gloria Steinem at the 1972 Democratic Convention

blocks.text: Gloria Steinem at the 1972 Democratic Convention
She would later remark that she had never wanted children because she had already had one - her mother.

In the late 1950s she went to India on a research scholarship, and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.

Steinem left India and moved to New York City in the early 1960s to start her career as a freelance writer. It was a time when male-dominated newsrooms made it difficult for women to get hard-hitting stories.
Breakthrough article

Her big break came in 1963, when Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny cocktail waitress and wrote A Bunny's Tale, an exposé for Show magazine detailing the seedy and sexist reality of Hugh Hefner's empire.
As soon as she arrived for the interview, a security guard called out, "Here bunny, bunny, bunny."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Steinem's undercover work as a Playboy Bunny revealed a world of misogyny and exploitation

blocks.text: Steinem's undercover work as a Playboy Bunny revealed a world of misogyny and exploitation
Using the fake name Marie, she lied about her age - telling Playboy she was 24 years old when she was actually four years older.
Steinem lifted the lid on the underpaid life of a Bunny, and the physical pain of wearing the high-heels and tight corsets for hours.
Despite the fame - and infamy - that followed, she still found herself struggling to be taken seriously by editors.
Though the Playboy exposé helped land her assignments for the New York Times and New York Magazine, often they were about ladies' stockings and the latest hairstyles.

"To this day when people don't like me they introduce me as a former Bunny, as a put-down," she told the New York Times in 2016. "On the other hand, I did improve the working conditions for those women."
All-female journalism
Undaunted, by 1968 Steinem was a columnist for New York Magazine, focusing on progressive social issues and women's rights.
Her article, After Black Power, Women's Liberation, external brought her national fame, making her the face of the US feminist movement in the 1970s.

"I was the only woman, and after I wrote an abortion article, my [male] friends there said to me: 'Don't get involved with these crazy women. You've worked hard to be taken seriously,'" she told Rachel Cooke for The Guardian in 2011.
So she took matters into her own hands.

In 1972, she launched Ms. magazine with a group of feminist activists. It was the first all-female founded and operated periodical, designed to be an alternative to other women's magazines that typically focused on housekeeping and fashion.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ms. magazine broke new ground, selling out within its first week of publication

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Ms. magazine broke new ground, selling out within its first week of publication
Critics - mainly men - were quick to write it off. News presenter Harry Reasoner said he gave it six months "before they run out of things to say".
The first issue sold out within a week and generated 26,000 subscribers. The magazine is still going today.
In 1978, Steinem wrote one of Ms. magazine's most infamous and widely read essays - If Men Could Menstruate.
Her satirical reflection on how different power, political and economic structures might be if men had menstrual cycles is still referred to in discussions about gender roles.

By the end of her career, Steinem had become a prolific and award-winning writer, penning numerous books including her own memoirs, a biography on Marilyn Monroe and a collection of her own famous quotes in the wryly titled, ‪The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off.
Abortion rights campaigner
Though still considered one of the world's best-known feminist activists, Steinem came to advocacy rather late in life - in her thirties.

At an abortion awareness rally in 1969 where women were sharing their experiences of having abortions, Steinem was encouraged to share her own story about terminating a pregnancy. It had taken place years earlier in London when she was 22 years old, just before going to India.

Abortion was illegal in the UK at the time, unless the woman's mental or physical health was in danger. The doctor took a great risk for Steinem, telling her: "You must promise me two things. First, you will not tell anyone my name. Second, you will do what you want to do with your life."
Nearly 60 years later, Steinem broke one of those promises, when she dedicated her memoir, My Life On The Road, to Dr John Sharpe.
She described that abortion speak-out event as a "light bulb moment" - when she realised the US needed a bigger women's rights movement.

Almost overnight, Steinem became a crusader for abortion rights, calling it "reproductive freedom". The phrase she coined is credited with making the subject more approachable for political discussion and continues to be used in abortion debates.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Joining Steinem at the 1989 March for Women’s Lives were Susan Sarandon, Gloria Allred, Jesse Jackson and Jane Fonda

blocks.text: Joining Steinem at the 1989 March for Women’s Lives were Susan Sarandon, Gloria Allred, Jesse Jackson and Jane Fonda
Steinem organised marches and quickly became a draw at demonstrations, although she admitted later that she found talking to the huge crowds "utterly terrifying".

After Congress failed to pass the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) in 1970 - legislation granting women equal rights to men - Steinem co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus with fellow feminist leaders and more than 300 women across the US. The group worked to include women in all aspects of political and public life.

The same year she testified at Senate hearings for the ERA, telling the predominantly male audience: "I have been refused service in public restaurants, ordered out of public gathering places and turned away from apartment rentals all for the clearly stated, sole reason that I am a woman."
Second-wave feminism continued to gain momentum, and Steinem was one of its most famous figureheads.
Too glamorous?

Critics, however, came from the left as well as right, targeting Steinem for everything from her looks to her motives. Some claimed she was too glamorous to be a true feminist, while others said she was successful only because of her appearance.

Betty Friedan, author of The Feminine Mystique, the book credited with launching second-wave feminism, was annoyed that Steinem became the face of the movement, accusing her of "ripping off the movement for private profit" when she launched Ms.
The media were trying "to make her a celebrity," fumed Friedan, "but no one should mistake her for a leader."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Steinem's sudden rise to become the face of second-wave feminism caught the ire of some activists

blocks.text: Steinem's sudden rise to become the face of second-wave feminism caught the ire of some activists

US President Richard Nixon was recorded during a secret conversation furiously ranting about Steinem, to which she responded: "There is some opinion that Richard Nixon is the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon".
Al Goldstein, the notorious pornographer and publisher of Screw magazine, launched a campaign of attacks that included publishing her phone number next to fake advertisements for oral sex.
He also printed a graphic centrefold image of a Steinem look-alike, and hung it open on display at the newsstand outside Ms. magazine's office building. She had to look at it every day.

As she got older, harassment to this degree became less common. However, given she was a recognisable figure in New York City, it was not uncommon for Steinem to be stopped on the street by strangers wanting to debate - sometimes with an edge of hostility.

But she welcomed the continued debate. In 2020, she was among a cross-section of public figures who signed an open letter denouncing cancel culture, saying it weakens open debate by shutting people down.
"If you care about having the conversation, surely you want to try in a humane way to convince the other person, not do away with them," she told the New York Times.
'I can't mate in captivity'

Gloria Steinem once quipped: "I can't mate in captivity" - a reference to her disinterest in marriage. But she publicly enjoyed a healthy dating life with a number of rich and famous bachelors, giving critics more ammunition to use against her.
They included Frank Thomas who was head of the Ford Foundation; film director Mike Nichols and Olympic decathlete Rafer Johnson (who helped tackle the man who assassinated Robert F Kennedy in 1968).
"I was the one always accused of using men, of being too sexual. Someone once sent me a cartoon of a tombstone that said 'at last she sleeps alone'," she wrote.
But in 2000, aged 66, she wed David Bale, a South African-born entrepreneur-environmentalist, and father of actor Christian Bale.
At the time, the union drew gasps of surprise and even disappointment from some feminists, who had spent years following Steinem's heated debates surrounding marriage laws.

But she said those laws had finally changed. "If I had married when I was supposed to get married, I would have lost my name, my legal residence, my credit rating, many of my civil rights. That's not true anymore. It's possible to make an equal marriage," she explained years later.
Steinem also confessed to it being a "green card marriage" because Bale's US visa was running out - but said that they loved each other and were going to be together regardless.

blocks.caption: Image caption, David Bale and Gloria Steinem, pictured with Maurine Rothschild

blocks.text: David Bale and Gloria Steinem, pictured with Maurine Rothschild
Bale died three years later from brain lymphoma.
Steinem had her own health scare with breast cancer in 1986, and underwent a lumpectomy.
'So much to do'
Gloria Steinem once said she wanted to live to 100 because "there's so much to do".
In her near-century of life, she even became a talented tap dancer.

She was given America's highest civilian honour - the Presidential Medal of Freedom - in 2013 by President Barack Obama, who credited her work with giving more women "the respect and opportunities that they deserve".
In 2024, she reached the age of 90. She lived alone in New York, content in the knowledge that Ms Magazine was still publishing.
Steinem seized the occasion to tell the BBC that she hoped her legacy "might help individual people... to become more the unique, valuable, loved and lovable person that they want to be."
She will be remembered for amplifying the voices of women in a way that mainstream media at the time either could not, or would not.
And, in so doing, she altered the landscape and language of women's rights in America.

articles.title: More than 80 migrants feared dead after boat rescued off Canary Islands
articles.summary: Rescuers found 44 survivors on board the vessel but bad weather meant they had to leave five bodies behind.

blocks.text: More than 80 people, including a baby, are feared to have died in a boat which was adrift in the Atlantic Ocean for 27 days.

Spanish Maritime Rescue teams located the vessel some 65 nautical miles southwest of Gran Canaria's coastal town of Arguineguín on Wednesday and found 44 survivors, with five dead bodies also on board.

The boat is believed to have departed The Gambia in West Africa in early August with 127 occupants on board. Human rights activist Helena Maleno Garzón, founder of Spanish charity Caminando Fronteras, said 83 people had lost their lives.
Rescuers were forced to leave the five bodies they found due to the rough sea conditions, Maritime Rescue said.
The organisation said it could not verify how many people were originally on board the vessel as it was not within its remit.
The 44 survivors are men from sub-Saharan Africa, Maritime Rescue said in a statement.
"Once the rescue was complete, adverse weather conditions in the area - featuring 20-knot winds and 2.5m waves - made it impossible to recover the five bodies found on board the vessel," it added.
Three of the survivors were airlifted to hospital in critical condition.
The rest were transported by sea to Gran Canaria, where they disembarked in the early hours of Thursday morning.

articles.title: Victims sue South African government over 1961 Sharpeville massacre that left 91 dead
articles.summary:
Claim relating to infamous apartheid-era shooting of protesters part of wave of litigation for apartheid-era crimes

The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South…

blocks.text: The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.

Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress. “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.

blocks.caption: Abraham Mofokeng, who was shot in the foot and back while protesting against South Africa’s apartheid pass laws during the Sharpeville massacre on 21 March 1960.  Photograph: Rachel Savage/The Guardian

blocks.text: Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.
The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.

As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.
Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South Africa government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.

The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.

blocks.caption: Dead and wounded South Africans lie outside the Sharpeville police station. Photograph: PN2

blocks.text: In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission. That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.
Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.

In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed that protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Colonel J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”

In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.

blocks.caption: Members of a choir perform during the commemorations of the massacre, at the Phelindaba cemetery in Sharpeville, on 21 March 2026.  Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.

The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.
Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of around 20,000 rand for six years.
“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”

blocks.caption: Paulina Mathinye, whose father Samson was killed by police in the Sharpeville massacre Photograph: Rachel Savage/The Guardian

blocks.text: The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father Samson was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.
Mathinye didn’t initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”

Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but couldn’t afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.

Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.

Sharpeville’s problems didn’t begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.

“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”

Maryland judge issues preliminary injunction blocking Trump’s executive order targeting what he termed ‘birth tourism’

A US…

blocks.text: Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order
Apple has renamed Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for US users of its Maps app, after an executive order from Donald Trump to change the name of the Great Lake amid his trade spat with Canada.

The Apple Maps app now displays the controversial new name for the lake, which sits between New York state and the Canadian province of Ontario, for users in the US. Apple users outside the country will still see the Lake Ontario name.
Apple had been reportedly mulling whether to submit to Trump’s new order after receiving a personal request from the president for the tech company to change the lake’s name.

Trump welcomed the news, declaring in a Truth Social post that the adoption of “Lake America” by Google Maps and Apple Maps meant the name change was “complete, ratified, and binding”. However, the US cannot compel Canada – or any other country – to also change the name.

The US president officially unveiled the name swap last week. He did not mention his escalating trade feud with the US’s northern neighbors in the order, but the timing suggested a retaliatory move after Canadian officials denounced Trump’s new sweeping tariffs and promised to instate tariffs of their own.

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, rejected the attempt to rename the body of water, saying in a post on social media that the lake’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.
Judge blocks new Trump bid against birthright citizenship
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
A US federal judge has blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a new executive order limiting who qualifies for birthright citizenship.
The move thwarts President Donald Trump’s latest attempt to restrict the constitutional right, which comes after the US supreme court rejected his previous effort, AFP reported.

US district judge Deborah Boardman of Maryland issued a preliminary injunction following an appeal by rights groups who challenged Trump’s executive order from 6 August targeting what he termed “birth tourism”.

“The supreme court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ’citizens at birth’,” Boardman wrote in her 35-page ruling, adding the president’s August order “is almost certainly unconstitutional”.

“When it comes to attacking birthright citizenship, the Trump administration has lost before this court, lost before the supreme court, and lost again today,” said Shana Khader, legal director at We Are CASA, a Maryland-based group.
Trump’s fresh executive order was aimed at those who he alleges enter the country under the guise of tourism while actually intending to give birth.

The president’s efforts to curb birthright citizenship are part of his wider campaign to limit immigration, which includes expelling millions of undocumented migrants and removing deportation protections from nationals of more than a dozen countries.
In other developments:

items: House Democrats rejected a constitutional amendment proposed by Republicans to ensure the size of the supreme court is permanently capped at nine justices. The proposal, a Republican effort to make the supreme court a campaign issue ahead of the November midterms, failed 212-206.

House Democratic lawmakers introduced a war powers resolution seeking to stop the Trump administration’s boat strikes. Gregory W Meeks, Adam Smith, Jim Himes and Bennie G Thompson said people have been killed “without due process” in attacks never authorized by Congress.

Senator Richard Blumenthal pushed back against a statement from the US Postal Service about its new system to screen millions of mail-in ballots for the upcoming midterm elections. “‘Just trust us’ is not acceptable,” he said.

Donald Trump celebrated the news that Apple had fulfilled his request to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for Maps app users in the US following an executive order that came amid rising trade tensions between the US and Canada.
The Pentagon introduced guidelines for the mandatory new ⁠testosterone deficiency screening required for service members age 30 and older, a policy introduced by Pete Hegseth last month.

articles.title: The US and Venezuela: a century-old relationship drenched in oil
articles.summary: A visual look at how Washington’s relationship with Caracas has gone from cordial to ‘predatory’
articles.byline: Oliver Holmes, Seán Clarke and Lucy Swan

blocks.text: Written in the middle of the last century, the US Department of State memo conveys its message in a curt and undiplomatically honest tone: the glue that binds Washington to Caracas is, and is always likely to be, oil.
“All US policies toward Venezuela are affected in greater or less degree by the objective of assuring an adequate supply of petroleum for the US,” the 1950 document reads.

Decades later, little appears to have changed. After a brazen night-time kidnapping of the country’s leader earlier this year, Donald Trump announced last week that the US was taking majority control over about a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves. That deal, according to the White House, “secures our energy dominance for the next century”. How much it will benefit Venezuelans is yet to be seen.

The country’s importance to the US has been proven time and time again over the past century. Home to what are now known to be the world’s largest known oil reserves, Venezuela kept allied planes, ship and tanks well fuelled during the second world war.

Washington and Caracas largely cooperated over the following decades, with US energy companies heavily involved in Venezuela’s oil industry, and profiting from it immensely. But relations took a nosedive in 1999, when Hugo Chávez became president.

A self-professed socialist and anti-imperialist, Chávez made alliances, and often oil deals, with China, Iran and Russia. Venezuela switched 180 degrees to become a natural adversary of the US, alongside its ally Cuba.

blocks.caption: Hugo Chávez pictured in 2010. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Relations deteriorated further when Chávez was briefly detained by his own military after a deadly crackdown on mass anti-government protests. The attempted overthrow lasted only two days and he was soon back in the presidential palace, accusing Washington of involvement in the failed coup.

Chávez deepened Venezuela’s dependence on oil exports in the years that followed. In 2007, he stepped up his battle with Washington with a wave of nationalisation in which he seized oilfields, including those that US firms had operated.

Caracas had nationalised the oil industry decades before, but had allowed US companies to profit from the extraction. Under Chávez’s new terms, however, the state oil company was given control of a majority share and foreign firms were offered minority stakes.
Among US oil companies, Chevron agreed to the worse terms, but ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips refused and were in effect pushed out of the industry.

Only Chevron, the second largest US oil company, has continued to operate in the country. ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips engaged in a years-long legal battle with Venezuela for compensation. The World Bank’s international centre for the settlement of investment disputes awarded them billions of dollars, but Venezuela has never paid the money in full.

Still, much of the country’s oil infrastructure was built with foreign involvement, and foreign companies are still active in the exploitation of the fields, among them Russian, Chinese and Cuban firms, as well as UK and European companies, including Shell, BP, Italy’s Eni and Spain’s Repsol.
When Chávez died in 2013, Nicolás Maduro rose to power. The former bus driver had worked as his foreign minister and continued an antagonistic policy towards the US.

Maduro’s rule was considered dictatorial. The UN estimated in 2019 that more than 20,000 Venezuelans had died in extrajudicial killings. Key institutions, such as the judiciary, were eroded under Maduro and the rule of law deteriorated.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Venezuela’s government protesting in Caracas on 3 January 2026 after the US seized Nicolás Maduro.

blocks.text: The US has portrayed the Maduro government as illegitimate. A Washington-led sanctions campaign compounded widespread corruption, and the Venezuelan economy suffered.
It did not help the relationship that Maduro kept close ties with Moscow and Beijing. About 80% of the crude oil Venezuela produced was exported to China before the US-imposed blockade in December.
China is the world’s biggest oil importer, and takes the shipments as repayment for loans it previously gave to Caracas, often at low prices.

Since the start of his second term, Donald Trump had repeatedly called for Maduro to be ousted, accusing him of sending drugs and criminals to the US – a claim experts say lacks evidence. He also claimed Maduro was stealing US oil, a reference to Chávez’s seizure.
In July last year, Washington announced a $50m (£37m) bounty on Maduro’s head, accusing him of being one of the biggest drug traffickers in the world.

Trump’s administration began to carry out airstrikes against alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean Sea and then to seize Venezuelan tankers, while building up the US military presence in the waters surrounding the country.

Trump gave Maduro an ultimatum to relinquish power in late November, offering him safe passage out of the country. But Maduro refused the offer, telling supporters he did not want “a slave’s peace” and accusing the US of wanting control of his country’s oil reserves.
This January, in the ultimate expression of a relationship breakdown, US forces carried out a pre-dawn raid on Caracas, capturing Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who are now on trial in New York.
Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, initially denounced Maduro’s capture as a kidnapping, but has since shown she is willing to work with Washington.

In the aftermath of Maduro’s abduction, Trump said the US would take control of Venezuela’s oil industry. And in August, after months of secret talks, Washington’s longstanding oil-focused policy was on display again when the US president announced the agreement to control millions of barrels of oil.

A White House press release described the agreement as the “biggest oil deal in world history” that gave the US government “powerful governance rights” over reserves. Further down in the document, the White House claimed private-sector growth would help drive a democratic transition in Venezuela, though few in Caracas will be holding their breath. Rodríguez has already been forced to defend herself against claims she is surrendering Venezuela’s natural resources to a foreign power.

One prominent Venezuelan economist has called the deal “predatory”, saying it was “done at gunpoint”. Francisco Rodríguez wrote that Washington’s actions in Venezuela had turned the country into “a protectorate in all but name”.
“Trying to run a country from the capital of an imperial power has been tried before,” he said. “And it has not ended well.”
​Additional reporting by Jillian Ambrose

articles.title: Palestinian teens killed during settler attack on West Bank village, officials say
articles.summary: Al-Mughayyir's council says they were trying to stop settlers stealing sheep, but the Israeli military says they threw stones at its troops.

blocks.text: Funerals have taken place for two Palestinian teenagers who local officials say were killed by Israeli settlers and soldiers in an attack on their village in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday.
The village council in al-Mughayyir told the BBC that Omar al-Nassan, 19, and Khalil Abu Alia, 16, were killed as they tried to stop Israeli settlers stealing sheep and that confrontations broke out.
The Israeli military stated that its forces had entered the village to provide security for an Israeli civilian and police trying to retrieve livestock.
It said they fired on and struck what it called "key instigators" of a "violent disturbance", in which Palestinians threw stones at its troops.
The deaths come amid a recent surge in settler violence in the West Bank, with more than three attacks per day on average recorded by the UN so far this year.
Al-Mughayyir, near Ramallah, has seen repeated settler attacks.

At least 81 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN's figures. At least 23 of those deaths have occurred in the context of settler attacks.
Three Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, the UN says.
The Israeli military has faced mounting criticism for actively participating in settler attacks on Palestinians, standing by, or failing to prosecute those responsible.

On Thursday, Israel's police force said a 19-year-old settler had been arrested on suspicion of participating in an attack on the Palestinian village of Qusra on Saturday. It marks the first such arrest in weeks of attacks on Qusra.
Dozens of masked settlers descended on the village, surrounding a house while Palestinians were trapped inside, and throwing stones.

Israeli soldiers who were deployed to the scene reportedly detained the trapped Palestinians but not the settlers, allowing them to leave. The Israeli military said troops removed "rioters" and protected residents.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
The settlements are illegal under international law.
In a separate development on Wednesday, Israeli forces demolished the Palestinian village of Khirbet al-Tabban, in the Masafer Yatta area.
Israeli human rights group B'Tselem said the village's 70 residents, including 28 children, were given no warning prior to the demolition and were not allowed to remove their property.
It described the demolition as the most significant in Masafer Yatta since May 2025.
In the 1980s, the Israeli military declared about 3,000 hectares in the South Hebron Hills, which includes Masafer Yatta, as a restricted firing zone for training purposes.
The military says the Palestinian homes there have been built illegally.

In 2022, Israel's Supreme Court ruled to allow the demolition of homes in the firing zone and the expulsion of their residents, who had argued that such a move violated international law and that their families had been living there since before the State of Israel was established.

B'Tselem says Khirbet al-Tabban is the 66th Palestinian community to be expelled by Israeli authorities since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023, which it alleges is part of a campaign of "ethnic cleansing" being carried out in the West Bank.

articles.title: 'Supersized' El Nino could be strongest on record, UN says
articles.summary: The current El Nino could end up being the strongest since records began 40 years ago, the UN warns. It says the phenomenon is being "supersized" thanks to exceptionally warm temperatures in the…

image.caption: El Nino is increasing the risks of extreme heat, drought and floods, according to the UNImage: Myo Kyaw Soe/Xinhua News Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: The El Nino weather phenomenon is set to intensify and will almost certainly last until February next year, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in an update Thursday.

The UN weather agency warned El Nino would develop into a "very strong" event in the coming months, heightening the risks of extreme heat, drought and flooding while threatening livelihoods and economies.

"El Nino is being supersized before our eyes," UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said in a statement. "The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up."

WMO head Celeste Saulo told a press conference in Geneva that, on the current trajectory, the El Nino, "may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began, so literally off the charts we have used for the past four decades."
What is El Nino?

El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon that happens every two to seven years and is not caused by climate change. But scientists say it can worsen the impacts of global heating caused by the continued burning of fossil fuels.
The WMO classifies El Nino events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong, with the current El Nino set to reach the highest intensity level on that scale.
This winter's El Nino could be strongest on record
The phenomenon begins with the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, triggering changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns around the world.
For example, it often brings dry conditions and drought to Australia, Indonesia and parts of the Amazon, while East Africa and the southern US may experience heavy rainfall.
El Ninos typically begin between March and June, peaking toward the end of the year and lasting around nine to 12 months.
Ocean temperatures already 'exceptionally' high

WMO head Saulo said there was "an exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100% that El Nino will persist through to February 2027," adding that it was the first time the organization had "expressed such a degree of certainty. "

Sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific region , which drive El Nino and reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometers away, are already well above average and continuing to rise, according to the UN agency.
"Subsurface ocean temps are also exceptionally high and in some areas more than 8 degrees Celsius above normal during July and early August," Saulo said.
While El Nino is expected to peak toward the end of the year, its knock-on effects will likely last well into 2027, she added.
Global average temperatures are often particularly high the year after an El Nino. For example, the 2023-2024 El Nino contributed to 2024 being the warmest year on record.
"We should not be surprised if this record is broken," Saulo said.
How climate change is teaming up with 'Super El Nino'
'We have no time to lose'
Saulo said droughts, floods and extreme heat were already causing disruption and devastation, and warned these impacts would "multiply and cascade as El Nino intensifies."

Saulo stressed that the weather phenomenon would "deliver a major blow to communities, economies and supply chains across the globe" and called for preparations to safeguard climate-sensitive sectors.
"We have no time to lose," she said.

articles.title: 'Beautiful, vibrant' Disney star Carla Jeffery dies at 33
articles.summary: Jeffery was known for playing cheerleader Bree in 2018 Disney Channel movie Zombies and two sequels.

blocks.text: US actress Carla Jeffery, who was known for appearing in 2018 Disney Channel movie Zombies and two sequels, has died at the age of 33.
Announcing the news, her agent Carla Alexander described her as a "beautiful, vibrant and incredibly talented woman whose radiant smile could light up any room".

Jeffery played cheerleader Bree in Zombies and its follow-ups in 2020 and 2022, and previously had a recurring role in Curb Your Enthusiasm as one of the Black family, who moved in with Larry David after Hurricane Katrina.
No cause of death has been given.
Her management company Alexanders Talent wrote on Instagram, external: "Our hearts are broken as we mourn the loss of our beloved Carla Jeffery.

"For more than 20 years, Carla was part of the Alexanders Talent Management family and watching her grow from a talented young girl into the beautiful, vibrant woman and actress she became was an incredible privilege.
"We will remember her infectious smile, her laughter, her talent, and the beautiful light she carried everywhere she went.

"Our deepest love and condolences are with Carla's family and loved ones. We ask that their privacy be respected during this incredibly difficult time. Rest beautifully, Carla. You will be deeply missed and forever loved."
Jeffery's twin brother Carlon, who is also an actor, reposted that statement as well as a clip of his sister on a beach and a screenshot of an undated text message.
"Hey Sis, call me back when you get this. I was just calling to see how your day went! I love you to the moon & back sis," it read.

"I just want you to know how proud I am of you. Your resilience, your grace, your infectious smile that lights up a room. You are truly a light that shines bright. Don't let anyone dim that light, even yourself.

"The light you carry is special and must be protected at all times. You are the best sister a brother could ask for. Pray we continue to grow closer to one another along this journey. I got your back in this life and the next."
Her co-stars also paid tribute, with Chandler Kinney, who played Willa in Zombies, writing that the actress's death "doesn't feel real".
"Carla. The sweetest, most sparkly gal. You made every day better and brighter with your infectious positivity," Kinney wrote.

"I think part of why you brought such effervescence to Bree (aside from your immense talent) is because that's really who you were in your heart; a bubbly, vivacious heart-of-gold cheerleader who loved nothing more than to uplift those around her."
Milo Manheim, who played Zed, shared a series of photos with the caption: "Love you Carlaboo, the sweetest, kindest, most loving person."
