articles.title: UN warns of 'supersized' El Niño as countries prepare for impact
articles.summary: The WMO has warned that the natural weather phenomenon could bring disruption to global economies.
articles.byline: Esme Stallard, Mark Poynting and Becky Dale, Yvette Tan, Tiffanie Turnbull and Nikita Yadav

blocks.text: Image source, Florian Plaucheur/AFP via Getty Images
El Niño brought intense flooding and landslides to southern Brazil in 2024
ByEsme Stallardsenior climate and science reporterMark Poynting and Becky DaleBBC Verify and Yvette Tan, Tiffanie Turnbull and Nikita Yadav
The world has entered a "danger zone of extreme weather" as the impacts of El Niño start to be felt globally, UN head António Guterres has warned.

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has released the latest data on the natural weather phenomenon showing it could be the strongest for more than 70 years and last until at least February 2027.
El Niño changes weather patterns around the world, pushing some regions into drought whilst others experience stronger typhoons and flooding.
Forecasters also say El Niño will boost temperatures in some places, coming on top of rising heat globally from human-induced climate change.
"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," Guterres said.

The BBC spoke with governments and scientists about the measures being taken globally to reduce the risk of deaths, displacement and environmental damage. Early warning systems have been strengthened and deployment of pre-emptive medical assistance, but the strength of this particular event has raised serious concerns particularly for vulnerable groups.
The WMO - a UN agency - said it has undertaken a "major mobilisation" to try to circulate its forecasts of potential extreme weather events, linked to El Niño, to as many communities as possible.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo warned: "El Niño has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world."
El Niño is a natural weather phenomenon that develops in the Pacific Ocean and is linked to a change in wind patterns. It allows warm water to spread eastwards and releases heat into the atmosphere.
Sea temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific have risen sharply in recent months - a clear sign of a strengthening El Niño.
In the Pacific's key monitoring region, surface temperatures have been well over 2C above average in recent weeks, putting it on track to be declared a "very strong" event.
But it is expected to surpass even that marker. Monthly sea surface temperatures could get close to 4C above average, forecasts suggest.
This would make it the strongest El Niño since at least 1950, by potentially a large margin.

blocks.caption: A line graph with the caption "El Nino is forecast to be very strong" and sub-headline "Sea surface temperature and forecast temperature in the tropical Pacific compared with 1991-2020 monthly average. A curved line from January 2026 rising to show +2C by July 2026, and then a forecast line from…

blocks.text: Temperatures are even more exceptional below the surface of the Pacific - in places more than 8C above average.
Above-normal sea temperatures are also expected in other parts of the world including the Indian Ocean, tropical Atlantic and around parts of the Australian coast.
With its rich marine life, changes in ocean heat are of particular concern to Australia.
It has been plagued by marine heatwaves in recent years - driven by climate change.
El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it tends to bring the kind of extreme heat which also drives those disasters, Dr Alistair Hobday, chief researcher at Australia's science agency, told the BBC.
This year, marine heatwave forecasts indicate the Great Barrier Reef will be spared the worst of the conditions, giving coral there more time to recover.
"[But] Southern Australia is getting slammed," said Hobday.
Last time a marine heatwave hit South Australia and Tasmania, there were starving penguins, fish kills, suffocating algae outbreaks, and jellyfish invasions.

Australia has recently introduced early warning systems for marine crises - this gives time for financial relief for fisheries to be established, relocation of crucial species and increased coral monitoring.
But this event is shaping up to be unprecedented - and Hobday admits he is quite worried.

blocks.caption: Two maps showing sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean. The map from December 2025 shows cooler-than-usual conditions, marked in blue, indicating a La Niña. The map from July 2026 shows much warmer-than-usual conditions, marked in red, indicating an El Niño.

blocks.text: Reduced rainfall brings drought and trade disruption
While the impacts on global weather are likely to be felt well into 2027, the WMO expects significant changes in rainfall patterns over the next few months.
Drier-than-usual conditions are forecast across large areas of South East Asia, Central America and northern parts of South America, increasing the risk of droughts and wildfires.
On Thursday, the number of vessels passing through the Panama Canal will be reduced by more than 10% in anticipation of lower rainfall.
About 14,000 ships per year use the artificial waterway - as well as being a crucial route for global trade, it is also a key source of income for Panama, bringing in about $3bn (£2.2bn) a year.

Indonesia is racing to contain wildfires that have burned more than 107,000 hectares of land nationwide this dry season. Like some other parts of South East Asia, it is facing a longer season this year.
A resident in Central Kalimantan told BBC News Indonesia he had been experiencing wildfires "for more than a month".
"The smoke has become quite thick. When we step outside, our eyes start to sting. The smell of the smoke is also quite strong," said Darwin Romy.

Authorities have said they are deploying cloud-seeding aircraft to trigger rains to extinguish these fires, and its government has promised resources to contain the fire and arrested dozens over allegations of using it to clear land.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Countries in Southern Africa, like Botswana, experienced severe drought during the last El Niño event

blocks.text: Image source, Monirul Bhuiyan/AFP via Getty Images
Countries in Southern Africa, like Botswana, experienced severe drought during the last El Niño event
Stronger typhoons and landslide risk
Thousands of miles away, China is expecting seven typhoons to make landfall in this year alone – something the country's experts have said is linked to the effects of a super El Niño.
In July alone, China experienced three typhoons - Bavi, Noul and Maysak - which left dozens dead.
And in August, more than 1m people were forced to evacuate their homes as Typhoon Dolphin hit – bringing heavy rains and strong winds.
Similarly, wetter-than-average weather is expected in parts of eastern Africa, southern Brazil and the southern US, raising the chances of flooding.

blocks.caption: Map of typical effects of El Niño episodes on precipitation patterns for each region. Key trends are drying in many equatorial regions (northern South America, central Africa, South East Asia and Australia), marked in brown. Southern United States generally becomes wetter than normal, marked in g…

blocks.text: "We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," said Prof Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the WMO.

This is all happening on top of long-term human-caused warming, making the impacts potentially more intense. Some scientists believe climate change could even be making El Niño events stronger, but this is not yet certain.
Peru is particularly vulnerable to El Niño, as its coastline borders the eastern Pacific.

Parts of the country, along with Ecuador and parts of Brazil, have previously experienced increased rainfall, resulting in flash flooding and landslides, particularly in urban centres where the water is less able to drain away.

Miguel Aréstegui, climate resilience lead at Practical Action, which helps countries prepare for extreme weather, said "we are significantly concerned, but that concern needs to translate into preparedness rather than alarm."

He said Practical Action had been working with partners over recent years to make sure the public had better access to early warning systems, including sharing information on river levels, flood risks and weather forecasts.

At the end of last month, the US announced it was deploying the vessel USNS Comfort to the Peruvian coast to provide additional medical assistance and technical equipment for when El Niño reaches its peak.

However, Aréstegui said El Niño "does not arrive in a vacuum". There are bigger, structural issues that make these events worse and which take much longer to resolve such as "housing in exposed areas, fragile water and sanitation systems, and a weak healthcare system", he said.

articles.title: DMW told to protect PH seafarers after deadly Strait of Hormuz attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Several senators on Thursday urged the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) to ensure the safety and protection of Filipino seafarers in high-risk areas following the death of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Several senators on Thursday urged the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) to ensure the safety and protection of Filipino seafarers in high-risk areas following the death of two Filipino crew members in an attack on a Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Sen. Raffy Tulfo both called for stronger safety measures for Filipino seafarers and assistance for those affected by the incident.

Their statements came after the DMW confirmed that two Filipino seafarers were killed after the Saudi-flagged M/V SIDR was hit by unknown projectiles while about to traverse the Strait of Hormuz on Aug. 31.
Fourteen other Filipino crew members aboard the vessel survived the incident unharmed.

“The deaths of two Filipino seafarers following an attack on a Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker while transiting the Strait of Hormuz earlier this week are deeply unfortunate. The DMW should ensure that the families of the victims, including those who survived the attack, immediately receive all the necessary assistance during this difficult time,” Gatchalian said in a statement.

“Hindi pa tapos ang kaguluhan sa Middle East kaya kailangang siguraduhin ng gobyerno ang kaligtasan ng lahat ng OFWs sa rehiyon, kabilang ang mga Pilipinong marino. Prayoridad dapat ang mahigpit na pagpapatupad ng safety protocols sa mga lugar at bansang itinuturing na high-risk areas,” the Senate president added.

(The conflict in the Middle East is not yet over, so the government must ensure the safety of all OFWs in the region, including Filipino seafarers. Strict implementation of safety protocols should be a priority in areas and countries considered high-risk areas.)

Tulfo, chairperson of the Senate Committee on Migrant Workers, likewise expressed his sadness over the incident and said his office is coordinating with the DMW to ensure the safety and welfare of the Filipino seafarers who survived.

“Sisikapin nating matiyak na sila ay ma-repatriate sa lalong madaling panahon at maibigay sa kanila ang lahat ng kinakailangang tulong, gayundin sa mga pamilya ng ating mga kababayang nasawi,” Tulfo said in a separate statement.
(We will work to ensure that they are repatriated as soon as possible and provided with all the necessary assistance, as well as the families of our fellow Filipinos who died.)

Tulfo also called on the DMW to ensure that manning agencies and shipping companies respect and enforce the seafarers’ “Right to Refuse Sailing” in high-risk areas such as the Strait of Hormuz without putting their entitlements and benefits at risk.
He said seafarers should also give informed consent and be properly briefed on the security risks before boarding and sailing.
Meanwhile, the DMW has likewise vowed support to the families and the colleagues affected by the incident, along with coordination with authorities.
The DMW also earlier said that it was arranging for the repatriation of the Filipino seafarers. /gsg

articles.title: Marcos orders aid for kin of PH seafarers killed in Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered immediate assistance for the families of two Filipino seafarers who died following a security incident in the Strait of Hormuz, Palace…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered immediate assistance for the families of two Filipino seafarers who died following a security incident in the Strait of Hormuz, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said on Thursday.

Saudi Arabian shipping company Bari confirmed on Wednesday evening the deaths of the seafarers after its crude oil vessel SIDR was involved in a security incident before transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Aug. 31 at 11:40 a.m.

“Unang-una po nakikiramay po ang Pangulo at ang administrasyon sa pamilya ng dalawang seafarer mula sa Cabuyao, Laguna at Daanbantayan, Cebu. At nag-utos na po ang Pangulo, agad-agad na tulungan ang mga pamilya ng dalawa nating kababayan na nasawi at ibigay lahat ng kailangan nila pati ang benepisyo, compensation, insurance proceeds na naaangkop na dapat ibigay sa ating kababayan na nasawi,” said Castro at a briefing.

(First and foremost, the President and the administration extend their condolences to the families of the two seafarers from Cabuyao, Laguna, and Daanbantayan, Cebu. The President has also ordered immediate assistance for the families of our two fellow citizens who perished, as well as the provision of all necessary support—including the benefits, compensation, and insurance proceeds—rightfully due to them.)
“Hindi po pababayaan ng gobyerno, ng pamahalaan, ‘yung naiwan ng dalawa nating kababatan. Muli, nakikiramay po kami sa pamilya ng dalawa po nating sefarers,” she continued.
(The government will not neglect the families left behind by our two fellow citizens. Once again, we extend our condolences to the families of our two seafarers.)
According to Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac, the ship had 16 Filipino seafarers aboard when a fire broke out after projectiles hit.
The ship has since been grounded off the coast of Oman, where the Filipino seafarers, including the deceased, were disembarked, he said in an online presser.
He said the 14 other seafarers were unharmed, and the agency is arranging their repatriation. /dl

articles.title: Nepal floods: Four hours under the rubble, 97 years above it
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Guna Maya Bohara sometimes sings at night. It is the same bhajan—Hare Ram, Hare Krishna—that she used to sing during her stay at the elderly care home and during temple visits.…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Guna Maya Bohara sometimes sings at night. It is the same bhajan—Hare Ram, Hare Krishna—that she used to sing during her stay at the elderly care home and during temple visits. Sometimes after singing, she asks a question: “Why did the water hit me?” The 97-year-old has asked the question more than once.

Apart from that, however, Bohara has mostly stopped speaking. Bohara is currently receiving treatment at Bir Hospital in Kathmandu. Her arms and legs have turned black and blue. She sometimes moves suddenly, almost involuntarily. She lies still for a while. Then another movement breaks the stillness. Doctors have diagnosed her with acute stress disorder.

On the morning of August 26, Bohara was in her room on the ground floor of the elderly care home at Devighat, a riverside town in Nuwakot. She was unaware that a glacier had collapsed high in the Himalayas. The collapse triggered a landslide, sending water and debris thundering down into the Trishuli River. The furious waters reached the ground floor, where Bohara was. It pushed her to the edge of the ground floor and left her there. The current was less intense on this side of the floor, witnesses say. Some of those caught in the current did not survive.

Nepal Police and Nepali Army personnel worked for about four hours to reach her, carefully clearing rubble carefully so as not to injure anyone still buried beneath it. Bohara’s relatives also rushed to the site. They brought a JCB excavator. With it, they worked together to move the debris away, inch by inch — moving, moving, moving, Dipak, Bohara’s great nephew, remembers, until there was space to lift her clear in its bucket.
Last Wednesday’s floods, however, were only the latest of Bohara’s ordeals in her long life.

At 97, Bohara has outlived her husband by 81 years. She was eight when she married him in Nuwakot’s Suryagadhi, at a time when child marriage was common practice. At 83, she chose on her own to move into a nursing home—Senior Citizens Welfare Foundation—in Devighat, close enough that her nieces could visit daily. She liked it there, among people her own age and looked forward to birthdays—her own and other residents—celebrated together.

By her twenties, she had already outlived nearly everyone who shared her blood: her husband, eight years into their marriage; both her parents, four years after that; her only brother, sometime later.
She never had children of her own.

What she had instead was her husband’s family, his three brothers, their wives, and in time their children. She raised thirteen nephews, twelve nieces as her own, sending every one of them to school, packing roasted maize for their lunch. Dipak says her family regards women of her generation as having quietly carried entire households through decades few now remember.
Bohara is the last of her generation left in the family.

Physically, she has proved more resilient than her age might lead one to expect. She has a pre-existing disability in her legs and an injury to her hand, caused by the torrents of water, is still being assessed, a CT scan and an X-ray pending. She survived on fruit juice for the first two days and has since moved to milk and full meals, Dipak said.

Of the people who share Guna Maya Bohara’s blood, none remain. Of the people who call her family, the nephews and nieces she once packed lunches for, there are twenty-five now, and they take turns at her bedside, waiting.

Dipak said that Bohara has not stopped asking, “Why did the water hit me?” He has tried to explain to her—more simply than what actually happened—that a lake, Gosaikunda, had burst far above them. She seems to understand, for a while. But hours later, she asks again: “Why did the water hit me?” /dl

articles.title: Filipinos’ visa-free stay in Thailand back to 30 days
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Thailand’s 60-day visa exemption will be replaced with 30-day visa free stays for tourists from 60 countries, including the Philippines, starting September 15, according to the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Thailand’s 60-day visa exemption will be replaced with 30-day visa free stays for tourists from 60 countries, including the Philippines, starting September 15, according to the Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT).

“From 15 September 2026, travelers previously covered by the 60-day visa exemption will instead be subject to the applicable 30-day visa exemption, 15-day visa exemption, Visa on Arrival, or other relevant entry arrangements, depending on nationality,” the TAT said, citing the measure published in Thailand’s Royal Gazette on August 31.
The change effectively halves the visa-free period that Filipinos have enjoyed since Thailand expanded its visa-exemption policy in July 2024.
For most Filipino tourists, however, the change is unlikely to affect typical short trips, as stays of up to 30 days will remain visa-free.
From September 15, passport holders from the following 60 countries and territories may enter Thailand visa-free for tourism and stay up to 30 days:

Australia, Austria, Bahrain, Belgium, Bhutan, Brunei, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Fiji, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, India, Indonesia, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malaysia, Maldives, Malta, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Oman, Philippines, Poland, Portugal, Qatar, Romania, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Taiwan, Turkey, Ukraine, United Arab Emirates, United Kingdom, and the United States.
TAT also explained that those using 30-day visa exemptions may enter through land-border immigration checkpoints no more than twice per calendar year. /dl

articles.title: NBI probes Russian national over yacht documents in Samar
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has taken custody of a Russian national after authorities found inconsistencies in his documents and questioned the circumstances…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has taken custody of a Russian national after authorities found inconsistencies in his documents and questioned the circumstances surrounding his entry into the Philippines aboard a sailing yacht that had earlier encountered engine trouble off Samar.

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said the yacht INGRID MARMARIS was towed on Aug. 29 to waters off Amandayehan, Basey, Samar, where its personnel and an NBI team inspected the vessel, its documents, and the Russian’s travel documents.
The yacht had earlier required assistance after experiencing engine trouble in waters off Marabut, Samar.
PCG search and rescue personnel aboard HSRB-031 began towing operations at about 7:30 a.m. on Aug. 29, bringing the vessel to the vicinity of Amandayehan.

At about 9 a.m., four NBI personnel from its Tacloban office arrived at the PCG motorpool area. The yacht, meanwhile, reached the area off Amandayehan at around 9:20 a.m., according to the PCG progress report.

About an hour later, PCG and NBI personnel boarded the yacht to inspect its documents, verify the identity and travel documents of its occupant, and examine other items relevant to the ongoing investigation.
During the inspection, the NBI team noted several inconsistencies and questionable circumstances in documents presented by Alexey Popov, a Russian national, according to the PCG.
The NBI also raised concerns over the circumstances of Popov’s entry into the Philippines, citing an apparent lack of appropriate documentation and/or authorization from relevant government agencies.
Popov was subsequently invited to proceed to the NBI office in Tacloban City for further investigation and verification.

At around 11:30 a.m., PCG and NBI personnel, together with Popov, left the yacht and proceeded to the NBI office. They arrived at about 12:05 p.m., where Popov was placed under NBI custody pending further investigation and coordination with other government agencies.
The PCG has taken custody of INGRID MARMARIS, which will be secured while the case is under evaluation.
The PCG said its personnel are continuing to coordinate with the NBI and other concerned agencies while maintaining the vessel’s security and preserving the investigation’s integrity./coa

articles.title: Russia to close branches of Germany's Goethe-Institut
articles.summary: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov announced the move in statements carried by Russian newswires. It comes after Germany said it would close the Russian House in Berlin.

image.caption: The Goethe-Institut offers courses in German language and culture Image: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said branches of Germany's Goethe-Institut would be closed on Russian territory.

Lavrov, in remarks carried by Russian news agencies TASS and Interfax, said Goethe-Institut locations would be closed in the Russian cities of Moscow, St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg. The statement came after Germany said Russia was responsible for a ‌drone ⁠incident at ⁠the Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Germany's response included closing a Russian cultural center in Berlin and a Russian consulate in Bonn. On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Moscow for the incident.

"They deliberately took this step — they could not have failed to understand — which means the end of their cultural presence in Russia," Lavrov said, according to state news agency TASS. He added the centers had remained open "despite all the Ukrainian complications in our relations with the West."

Russia's first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, shortly after the collapse of the Soviet Union. In 2018, Russia ordered the closure of the British Council following a diplomatic dispute with the UK.
On Wednesday, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko said Moscow would retaliate "very soon" over Germany's closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn.

articles.title: Trump $1 coin makes him first living president on US currency in a century
articles.summary: The US Mint special edition is stamped with a portrait of Trump alongside the words "LIBERTY" and "IN GOD WE TRUST"

blocks.text: Donald Trump's portrait has made its way on to a US coin - the first time a living president has appeared on American currency in a century.
On Wednesday, the US Mint launched the $1 coin with a portrait of Trump alongside the words "LIBERTY" and "IN GOD WE TRUST", to celebrate America's 250th anniversary.
The special-edition coin captures "the spirit, pride, and legacy of a nation approaching its landmark anniversary", the US Mint said.

The coins - priced at $61 (£45) for a roll of 25 and $154.50 for a bag of 100 - were "not currently in stock" on the mint's website within hours of going on sale. The BBC has contacted the US Mint, the Treasury and the White House for further details.

The coin has been "created to celebrate this historic national milestone" with a "once-in-a-generation anniversary design destined to become a standout addition to modern collections", the US Mint said.
They are also being sold in vending machines at the US Mint store in Washington DC.
While the coins have a golden colour they do not contain any actual gold. According to the US Mint, they are 88.5% copper with the balance being made up of zinc, manganese and nickel.

articles.title: AirAsia seals first codeshare with Pegasus, bridges Asia and Europe
articles.summary: AirAsia has signed its first-ever codeshare agreement, teaming up with Turkey’s largest low-cost carrier, Pegasus Airlines, to open seamless connections between Southeast Asia and Europe…

blocks.text: AirAsia has signed its first-ever codeshare agreement, teaming up with Turkey’s largest low-cost carrier, Pegasus Airlines, to open seamless connections between Southeast Asia and Europe through Istanbul, the two airlines announced at AirAsia’s headquarters in Sepang, Malaysia, on Wednesday.

The partnership, unveiled before members of the media and witnessed by Turkey’s ambassador to Malaysia Nevzat Uyanık, will progressively open access to more than 100 routes between Asia and Europe, combining AirAsia’s Southeast Asian network with Pegasus’s reach across Europe from its hub at Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen Airport.

Five European destinations will be added from launch: Stansted (London), Vnukovo (Moscow), Esenboğa (Ankara), Zurich and Athens, all connecting through Kuala Lumpur and Istanbul. AirAsia will also lift its Kuala Lumpur–Istanbul frequency from four times weekly to daily by February 2027, up from the direct link AirAsia X has operated since November 2025.

blocks.caption: Farouk Kamal

blocks.text: Opening the event, Farouk Kamal, Deputy Group Chief Executive Officer of AirAsia Group Berhad, told guests the tie-up “marks the start of many more opportunities to come between the two airlines” and reaffirmed the group’s ambition to become the world’s first low-cost network carrier.
He said he had personally tried the product being announced on a trip last year and described the experience as “great” before handing over to colleagues to reveal the details on stage.

blocks.caption: AirAsia Seals First Codeshare With Pegasus, Bridges Asia and Europe

blocks.text: ‘Meaningful milestone’ in 25th year
In a statement accompanying the announcement, Bo Lingam, Group CEO of AirAsia Group, said the codeshare was a landmark moment as the airline marks its 25th anniversary.

“As AirAsia’s first-ever codeshare, this partnership marks a meaningful milestone in our 25th year and the next chapter in our evolution from a leading Asean low-cost carrier into a truly global travel network,” he said. “By connecting our extensive network across Asia with Pegasus’s strong European network from Istanbul, spanning 160 destinations across 56 countries, we are making Europe more accessible to our guests while creating a gateway for European travelers to discover Asean and beyond.”

blocks.caption: Elifnur Dogruoz

blocks.text: On stage representing Pegasus was Elifnur Dogruoz, the airline’s Group Head of Network Planning and Airline Collaborations, who told the audience the two carriers shared a common philosophy despite operating at opposite ends of Asia.

“At AirAsia your promise is ‘now everyone can fly.’ At Pegasus we say everyone has the right to fly – different words, but the same belief that air travel should be accessible for more people across more places,” she said, adding that Sabiha Gökçen was “more than a home” for Pegasus and a key gateway between Europe and Asia, just as Kuala Lumpur was for AirAsia.

blocks.caption: AirAsia Seals First Codeshare With Pegasus, Bridges Asia and Europe

blocks.text: She thanked Malaysia’s civil aviation authorities and airport operators for supporting the deal.
Pegasus chief executive Güliz Öztürk, who also did not attend the Kuala Lumpur event, added in a statement issued alongside the announcement:

“Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen is a natural connecting point between Europe and Asia. That AirAsia’s first-ever codeshare is with Pegasus Airlines is a source of pride: it reflects the network we have built from Istanbul over two decades and a hub that continues to grow. Our guests can now reach Kuala Lumpur seamlessly and, from there, AirAsia’s network of more than 140 destinations across Asia-Pacific.”

blocks.caption: Amanda Woo

blocks.text: Presenting the mechanics of the partnership to media, AirAsia’s Chief Commercial Officer, Amanda Woo, explained that travelers booking through AirAsia will receive both boarding passes at check-in, with baggage checked straight through to their final destination.

“One journey, one itinerary, a seamless experience,” she said, describing how a passenger flying from Kuala Lumpur to Athens via Istanbul would simply follow the signs to their next gate in Istanbul without needing to check in again or collect their bags.

Woo said the combined network would ultimately connect more than 100 routes between Asia and Europe and confirmed a further sweetener for early bookers: AirAsia will raise its Kuala Lumpur–Istanbul service from four times weekly to daily next year to meet expected demand.

The new connectivity also runs in reverse, with European travelers able to connect through Istanbul to Kuala Lumpur and onwards across AirAsia’s Fly-Thru network spanning Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, China, Vietnam and beyond. /dl

articles.title: Seven Thai airlines offer free 10kg fruit check-in at 20 airports
articles.summary: BANGKOK — Passengers can check one 10kg box of fresh fruit for free at 20 Thai airports under a year-long scheme that began on September 1. Seven airlines will allow passengers to check up to…

blocks.text: BANGKOK — Passengers can check one 10kg box of fresh fruit for free at 20 Thai airports under a year-long scheme that began on September 1.
Seven airlines will allow passengers to check up to 10 kilograms of fresh fruit into the aircraft hold free of charge under a year-long program covering 20 airports across Thailand.

The Commerce Ministry, through the Department of Internal Trade, has signed a cooperation agreement with the Transport Ministry’s Department of Airports and seven airline partners: Thai Airways International, Thai AirAsia, Bangkok Airways, Nok Air, Thai Lion Air, Thai Vietjet Air and EZY Airlines.

blocks.caption: Seven airlines offer free 10kg fruit check-in at 20 airports

blocks.text: The program will run from September 1, 2026, to August 31, 2027, and is intended to help farmers distribute seasonal produce, encourage consumption of Thai fruit and support domestic tourism.

Banjongjitt Angsusingh, adviser to the commerce minister, said the government was seeking a wider range of distribution channels for agricultural produce entering the market. Her English name and title follow the Commerce Ministry’s official listing.

The cooperation would use the capabilities of airports and airlines to help travellers carry fruit home from producing areas and tourism destinations without having to pay additional transport charges, she said.

blocks.caption: Seven airlines offer free 10kg fruit check-in at 20 airports

blocks.text: One free 10kg box per passenger
Passengers using the service will be entitled to one standard fruit box with a maximum weight of 10kg.

The Department of Internal Trade will supply the boxes to participating airports from September 1. It will also work with provincial commerce offices to bring farmers into airport sales areas to sell seasonal fruit directly to travellers.
The Department of Airports will provide collection points for the boxes, assist passengers using the service and allocate temporary sales spaces for farmers at airports under its supervision.
The seven partner airlines will carry the fruit in their aircraft holds free of charge, subject to the 10kg limit per passenger, and promote the programme through their communication channels.
EZY Airlines is the official branding used by the participating Thai regional carrier.

blocks.caption: Seven airlines offer free 10kg fruit check-in at 20 airports

blocks.text: Twenty airports join pilot programme
The service will initially be available at airports in:

Nan, Lampang, Tak, Phitsanulok, Loei, Udon Thani, Khon Kaen, Sakon Nakhon, Nakhon Phanom, Roi Et, Ubon Ratchathani, Buri Ram, Prachuap Khiri Khan, Chumphon, Ranong, Surat Thani, Nakhon Si Thammarat, Krabi, Trang and Narathiwat.
Passengers should contact the designated service point at the airport to receive their fruit box before checking it into the hold.
The authorities initially aim to distribute 100,000 boxes, representing capacity for approximately 1,000 tonnes of fruit.

blocks.caption: Seven airlines offer free 10kg fruit check-in at 20 airports

blocks.text: Fresh fruit only, with strict packaging rules
Only fresh fruit will be accepted under the programme. The total weight must not exceed 10kg, and the fruit must be dry and free from moisture.

Passengers must use the official box supplied by the Department of Internal Trade at the airport service point. The container must be securely closed with adhesive tape or straps to prevent ants, insects and foreign objects from entering, as well as to stop liquid or odours from escaping.
Durian and other strongly scented fruit will not be accepted either in the cabin or as checked baggage because their smell could disturb other passengers.
“Before bringing fruit on a flight, passengers should ensure that it is packed properly,” Banjongjitt said.

“Durian and other strongly scented fruit must not be carried on board or placed in the aircraft hold, so that the smell does not disturb other passengers and everyone can enjoy a convenient and smooth journey.” /dl

articles.title: Vietnam arrests deputy minister on bribery charge
articles.summary: HANOI — Vietnamese police arrested a deputy health minister on Wednesday for allegedly accepting huge bribes, part of a probe into a company accused of smuggling medical equipment, authorities…

blocks.text: HANOI — Vietnamese police arrested a deputy health minister on Wednesday for allegedly accepting huge bribes, part of a probe into a company accused of smuggling medical equipment, authorities said.
Communist Vietnam has pursued a high-profile anti-corruption campaign in recent years that has netted dozens of business leaders and senior government figures.

Deputy Health Minister Tran Van Thuan, a leading oncologist in Vietnam, was taken into custody “due to his acceptance of bribes involving a large sum of money”, the public security ministry said in a statement, without specifying the amount.
Thuan, 56, was appointed deputy health minister in 2020 and chairman of the National Medical Council in 2024.

His arrest came as part of a police investigation involving “smuggling” and “violations of accounting regulations causing serious consequences” at Viet My Medical Investment Joint Stock Company, the ministry’s statement said.

Police have arrested two executives and an accountant at the firm, which was allegedly set up to trade, resell and inflate the prices of medical equipment and pharmaceuticals before importing them from Singapore and Hong Kong into Vietnam, state media said.
Police also accuse company leaders of attempting to illegally import medical equipment.
AFP was unable to contact the company for comment.
Vietnam’s sweeping anti-corruption drive, accelerated by President To Lam, has removed many of his opponents, according to analysts, leaving him as the country’s most dominant leader in decades.
In May, former health minister Nguyen Thi Kim Tien was imprisoned for six years over her mismanagement of hospital projects, state media said.
Tien was rocked by corruption scandals in previous years, and was once voted the least popular official by lawmakers in the one-party state. /dl

articles.title: 'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
articles.summary: More than 80 people have been killed in the mob violence, the BBC finds after gathering data from six African nations.

blocks.text: More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries.
The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media.

"They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief.

His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen.

Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread. Social media has amplified these fears.
The recent wave of rumours appears to have started last year in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where similar claims had surfaced in 2008.
They progressively spread across the region to Burundi, Zambia and Tanzania as well as Mozambique, Angola, Malawi and Kenya.
In Zambia, the hearsay about disappearing genitals first gained traction in March when a woman was lynched, going on to spread panic across the border in Tanzania.

At his home in Mpemba near Tunduma, a busy trading town in Tanzania by the border with Zambia, Mgala traces his fingers along the sickle-shaped scar that runs down the right side of his head as he reflects on his traumatic experience.
"If I had known how close I would have come to death on that day, I wouldn't have gone into that restaurant to eat. Only we don't know how close death is," the mechanic says.

He and his friend had gone into Tunduma on 1 April to meet a client about a car sale and decided to eat lunch beforehand. They had not long sat down in the restaurant when they were dragged outside by a mob.
Two smaller scars on his chin and a missing tooth are other visible marks of his ordeal.
Amid the beating, he lost consciousness. Mgala regained awareness in hospital two days later to news that his friend had been killed.
Back at his house where he lives with his wife and their four children, he now walks with a limp and says he also suffers from constant headaches.
He has not been able to return to work at his mechanic shop but says neighbours and friends have helped cover the cost of some of the medicine he needs.

On the same day that Mgala and his friend were attacked, commercial photographer and businessman Michael Silavwe says he witnessed another similar assault in Tunduma, where he says anxiety had been building after videos about stolen genitalia had begun circulating on TikTok.
Outside his shop he saw people running and says he learned that a man had been accused nearby and was being beaten - and later set on fire.
"After they set him on fire, the police arrived at the scene and everyone scattered and ran away," the 23-year-old told the BBC.

In a video of the attack verified by the BBC Global Disinformation Unit and viewed more than 100,000 times across TikTok and Facebook, a group is seen beating a man while demanding he return the victim's allegedly stolen genitals.
"Those incidents kept escalating and people kept getting beaten," Silavwe said, adding that at the time young people like him did feel scared, but he understands now there is no truth to the rumours.
Asha Steven Mwakilasa, a 50-year-old tailor and fashion designer in Tunduma, which is in Momba district, agrees: "I came to realise it was not true."
This does not stop her anxiety - especially if her husband or sons are out, but she says she is grateful that the police are now mounting patrols.

Momba district commissioner Elias Daniel Mwandobo told the BBC local investigations suggested there was deliberate criminal intent behind some of the incidents: "Individuals conspired to commit a crime and incite public panic for their own benefits."

Another video recorded in Tanzania's main city of Dar es Salaam shows a crowd marching a man down a dusty market street, pushing, grabbing and striking him and insisting he returns the genitalia, as the man pleads his innocence.
The BBC Disinformation Unit verified similar videos of attacks in Mozambique and Kenya.

Dozens of these recordings of mob violence, alleged first-person accounts, warnings about alleged incidents, commentary and videos framed as reports of events in particular areas are circulating across TikTok and Facebook.
Many of those analysed by the BBC, including some showing mob violence, remain online.
"We are reviewing the content shared with us and will take action on those that are found to violate our policies," a Meta spokesperson told the BBC.
TikTok has yet to respond to a BBC request for comment.
With some social media creators, who warn viewers to be vigilant, it is often unclear whether they believe the claims or are primarily seeking engagement.
Alongside these posts, some users promote so-called charms said to protect against genital theft, while comedians have parodied the claims through comedy skits.
Smartphones and social media make rumours spread faster, reach larger audiences and become more difficult to control once they begin circulating, says author Julien Bonhomme.
His book, The Sex Thieves: The Anthropology of a Rumor, examines how hearsay about "sex thieves" spread and why people believe them.
People are not simply hearing claims that someone has lost his genitals - they are seeing distressed men say it has happened to them, or watching crowds respond to accusations, he says.

Videos shared on social media can make unverified claims appear more believable, he says, because of their immediacy, describing this as "one of the most significant differences" between the current digital environment and earlier outbreaks.
The worst-hit country has been Mozambique, where the police said in May that 55 people had been killed in six weeks, including a police officer, health workers and civil servants.

Mozambique's President Daniel Chapo publicly condemned widespread rumours and deaths, saying the claims were false and the government had found no medical evidence to suggest anyone had lost a part of their body.

The two healthcare workers were attacked at their home and workplace in April in Cabo Delgado province - a region that borders Tanzania which has been affected by an Islamist insurgency for nearly a decade.
The health facilities in the areas of the attacks had to close for weeks while the authorities launched public awareness campaigns to counter the claims.
As part of the health campaign, the government said some of the fears could be linked to Koro syndrome, a mental illness otherwise known as missing or genital retraction hysteria.
The most recent incidents of violence have occurred in Kenya, where five people were killed by mobs in the coastal counties of Kwale and Mombasa.

After the first incidents were reported in July, Mombasa County Commissioner Mohamed Noor blamed some content creators for spreading the claims to boost engagement "simply to attract views and attention".
"Such misinformation can easily lead to loss of life," Noor told the BBC.

He said police had since contained the violence and made several arrests, including a father and son who were sentenced to a year in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a woman they accused of causing men's genitals to disappear.
Similar claims also fuelled mob attacks in Malawi, leaving eight people dead.
Back in Tunduma, in neighbouring Tanzania, even as mechanic Mgala recovers from the physical impact of the assault, the emotional pain is still raw.
"It still hurts me deeply when I think back to the senseless manner my friend died because I still don't know what was going on," he said.
"To suddenly find yourself being pelted with stones for no reason, and then end up losing your life?"

articles.title: Why Nepal floods should worry India
articles.summary: The disaster comes as a warning as climate change raises shared Himalayan risks.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Image
The death toll in Nepal from devastating floods on the border with Tibet has crossed 1,000
Nepal's devastating floods have exposed a risk that does not stop at its borders.

India and Nepal share the rivers that rise in the Himalayas, but the relationship between a flood in Nepal and a disaster in India is more complicated than a simple story of water flowing downstream, say experts.
Some floods can race out of the mountains carrying enormous quantities of mud, rock and debris. Others may lose much of their force as they reach the plains, leaving behind a more conventional flood.
And whether that water becomes a disaster in India depends not only on how much rain has fallen in Nepal, but also on rainfall, river levels, embankments, drainage and development on the Indian side.
Nepal's floods are a warning for India - not simply because water flows south across the border, but because the two countries share a vast and increasingly volatile Himalayan river system.
How many Nepal rivers flow into India?

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges

blocks.text: Image source, Universal Images Group via Getty Images
Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges
Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges.
Three major systems dominate: the Kosi in the east, the Gandaki (Gandak in India) in the centre and the Karnali (Ghaghara in India) in the west, with the Mahakali (Sharda) along the western border.

A dozen smaller rivers rising in the Siwaliks and Chure - including the Bagmati, Kamala, Rapti and Babai - are less famous but can produce faster, more unpredictable floods because their catchments are small and steep.

Seven to nine major rivers flow from Nepal into the Indian plains, and they are responsible for flooding in India, according to Manish Shrestha, a hydrologist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD).
India's Central Water Commission identifies the Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati and Ghaghara as some of the main transboundary rivers.
Which Indian states are most exposed?

blocks.caption: Image caption, Bihar is India's worst flood-prone state

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Bihar is India's worst flood-prone state
Bihar is by far the most exposed Indian state, with roughly three-quarters of north Bihar officially classified as flood-prone.
Almost all the major rivers that flood the state originate in Nepal, with the Kosi - the "sorrow of Bihar" - the most notorious, followed by the Gandak, Bagmati and Kamala.
But the risk extends beyond Bihar.
Eastern Uttar Pradesh is vulnerable to the Ghaghara, Rapti and Gandak rivers. Districts like Gorakhpur, Bahraich, Lakhimpur Kheri and Shravasti are regularly affected.
Uttarakhand state shares the Mahakali-Sharda rivers. North Bengal receives the Mechi and Mahananda.
"Bihar dominates in scale. Uttar Pradesh is second and often under-reported," says Pradeep Man Dangol, hydrologist at ICIMOD.
Bihar bears the greatest burden, but Uttar Pradesh is a significant and often overlooked part of the risk.
When Nepal floods, what determines India's fate?

blocks.caption: Image caption, A view of a flood-affected district in India's Bihar in 2008

blocks.text: A view of a flood-affected district in India's Bihar in 2008
Think of it as a three-part chain, say hydrologists.
First, the rain: where it falls and how heavily.
Flood peaks reaching India are often generated not in the high Himalayas but lower down, in the Siwaliks, Chure and Terai, where intense monsoon rain can fall on steep, small catchments.
Second, the river.
Nepal's rivers cross a sharp break in slope at the mountain front, drop their sediment, and spread across the plains as braided, shifting channels.
Third, when the water meets India.

How bad the flooding becomes depends on what the water encounters - the volume of rain on the Indian side, how full the Ganges is, embankments and barrages, and blocked drainage from roads, railways and settlements on the floodplain.
So the peak flow at the border is largely determined by rainfall in Nepal. The severity of flooding depends at least as much on conditions in India.
The 2008 Kosi disaster shows why: the river was carrying far less water than the embankment was designed to handle. The catastrophe was caused by the embankment failing, not by an exceptional flood.
So how much depends on Nepal v India?

"For the peak flow arriving at the border, largely Nepal's rainfall; for the severity of flooding once it arrives, at least as much on Indian conditions," says Saswata Sanyal, ICIMOD's intervention manager for disaster risk reduction.
How Nepal's rain becomes India's flood risk
The 2008 Kosi disaster is a powerful illustration.
Nearly 400 people died in Bihar after the Kosi breached an embankment in Nepal. But, remarkably, it was not an extraordinary high-flow event on the river.

According to Rajiv Sinha, a professor of earth sciences at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur, the flow was only about a tenth of the river's carrying capacity. The catastrophe was caused by a breach in an embankment built decades earlier and inadequately maintained.

"The embankments constructed in the 1950s and 1960s had not been properly maintained. They had become eroded and eventually developed a weak point. The river breached its embankment through these vulnerable points and entered parts of India that had not seen flooding for perhaps 100 years," says Sinha.
The failure, in other words, was "structural, not hydrological", adds Sanyal.
How much warning can India get from Nepal?
For ordinary monsoon floods, India may have "roughly 12 hours to two days of warning", according to Sanyal, depending on how quickly the water travels downstream.
Water can take about a day to reach the Bihar plains from the Nepal mountain front along the Kosi and Gandak, and somewhat longer along the Ghaghara.
Flash floods from the Chure rivers can arrive within hours.
A landslide-dam burst or debris flow can be even faster - in the current floods, the peak surge from Rasuwa reached Triveni, near the Indian border, in about seven-and-a-half hours.

India and Nepal do share real-time rainfall and river-level data from a network of stations. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology feeds rainfall and river levels to India's Central Water Commission, which uses them for flood forecasts.
But important gaps remain, says Sanyal.

They include too few real-time monitoring stations in the fastest-flowing Chure catchments. There's also no single shared forecasting model between the two countries; and limited routine sharing on embankment conditions, river-channel changes and sediment.
And then there's, crucially, the last mile.
A warning reaching a district office is not the same as reaching a family in danger.

For these transboundary rivers, Sinha says, "cooperation on information sharing and early-warning systems is extremely important. We need rapid continuous monitoring of glacial lakes, their outflows and how they are changing over time".
What is the biggest misconception around Nepal and floods in India?

blocks.caption: Image caption, The confluence of Dhauliganga and Rishiganga rivers in India's Chamoli district

blocks.text: The confluence of Dhauliganga and Rishiganga rivers in India's Chamoli district
A common misconception is that Nepal "releases" water into India, say scientists.
Nepal has almost no large reservoirs capable of doing this: its main storage dam, Kulekhani, holds less than a tenth of a cubic kilometre, "so there's nothing to release", says Sanyal.
The Kosi and Gandak barrages are operated by India. When floodwater reaches the border, it is overwhelmingly because rain has fallen upstream - not because Nepal has opened a gate.

But there is an important truth behind the claim: much of the water that floods north Bihar and eastern UP has fallen as rain in Nepal, so Nepal's rainfall largely determines the timing and size of flood peaks reaching India.
Nepal supplies around 40% of the average annual flow of the Ganges - and a much larger share in the dry season - making its hydrology critical to India.
"What is too simplistic is treating that as a story of cause and blame. Rain is not a decision," says Sanyal.
Whether a given flow becomes a disaster depends on conditions in India as much as in Nepal the Ganges' level, Indian rainfall, embankment integrity, drainage and sediment.

"And the effects run both ways: embankments and barrages built for India's protection have raised water levels and caused backwater flooding in Nepal's Terai, which is Nepal's long-standing concern,' says Sanyal.
Nepal and India share one river system, with one country upstream and the other downstream.
The answer is therefore not blame, but better shared data, forecasting and river management.
So what should worry India the most?

blocks.caption: Image caption, A massive cloudburst triggered heavy rains and flash floods in Dharali, India, in 2025

blocks.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images
A massive cloudburst triggered heavy rains and flash floods in Dharali, India, in 2025
"India should be worried. but not necessarily because of the Kosi river in Nepal," says Rajiv Sinha.
In other words, experts say, the real warning is about what is happening in the Himalayas - and what happens when water, rock, ice and enormous quantities of sediment suddenly combine.

Sinha says the latest Nepal disaster resembles a series of catastrophic events that India has experienced in recent years, including the 2021 Chamoli disaster and the 2025 Dharali disaster in Uttarakhand. The Nepal event, he says, was "perhaps five to 10 times larger".
"The fundamental point is that these are not normal hydrological floods," Sinha says.

A conventional flood is largely water. But when water from intense rain, melting ice or a sudden discharge mixes with huge quantities of sediment, the result can become a thick, high-energy slurry capable of destroying almost everything in its path.

That was the lesson of the Chamoli disaster in 2021, when a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people and damaged hydropower infrastructure.
It was also evident at Dharali in Uttarakhand in 2025, after heavy rains triggered a flash flood and the flow of debris buried parts of a village under metres of material.
And then there's climate change.

Extreme rainfall is intensifying: the region is warming faster than the global average, a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, and the monsoon is delivering more rain in fewer, heavier bursts, say experts.

High-mountain hazards are also growing. As permafrost degrades, glacial lake outbursts and rock-ice avalanches are expected to increase, producing faster, debris-laden floods that are harder to forecast.
And more extreme events mean more landslides and sediment in rivers, raising riverbeds and reducing channel capacity on both sides of the border.
They are manifestations of the same broad Himalayan hazard system. And India's exposure is considerable.

articles.title: Rare train of Pacific cyclones fueled by historic El Niño
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — Two powerful hurricanes and a strengthening tropical storm on Wednesday were churning through the Pacific Ocean where waters were being warmed by a historically strong El Niño…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON — Two powerful hurricanes and a strengthening tropical storm on Wednesday were churning through the Pacific Ocean where waters were being warmed by a historically strong El Niño climate episode.

Furthest west is Hurricane Lowell, followed by Hurricane Karina. Both of the Category 4 storms are anticipated to pass well to the south and to the northeast of Hawaii, respectively, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).
However, uncertainty remains over their tracks, with the possibility Lowell could pass close to the archipelago’s westernmost islands.
Hawaii is still recovering from the impacts of Hurricane Lala, which brushed past the southern part of the Big Island last month, bringing destructive winds and severe flash floods.
Lowell and Karina are trailed to the east by Tropical Storm Marie, currently a few hundred miles south of Baja California and “expected to become a hurricane later today,” the NHC said.

“El Niño warming sets the stage for these storms, which are fueled in large part by warm waters — when the tropical Pacific is warmer than normal we see an increase in strong storms,” Julia Cole, a climate scientist at the University of Michigan, told AFP.
A train of three cyclones “is definitely rare to see,” she added.
A similar train of four cyclones happened in 2015, another intense El Niño year, when Typhoon Kilo, Hurricane Ignacio, Hurricane Jimena and Tropical Depression 14E crossed the Pacific at once.
“The climate system has significantly warmed over the last 20 years or so,” said Benjamin Kirtman, an atmospheric scientist at the University of Miami.
Warm waters provide fuel for storms, and El Niño’s effect on the atmosphere leaves little vertical wind shear over the Pacific, creating favorable conditions for hurricanes to intensify.
“There’s no other way to put it — it is juicy out there right now,” he told AFP.

What’s more, the sea surface temperature anomaly — how much warmer the ocean is compared to average — is already near record high, right in the middle of the Pacific hurricane season, Kirtman explained.
Impacts felt worldwide

This year’s El Niño has a 69 percent chance of becoming the strongest on record, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and is already unleashing extreme weather across the globe even though it is not expected to peak until October-December.

Peru, the world’s largest catcher of anchovy, is facing a devastating blow from warming seas that have gutted production, according to industry officials. In Sudan, El Niño is blamed for delaying crucial rains that have led water levels in the Nile to drop precipitously.
El Niño is the warming phase of a natural cycle in the tropical Pacific known as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), and comes along every two to seven years.
It sets in when east-to-west trade winds ease, allowing warm water which normally piles up in the western Pacific Ocean to slide back east and rise to the surface.

When those warmer-than-average surface temperatures last for a few months, they cause more storms and clouds over the region, which in turn cause ripple effects through the entire global atmosphere: hotter and drier conditions in some places, cooler and wetter in others.

Climate change increases El Niño’s impacts. A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so El Niño-linked rains can turn more extreme. It also dries out soils, deepening drought where El Niño brings drought. /dl

articles.title: Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice in South Africa
articles.summary: At least 69 people were shot dead in 1960 but no-one has been prosecuted and victims want restitution.

blocks.text: Abraham Mofokeng was 20 when he joined a peaceful protest in Sharpeville
ByPumza Fihlani
Reporting fromSharpeville

Abraham Mofokeng still carries the wounds of the bloody suppression of a protest in South Africa 66 years ago. In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators.
A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg.
"We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government.
"All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told."

The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted.
Mofokeng is now part of a legal case set to be announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.
At least 69 protesters were shot dead by police on that day in 1960, becoming a pivotal event in the history of the anti-apartheid movement.
Though Sharpeville may be a place name rich in historical resonance, it scarcely looks like a site that symbolises the struggle: the township is slowly crumbling.

The once tarred roads of this area south of Johannesburg are returning to dirt. Many of the houses are still the small, brown-faced brick homes built under the apartheid-era government. The earth is dry and barren - heaps of rubbish are piling up throughout the neighbourhood.
While the legalised system of racism was buried in 1994 when the country held its first democratic election and elected Nelson Mandela as president, its scars remain.
There have been attempts at redress - not least through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) - set up by Mandela's government to investigate crimes committed during the apartheid era.
But the Sharpeville survivors feel they have not seen justice.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters started fleeing as the police opened fire

blocks.text: Image source, Universal History Archive/UIG via Getty images
Protesters started fleeing as the police opened fire
Sharpeville's local memorial park, the Human Rights Precinct, tells the story of how the streets of township became the scene of a bloodbath.
Inside the park stand 69 white pillars, one for each life lost.
The victims were killed while demonstrating against the racist pass laws.
At the time, black people were forced to carry a document known as a passbook, known as "dompas" in Afrikaans, which restricted their freedom to move around the country.
A person could be beaten and jailed if found without it - or if found in a "whites-only" area without permission.
Many heeded the call from the leaders of the Pan Africanist Congress in March 1960 to march in protest against the dompas, including then-20-year-old Mofokeng.

"The life we were living under apartheid was a life of oppression. We could not move around freely. We ended up planning to march to the police station against these passbooks that were being used to oppress us," he says.
Thousands turned up to what they thought would be a peaceful protest.

"[The police] had rifles, machetes, even shields. We explained to the police that we didn't want the passes anymore and we were prepared to go to prison. There was a commotion, then all hell broke loose when the police started shooting."
Mofokeng was among the more than 200 people injured and recent estimates by South African researchers have revised upwards the number who died to as many as 91.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Larazus Magotsi witnessed police shooting at some who were trying to get up from the ground

blocks.text: Larazus Magotsi witnessed police shooting at some who were trying to get up from the ground

Another survivor, Larazus Magotsi - now 90 - walks along the long row of graves in the cemetery where most of those who died are buried. Among them is a headstone marking where a 12-year-old was laid to rest.
Magotsi's eyes are filled with tears as he struggles to compose himself.
"We heard gunshots and ran and hid inside a store, peeping to see what was happening outside," he says.
"People were lying on the ground. When we looked out again, we saw that some were trying to get up, but the police were just shooting at them.
"Others were using machetes to strike the heads of people who were still moving."
It is thought that more than 1,300 bullets were shot into the crowd. Archive photos show policemen walking among the corpses, lying where they fell, in the immediate aftermath of the massacre.
The only legal case that followed the killings was a failed attempt to charge the protesters with affray.
Now, survivors and relatives of those who were killed are hoping to overturn the law they say prevents them from getting justice.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The photographer Ian Berry later told the BBC that it seemed the man in the centre of this picture was holding his jacket up "as though to protect himself from the bullets"

blocks.text: The photographer Ian Berry later told the BBC that it seemed the man in the centre of this picture was holding his jacket up "as though to protect himself from the bullets"

The 1961 Indemnity Act was passed by the apartheid government in the wake of the massacre and protected the police and government from having criminal charges or even civil claims brought against them in relation to what happened at Sharpeville.
Despite more than 30 years of democratic rule, that law remains on the statute books.

But now South African non-governmental organisation Lawyers for Human Rights, together with UK-based law firm Leigh Day, has filed a case at the High Court arguing that the law is unconstitutional under the new constitution that came into effect in 1994.

"Apart from the individual damages, what the community's looking for is basically reparations to enable their healing. They feel as though Sharpeville is a forgotten community," says Charne Tracey, one of the lawyers on the case.

Part of their court application includes getting a class action certified - if approved this would mean that for the first time dozens of victims and relatives of those killed could collectively sue the state. It could also possibly lead to criminal charges being brought against the alleged perpetrators, if any are still alive.

"Nothing has been done that assists with their healing and improvement of their quality of life, or remedy the long-term effects of what they've suffered," Tracey says, adding that 70 people could be involved in the class action.
Constitutional law expert Prof Frans Viljoen believes having the old law repealed is important because it would help to "clean up" the legislation and "close a chapter on the past".
"Although South Africa has a very transformative constitution… The principle of continuity of statehood still applies, which is why the case can be brought against the current state," says Viljoen.
"So if there were laws in our statute book in 1994, the constitution explicitly says they remain in force until parliament repeals them, abolishes them or changes them," he adds.
But he backs attempts to declare the Indemnity Act unconstitutional "to cleanse us of that past".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Many of those who died in the massacre are buried in a long row in a cemetery in Sharpeville

blocks.text: Many of those who died in the massacre are buried in a long row in a cemetery in Sharpeville

The TRC, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was generally praised for bringing together victims and perpetrators who were granted amnesty as long as they, among other conditions, fully disclosed what they had done.

But the greatest criticism of the process was that it did not bring about justice for some as people were not jailed for their acts and no police officers applied for amnesty for the Sharpeville shootings.
The government told the BBC it had supported apartheid victims over the years, and would continue to do so, but did not oppose survivors and families pursuing legal remedies.

When it comes to reparations the justice department said 560 TRC-recognised victims of apartheid-era violence had received individual grants amounting to some $31m (£23m) and though not all Sharpeville survivors and relatives had been identified it encouraged them to come forward.
For many in the community of Sharpeville, there is hope that restitution will help heal decades of lingering trauma.
"Apartheid is dead and buried. A win would bring complete healing, not just for us, but for future generations as well," says Mofokeng.
"Considering how people died, many have not completely healed."

articles.title: China’s falling emissions amid Iran war spark hope of decarbonisation watershed
articles.summary:
Oil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price falls

China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the…

blocks.text: China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows.

The report reveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy.

China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed for Carbon Brief by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months after the first US airstrikes in late February.

How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand.

blocks.caption: Wind turbines on the Yellow Sea coast of Yancheng, China. Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPA

blocks.text: The country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport. While large numbers of petrol and diesel vehicles stayed off the roads, there was a surge in journeys by electric cars, buses, trains and trucks.

This electrifying trend had begun long before the strait of Hormuz crisis. China is by far the world’s biggest manufacturer, user and exporter of batteries, e-vehicles, wind turbines and solar panels. The disruption of oil supplies from the Gulf has strengthened the economic and strategic imperative of reducing petro-dependence.
In the first half of 2026, China’s shift towards electric vehicles displaced the equivalent of the UK’s entire oil consumption over a six-month period.
after newsletter promotion

Analysts predict much of this demand will not return even if global oil prices fall. “In a qualitative sense, there’s no question that the transport sector decarbonisation has been accelerated,” said Lauri Myllyvirta, the lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “It’s a validation of the energy security strategy that China has in place … It’s very clear that electrification is the winning strategy to insure against these kinds of shocks.”
Myllyvirta noted this was the first time China’s overall emissions had fallen due to a reduction in oil use rather than in coal consumption.

In fact, coal generation rose during the quarter due to shifting economic incentives and delays in adapting the country’s grid, which caused considerable wastage of wind and solar power. Despite this, observers believe the longer-term trend in China is away from fossil fuels.

Dr Muyi Yang, a senior analyst at Ember, which will next week publish a separate overview of China’s energy trends, said a fossil fuel peak was coming into view at the provincial and sectoral level. “The Iran crisis reinforces the case. The way China has been able to absorb its impact strengthens the confidence to go deeper and further.

“The risk of oil-import dependence increasingly comes from the geopolitical domain. This is a risk no country can effectively manage. So the more effective strategy is to reduce that exposure altogether. And China’s experience is demonstrating that this works.”

articles.title: New youth trend: ‘Aura farming’ gets competitive
articles.summary: LIMA, Peru — Dozens of young people gathered recently on a beach in Peru’s capital to dance, pose and show off their most creative moves—all in pursuit of one thing: aura. They were taking part in a…

blocks.text: LIMA, Peru — Dozens of young people gathered recently on a beach in Peru’s capital to dance, pose and show off their most creative moves—all in pursuit of one thing: aura.
They were taking part in a so-called aura battle, a real-world spin on the internet trend known as “aura farming” that is sweeping across Latin America.

Dressed up as characters from comic books or animated films, competitors engaged in dance battles of sorts, vying for the crowd’s applause. Those with the loudest cheers and the most creative moves advanced to the next round.

One competitor dressed up as Spider-Man performed forward rolls and push-ups, as techno music played in the background. Another hopped on one leg while kicking the other forward, in a move that looked straight from a video game.
Shed off all ‘shame’

“Aura farming is about letting your essence flow in a place where people are watching you, but where there is no shame,” said Liam González, a 20-year-old film student who attended dressed up as the movie character Shrek.
Gonzalo Cornelio, 19, came dressed as former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, wearing a grey tracksuit like the one worn by the deposed leader the night he was captured by the US military.
Aura farming competitions first emerged in Brazil and spread through social media. Now, teenagers and adults are holding aura battles across Latin America.
“It’s not about being popular,” said María Paula Martínez, a professor in the arts faculty at Colombia’s Los Andes University. “It’s about showing off good vibes, and having others recognize that.”

Like video game characters who farm for points, people who go aura farming are trying to earn a reward. In this case, it’s about generating good vibes, and thus improving their “aura,” a term that, according to some spiritual traditions, refers to an energy field that surrounds people.

Fernando Lícito, a Peruvian content creator, said that in aura battles participants do not touch each other or trade insults. “They are simply farming their aura,” said Lícito, 25. “And whoever gets the crowd to make more noise wins.”
From digital to physical
Lícito said he saw a video in June of an aura farming contest in Brazil, and decided to bring the idea to Peru. So far, he has organized three aura battles there.
During the contests, some participants imitate soccer star Cristiano Ronaldo’s goal celebration, extending their arms downward and making a sound that sounds like “siuu.”

Aura battles have spread to cities across Latin America, including Mexico City, Quito and Buenos Aires, where dozens of people staged a battle in front of the Obelisk, one of the most iconic monuments in the Argentine capital.
The contests have also reached Spain, with events taking place in Madrid, Burgos and Zaragoza.
Martínez, the Colombian arts professor, said that the concept of aura farming has moved beyond the digital world into physical spaces, enabling teenagers to socialize.
Not everyone amused
But some aura battles have met some resistance.
In Lima’s Miraflores district, officials recently canceled an aura farming event, saying organizers had not obtained the permits required to hold it in a public space.

In July, the mayor of Cuiaba, a city in southwestern Brazil, denied permits for an aura tournament, arguing it was not in the public’s interest. The event was transferred to a university campus. And in Costa Rica, the ministry of education banned aura battles in public schools arguing they could create conflicts between students or disrupt learning.
In Mexico, by contrast, the education minister embraced the trend, posting a video in which he smiles and says he is “farming good education” as the country prepares for the new school year.

González, the aura farmer who dresses up as Shrek, said that this hobby gives him a way to have fun and express himself, even if his grandmother doesn’t get what he’s doing and thinks it’s silly. “We were born in a different era,” he said. /das

articles.title: Journalists’ code of ethics getting an AI-era reboot
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Walk into a corner of a newsroom somewhere and you can often find it affixed to a bulletin board, perhaps peeking out from behind the coffee pot: the Society of Professional Journalists’…

blocks.text: NEW YORK — Walk into a corner of a newsroom somewhere and you can often find it affixed to a bulletin board, perhaps peeking out from behind the coffee pot: the Society of Professional Journalists’ (SPJ) Code of Ethics. It’s less than a thousand words, fitting neatly on a poster.
But those words—organized around four key journalistic principles—are important enough, asserts Dan Axelrod, that they just might save our democracy.
